Because they do not attain the happiness connected with this birth that they had experienced before. Just as people whose senses are impaired by bile and other disorders lose their desire for particular foods and drinks, so too they are tormented when desire ceases: the sole cause is the interruption of a delight they had previously experienced. Thus it is unreasonable to deny the happiness each person directly experiences. We see that this account has been offered simply to placate people attached to pleasure. Therefore pleasure is something other than the mere removal of suffering, and this is the primary meaning of the word “bliss.” When scripture is the means of knowledge, its words should be understood according to their ordinary meaning. Acting toward that bliss is not action rooted in attachment. Desire alone is not attachment: attachment is the superimposition, prompted by ignorance, of a quality that is not really there. A mind made clear by seeing reality has appreciation and desire for what is real; these do not belong to the class of attachment, just as the disquiet born of seeing the insubstantiality of worldly existence does not belong to the class of hatred. Otherwise, action toward the reality that transcends all suffering would be driven by hatred of it, and worldly bondage would continue.

Moreover, even those attached to the excellence of visible pleasures are instructed to conquer the senses as a means to that excellence, by abandoning desire and the like; the same will apply here. How, then, could attachment to desired objects be forbidden while attachment to other objects is not? If all attachment were forbidden, no activity would be seen. In the same way, one turns away even from a pleasure that has come within reach because one is attached to a higher pleasure. As it is said, “A life governed by desire is not commendable, but neither is desirelessness found here.” Someone may object: if bliss is something experienced in Brahman, there is a duality between the experiencer and what is experienced. The relation of agent and object requires an action and an instrument, so the statement “Brahman is bliss” could not hold. If bliss is predicated of Brahman as a quality, the claim that Brahman is nondual also fails. If bliss is not experienced, then, though it may exist, it is as good as nonexistent and there is no point in mentioning it. It is mentioned because it is a human goal; how can something unexperienced be a goal?

The answer is that this should be understood in the same way as the result of cognition and as the knowing subject. Thinkers on every side hold and experience that the result of a means of knowledge is either different from the cognition or not different from it. Yet it is not unexperienced: if it were, nothing could ever be experienced, since the experienced status of things depends on it. Nor is it experienced as an object, because there is no further result of that experience, and an endless regress would follow. Therefore it is experienced, because it is self-illuminating; and it is not experienced as an object, because it does not occupy the role of an object. In the same way, if the knowing Self were not experienced, there would be no cognition at all. One could not say, “I have known this”; the Self could not be connected with the result of knowing or with its object. If the Self were not connected with them, what difference would there be between what is known by oneself and what is known by another? Yet the Self is not experienced as an object, for if it occupied that role it would be separate from the knowing subject and would not be the Self. Its knowability, therefore, consists precisely in its being self-illuminating.

Likewise, bliss, whose nature is the self-illumination of Brahman, is not experienced as an object, because it does not occupy the role of an object; nor is it unexperienced, because it is self-illuminating. The statement “By what should one see what?” is also a denial concerning objects. It is said specifically because all relations to objects have come to rest, as the scripture declares, “When everything has become nothing but the Self.”

Others hold that qualities are of two kinds: positive and negative. Negative qualities do not obstruct nonduality, as in the statements “one,” “immortal,” and “unborn.” The cessation of distinctions that arise and pass away is not itself some entity that would introduce duality. Bliss, however, if positive, must be either a quality or the bearer of a quality. If it is a quality, consciousness would be the bearer; if consciousness is the bearer, bliss would be its quality. One thing cannot have two distinct natures, because they would conflict. Thus, if “consciousness” and “bliss” in the statement “Brahman is consciousness and bliss” are both positive, their relation as quality and bearer would destroy nonduality. One might reply that a quality is not different from its bearer, since, if it were different, the relation between quality and bearer could not hold any more than a cow could be related as a quality of a horse. That is not sound either: if the two are identical, the relation still cannot hold, because the quality would then be no different from the bearer. A quality must therefore be different in some respect. But then the scriptural statement that there is absolutely no difference, “One alone, without a second,” could not apply. The same difficulty applies to anyone who accepts two distinct natures in a single thing.

Accordingly, they say, bliss is only a limiting condition of consciousness: the word “bliss” denotes the absence of suffering in consciousness, just as terms such as “not gross,” “not minute,” and “not short” denote the absence of those limiting conditions. Consciousness and bliss cannot simply be identical, because then the two words would be redundant. How could oneness be conveyed by two words that are not synonyms? Thus, they conclude, “bliss” means only the cessation of suffering.

The reply is that there is no fault in two words conveying one particular thing by expressing consciousness qualified by the distinctive character of bliss, just as two words express the moon’s light. For example, “the Sun is brilliant light”: “brilliant” and “light” are not synonyms, yet together they convey a single distinct light. Indeed, no...

The distinction may be between the Sun and some other light, or between the Sun’s nature as light and its excellence; it is not a distinction between two separate lights. Rather, the two words convey a particular kind of light. Similarly, the two words in “Brahman is consciousness and bliss” convey Brahman either as bliss distinct from consciousness or as consciousness distinct from bliss. Some hold that this bliss is supreme because it is free from suffering that depends on means and is subject to destruction. But, where scripture is the means of knowledge, that interpretation should not be accepted against the words themselves. If supreme bliss is impossible by nature, it is not reasonable to call the absence of opposing suffering a figurative form of it. It is therefore right to say that Brahman is the self-illumination that is the highest nature of the Self. Ordinary pleasure is a fraction of this, since it is limited. It is difficult to make the same account fit the mere cessation of suffering.

There is another reason for saying that the Self is bliss by nature: it is the object of supreme love. Scripture states that it is “dearer than a son.” This is also evident in experience. Everyone wishes, even a worm, “May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist.” That wish is fulfilled in what is dear. Love belongs to what is blissful by nature; it does not belong to what is painful, nor to something that is neither painful nor pleasurable, since toward the former there is hatred and toward the latter indifference.

Others say that one experiences happiness in the Self during deep sleep, recalling, “I slept happily.” Such a recollection would not be possible without experience, and the state of deep sleep is accepted. Nor would one recall it as happiness if the experience had been of some other kind. There is nothing else there to be experienced apart from the Self. Scripture likewise says that one reaches Brahman every day. Others respond that the recollection is equally explained by the cessation of suffering, so it does not establish beyond doubt that one was happy. The reply is that, if another meaning is established, the word “happiness” may be taken as signifying the cause that removes suffering; otherwise its primary meaning is the reasonable one. They then say that, since both usages occur and both are plausible, the meaning cannot be established from usage alone. Enough of this extended discussion.

Some now argue for duality on the grounds that experiences are arranged in distinct ways, that a distinction between the liberated person and the one in worldly existence is intelligible, that seeing has a purpose, that there is a contradiction in the Self acting upon itself, that the seer is inferred from what is seen, and that what is seen is experienced as divided into sound and other objects, and into pleasure, pain, and delusion. They therefore take the scriptural statement of oneness to be figurative, based on the absence of divisions of class, place, and time. They also take “the Self alone is all this” figuratively, on the ground that everything belongs to it. The author answers: “One.” The scriptural statement “Indra, through his powers of illusion, appears in many forms” plainly shows that the perception of many forms depends on illusion. How, then, can the statement of oneness be called figurative? Scripture plainly denies multiplicity: “Here there is no multiplicity at all.” It censures the perception of multiplicity: “He goes from death to death.” It also says that the vision of difference is like seeing difference in a confused state: the word “as if” in “the one who sees here as if there were multiplicity” cannot be used to make oneness figurative. Even if one grants that oneness is figurative, that does not remove the actual multiplicity they claim. If they say that the denial of multiplicity is figurative too, there is no purpose for saying so. Figurative usage is justified when there is a reason for it and some purpose; we see no purpose in making the removal of multiplicity figurative. Indeed, this reverses the point. One might make the denial of multiplicity figurative for prosperity or for the highest good, but that denial removes distinctions such as means and ends and manifests the identity of the Self everywhere, and thus would run counter to both. It is agreed that the highest good is the complete cessation of worldly entanglement. Further, the emphatic “one alone, without a second,” with both the force of “alone” and “without a second,” repeats the same meaning, and so the scripture is understood to deny every kind of difference. Repetition intensifies meaning, as when someone says, “How beautiful, how beautiful!” It does not weaken it. The idea that the statement is figurative is therefore remote.

As for the argument from the arrangement of experience, an imagined difference is enough to explain it. Even when there is just one Self—whether all-pervading, as large as the body, or atomic—experiences are arranged according to imagined differences: “My foot hurts,” “My head hurts.” Neither the foot nor the head is actually connected with the pain, since neither is conscious. Even for someone who holds that the Self is the size of the body, its parts are not themselves the experiencers of pain, for then the Self itself would be left without experience. Someone may object that, if there is only one Self, the experience of one body should be recalled through another body. But that is a different matter: an arrangement of experiences exists in any case. Even in that account, one bodily region does not recall the pain of another region, just as one living being does not recall the pain of another; the cases are alike. Moreover, distinctions in the colors and shapes of pleasure and other experiences are observed in a jewel, a sword, and a mirror even without a real division in the conscious subject. In this way a distinction between the liberated and the worldly person is also intelligible: the one Self, connected in one place with pleasure, pain, and the like, appears bound there, and elsewhere appears liberated...

In the same way, the one Self appears divided by a limiting condition: as a face looks dirty on a soiled mirror, yet looks clean in a clean mirror, and, when seen without the mirror, is understood not to be touched by the mirror’s impurity. One may object that imagination is a quality of the knower’s cognition and cannot determine an object. Objects do not change as the knower’s cognition changes; nor can a result follow from something merely figurative. A boy who is only figuratively called fire does not burn. The example, however, was given to show how experience can be arranged. The reply is that this too is a case of error, and there is no reason to rule out error here. Even an imagined snakebite can cause death, and a reflected sun can produce the effects of light.

The argument that the seer must be inferred from what is seen, and that the observed distinctions in pleasure and other experiences establish multiplicity, is also unsound. It has already been explained that what is seen cannot be established if the seer is not luminous. Nor is a distinction in what is seen actually established, as will be shown: the means of knowledge does not delimit such a distinction. The power of seeing has a purpose through its own use by the Self; there is no contradiction in its operating in the Self, as has been explained by the examples of a lamp and of the result of cognition.

Furthermore, the relation between seer and seen is intelligible only if there is oneness: the conscious Self itself appears, or transforms, in different ways. If there were multiplicity, the two would have entirely distinct natures, unmixed with one another and unrelated; what kind of relation between seer and seen could there be? Consciousness cannot coherently cognize something that is wholly unrelated to it. If someone says that there is a relation because consciousness enters the mind, that is not so: consciousness is pure, does not transform, and does not pass into another thing. If the mind, which is seen, appears changed by the proximity of consciousness and by its reflection, what is meant by saying that it has a reflection of consciousness? It means that something which is not consciousness appears as consciousness. In that case, what is seen is not seen as it truly is. It is difficult to maintain that something separate from the seer exists in ultimate reality while never being seen in ultimate reality.

Another view is that the seen is established simply by being seen, not through a relation; seeing, it is said, is directed outward and has the form “this.” The reply is: certainly it has an outward-directed form. But it is the one Self itself appearing in different ways, or transforming, like a person’s own face seeming divided from the person on the surface of a mirror. It is difficult to understand how something divided from consciousness and wholly unrelated to it could be cognized by consciousness. Scripture likewise teaches that the seen is not other than the seer: “When the Self is known, all this is known.” Thus “one” was rightly said.

Those who hold that the Self is momentary cognition say that attaining Brahman is simply the cessation of cognition, brought about by ending the latent afflictions and impressions. Scripture says, “After death there is no recognition.” Others say that it is the arising of purified knowledge, freed from every latent impression and from the distortions that take the form of objects. If reality were beginningless and endless, they argue, there would be nothing to remove or to attain; the scriptures and the actions undertaken for their sake would be pointless. If the nature of reality were knowledge, there would be nothing to remove or attain, because ignorance would be absent and knowledge already present. If its nature were ignorance, and ignorance were eternal, its former nature could not be abandoned and another nature could not arise. The same applies if one says that reality has both natures: knowledge would already be attained, and ignorance could not be eliminated. The author answers them with the words “immortal” and “unborn.”

The scriptures and the practices undertaken for liberation are not pointless, because ignorance can be removed. In every system, even beginningless ignorance is accepted as removable. We do not say that what is beginningless cannot be removed; we say that the nature of Brahman, which is eternal, cannot be removed. If ignorance is not Brahman’s nature, one may object, then it must be something other than Brahman; otherwise it would not exist, and what would there be to remove? If ignorance is non-apprehension, how could it be a distinct thing? And it is not irremovable, since all the operations of the means of knowledge are directed toward removing non-apprehension.

That is also unsound. Ignorance, which consists in not grasping reality, is removed by knowledge; and that ignorance is eternal in Brahman. There is no being other than Brahman whose failure to grasp reality could be removed by knowledge that is attained through effort. Yet grasping and not grasping Brahman at the same time are contradictory. If they were not contradictory, ignorance could never at any time be removed. For one who holds that ignorance is mistaken cognition: if that were Brahman’s nature, how could it be removed if it were eternal? If it were not Brahman’s nature, it would be something other than Brahman; then to whom would it belong, given that there is no being other than Brahman? If it belongs to Brahman alone, that is contradictory, since Brahman is knowledge by nature. If it is not contradictory, then by what could it be removed?

The reply is that ignorance is not Brahman’s nature, is not something other than Brahman, is not absolutely nonexistent, and is not existent. This is precisely what is called ignorance, māyā, or false appearance. If it were the nature of something, whether identical with or different from that thing, it would be real and therefore not ignorance. If it were absolutely nonexistent, like a hare’s horn, it could not function or be spoken of...

Therefore ignorance is indeterminable. All schools must accept it in this way. For the Buddhist who holds that only what is empty exists, what is seen correctly cannot be ignorance; if it were as nonexistent as a hare’s horn, it could not enter into any transaction. The idealist who holds that only cognition exists likewise cannot deny what appears as it appears: blue, yellow, and other forms appear outwardly as objects of knowledge, and if they were absolutely nonexistent, their outward appearance would be impossible, like a hare’s horn. Realists too could not call appearances such as permanence in what is impermanent, or silver where there is only something else, “ignorance,” if the appearance itself were real. If it were absolutely nonexistent, no practical activity could be based on it.

Someone may object: perhaps the form that appears is not real, but the appearance itself is real, and that is what is called ignorance. This is not sound. If there were nothing that appeared, it would be difficult to explain how its appearance could truly exist. There might be appearance alone; but even the phrase “its appearance” would then be an error. Therefore ignorance is neither existent nor nonexistent. And because its nature is not firmly established, it can be removed: it is only māyā. If it were firmly established in its own nature, how could it become otherwise without losing that nature? If it were empty, it would already be removed by itself. Thus nonduality is not lost, and there is no need to claim that what must be removed is absent.

As for the question, “Whose ignorance is it?” we say: it belongs to living beings. One may object that living beings do not differ from Brahman, since scripture says Brahman enters them as their Self. That is true ultimately; they differ only in imagination. But whose imagination produces the difference? It cannot be Brahman’s, since Brahman is knowledge by nature and free from imagination. Nor can it belong to living beings, since before imagination they do not exist; that would make each depend on the other, because the division into living beings depends on imagination, while imagination would depend on those living beings.

Some answer that this objection applies only where real things are established. Something unestablished, mere māyā, is not subject to the fault. Māyā is precisely something that cannot be made coherent; if it were coherent, it would be reality rather than māyā. Others explain that ignorance and living beings are both beginningless, like the succession of seed and sprout, and so they do not create a mutual-dependence problem. Those who hold that ignorance is the material cause say, “Ignorance is beginningless and has no purpose.” Because it is beginningless there is no circularity; because it is purposeless, there is no basis for asking why it produced the manifold world.

Some challenge this with the saying, “No one, however foolish, acts without aiming at a purpose.” They say that Brahman must have had some purpose in producing the world. It cannot have been compassion toward others, since before creation there were no beings to receive compassion, and creation is accompanied by suffering. Nor can creation have been play for Brahman’s own sake, since Brahman’s desires are already fulfilled. If creation is caused by ignorance, however, no purpose is required: illusions such as a city of heavenly musicians do not arise for an intended purpose.

Nor does the creation of a world of distinctions imply that pure Brahman has an impure transformation. The saying, “A pure person cannot undergo an impure change,” is being applied here to a world of distinctions produced by ignorance. There is no fault of partiality or cruelty. A magician who displays a manifold spectacle does not display preference or hatred according to whether the bodies shown are whole or incomplete. Nor is a painter at fault for making some pictures whole and others incomplete, or children for playing with varied figures made of clay. The teachers say that the world’s variety, arranged in accordance with the accumulated actions of beings, is not a fault.

Nor does it follow that Brahman lacks sovereignty. A lord does not cease to be a lord when he gives different results according to differences in the services performed. A pure cause may also yield an impure effect: cause and effect are neither absolutely alike nor absolutely different, since otherwise there could be no relation of cause and effect. Water, which is fluid, produces a hard pot; and, in the other direction, a conscious scorpion is said to arise from unconscious cow dung. Many differences between a cause and its effects must be admitted.

One may object that living beings too are pure by nature, since they are not different from the reality of Brahman; how, then, can ignorance have any place in them? This is apt. A clear face, however, is reflected in swords and other surfaces, and its reflection may appear dark or otherwise impure. If one says that this is an error, the case is the same for the impurity of living beings: it too is error. Otherwise, as has been said, purity would be almost impossible to attain. Someone may object that swords and the like are causes of error, and that a cause of error must likewise be stated here. But searching for a cause of beginningless error is inappropriate. This answers the question, “What causes ignorance to arise, as in a dream?” One may still object: if ignorance is beginningless, natural, and without a cause, how could it be cut off?...

All the scriptures, at any rate, are directed toward ending natural ignorance. The dark color of particles of earth is also removed by the color produced through baking. One may object that even something natural can be removed when a distinct cognition arises; but, for those who hold that there is only one Self, there is no incoming real thing, so how could ignorance be removed? Knowledge that is itself the nature of the Self cannot remove ignorance, since the two could coexist without contradiction. If they did contradict one another, the world would be eternally liberated because ignorance would have been removed forever. Nor can some other, incoming knowledge oppose ignorance: on the doctrine of oneness, nothing real can be separate from Brahman, and something that arrives cannot be the nature of Brahman. It has been said:

“No one can remove the ignorance that is natural;
only when something distinct arises can what is natural ever perish.
But there is no distinct cause for those who accept the means of oneness.”

The reply is that ignorance has already been shown to taint living beings, not Brahman. Brahman is always pure, eternal illumination, not something that arrives. Otherwise, ignorance would not cease even for one who had attained identity with Brahman, and there would be no liberation. If Brahman itself were the one that passes through worldly existence and is then liberated, the liberation of one would entail the liberation of all. For it would be Brahman itself that transmigrates when it sees difference and is liberated when it sees non-difference. The ignorance that arises naturally in living beings can be removed when knowledge arises as a cognition opposed to it. Knowledge does not arise naturally in living beings; ignorance alone is natural there, and it is dissolved by knowledge that arises later. Although living beings are not different from Brahman, the arrangement of knowledge and ignorance has been explained by the analogy of an original image and its reflection.

By what means is ignorance removed? By the means prescribed in scripture: listening, reflection, sustained meditation, celibacy, and the other disciplines. How? Sustained meditation, preceded by listening and reflection, on the Self—described as “not this, not this” and as excluding the entire manifold of differences—is plainly opposed to seeing difference and removes it. It dissolves the perception of difference in general, and, being itself included in that general dissolving, it too subsides. Listening and the other disciplines do not aim to remove one separate division by means of another division, such as the division between the listener, the act of listening, and what is heard; they dissolve division in general. When that, too, has subsided, the Self shines forth clear and purified. Just as muddy water, when a particular powder is added that gathers up the dirt, becomes clear as the powder itself settles, so when perception of difference is dissolved by listening and the other disciplines, all particular distinctions disappear with it, and the living being rests in its clear and purified nature. A living being is separated from Brahman only by ignorance; when that is removed, its own nature is Brahman. When the distinctions between pots and the like are gone, the space within them is simply the pure, immeasurable space.

Someone may object: how can division be removed by division itself? The reply is that it is opposed to division, just as one kind of powder removes dirt, as has been explained. The means of listening, reflection, and sustained meditation are plainly opposed to seeing difference in Brahman, which is beyond difference, even while the means themselves remain associated with ignorance. Milk digests milk; poison neutralizes another poison and itself subsides. As it is said:

“Whoever knows both knowledge and ignorance together
crosses death through ignorance and attains immortality through knowledge.”

This means that knowledge and ignorance are joined in the relation of means and end. Knowledge does not arise without ignorance. If knowledge is something to be brought about, it would be constructed and therefore impermanent. The verse therefore says, “Through ignorance one crosses death.” Its meaning is not that ignorance is the means to knowledge; rather, ignorance in the form of listening and the other disciplines removes ignorance. “Death” is the name for ignorance. When ignorance ceases, one attains the immortal reality indicated by knowledge: abiding in one’s own nature, like a crystal that ceases to take on a color imposed by a limiting condition. Without any further effort, one remains in the nature that is knowledge.

Another interpretation is that ignorance never exists without knowledge. Even perception of difference is not without illumination: unless it were illuminated, the difference could not appear. Therefore it is the supreme illumination itself that shines in this or that way. As it is said, “Everything follows the shining of that alone; by its light all this shines.” It is only bound up with ignorance, as stated: “This inner person imagines every perception, undiminished and without conceptual division, as though it were divided.” Similarly, knowledge in the form of listening to statements of oneness and the other disciplines is never without ignorance, since it remains bound to distinctions such as the listener, the hearing, and what is heard. Through ignorance itself—knowledge that is close at hand and opposed to it—one sees these distinctions, crosses ignorance, and rests in the eternal nature called knowledge, like water clouded by a reflection that becomes clear when the reflection ceases. Someone may object that, since division is unreal in oneness, the listening and other means that are its basis...

...could be false, and how could it bring about any result for anyone? Knowledge of what is true that comes from something false would itself be false, just as mistakenly taking vapor to be smoke would make an inference from it false. The reply is that there is no rule that something false cannot be the cause of any result. Māyā can be a cause of pleasure or fear, and something false can lead to correct knowledge, as do drawings of cows and written letters. One may object that these are real in their own nature, not empty; but, for those who hold that there is only one Self, the means themselves are false even in their own nature. The reply is: let them be real in their own nature. The form through which they convey meaning is false, and a reality that serves no purpose in producing the result would be irrelevant. Moreover, the means for seeing oneness are not false in their own nature, since Brahman itself is their nature. Brahman, bound by ignorance, serves as a means to the attainment of Brahman, just as written marks communicate the letters “ka” and “ga” through forms that do not actually exist as cows.

Someone argues that a drawing of a cow does not lead one to understand a cow by being a cow; it does so through resemblance, while a written mark does so by convention, so that one remembers, “When I see a mark like this, I should recall this letter.” This contradicts common practice. In ordinary life, children are taught letters as letters, and both the person who points them out and the learner speak without distinction: “This is a cow,” and “I have seen a cow.” Likewise, it is not false to infer from an unreal image a real object whose reflection has not been seen, situated in a particular place. Nor is it false to infer the difference in meaning from an eternal word, despite unreal divisions into long and short sounds. A falsely imagined snakebite can cause death; therefore an inference of death, fainting, and the like from it is not false, just as it would not be false after a real snakebite marked by the passage of time and other distinctions.

For the one who holds momentary cognition to be the Self, the scriptures and disciplines directed at liberation are pointless: nothing can be added or removed from something momentary. It comes to an end by itself, and no excellence can be added to it, since a single moment admits no division into what is specific and what is not; a moment cannot be divided. One may answer that something can be added or removed in the continuum. That is not sound. The transmigrating being is the agent and experiencer, but a continuum, because it is not a real thing, cannot be an agent or experiencer. How can something unreal be bound or liberated? Another may say that the continuum is neither absolutely unreal nor real, but exists by imagination; the scriptures and practices are directed toward liberation from it. Then it is something imagined that transmigrates and is liberated, and the imagined objects of transmigration and liberation are themselves imagined. Why is this not the very account we give? It has already been said: transmigration and liberation have only an imagined object; they do not belong to the highest reality.

Even granting momentary cognition, however, transmigration and liberation of a beginningless and endless continuum are impossible. There is no arising, since the continuum is beginningless and transmigration is unreal. Nor can it be destroyed: it is unreal, and there can be no final moment. That last moment must either begin some effect or not. If it begins an effect, it is not the last moment, and the continuum is not destroyed. If it begins no effect, it lacks every power and has the character of nonexistence. When that moment does not exist, every member of the continuum is likewise nonexistent on the same grounds. With the members gone, there is no continuum at all; what, then, could be destroyed?

One may say that the last moment does begin an effect, such as omniscience in another continuum. But if cause and effect are present, how can that be another continuum? Nothing other than the relation of cause and effect distinguishes one continuum from another. Yet cause and effect alone do not establish a single continuum: it is the relation of appropriating cause and effect that does so. The final moment of omniscient cognition is an object-condition, not an appropriating cause. Omniscience arises from a preceding cognition in its own continuum; the final moment of the other continuum is only its object-condition. If one requires an appropriating cause of the same kind, then the cognition of a liberated mind and the omniscient cognition are not of the same kind. One who says that a continuum is cut off by producing an effect of a different kind would have to accept that a stream of color-perception ends as soon as a cognition of another object arises. The discussion could be extended, but enough.

Some hold that the reality of the Self is not itself consciousness, but has consciousness as an attribute. They say that reaching Brahman means abiding in a state where all special attributes have been uprooted. Since it is all-pervasive, independent of body and senses, and eternal in the form of knowledge, if the Self’s nature were knowledge, a variety of knowable objects in its vicinity would make worldly existence even more extensive. If it knows nothing, however, it is not knowledge by nature. The verb “to know” requires an object; it cannot be used when there is no relation to an object. The author answers them with the word “consciousness.” For scripture says, “Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.” ...

The scripture continues, “consciousness and bliss,” and so on. There is no fault in this. A fire that burns can burn only what is brought near and is combustible, not what is not brought near or cannot burn. Likewise, a crystal, mirror, or other clear surface, though luminous by nature, displays through reflection only what is placed before it and is suitable to be reflected. In the same way, a person residing in a body that is the seat of experience enjoys sounds and other things brought within reach by the sense faculties that enable experience, even though consciousness itself is eternal. Therefore, it does not follow that everyone would perceive everything.

Nor does liberation involve the enjoyment of external objects. Someone may object that, since the Self is all-pervasive, everything is present to it as an object; what, then, must be brought near? The reply is that even for those who hold the ignorant Self’s cognition to arise from conjunction with the mind, all minds are in conjunction with all Selves, so how would there be any ordering of experience? All objects would be present to it through the mind’s contact. If, as they say, the arrangement of experience is determined by karma, that same explanation can be admitted by those who hold the Self to be consciousness itself.

Further, when seeing oneness is complete and everything has become the Self, there is no seen object; thus, though seeing is the Self’s nature, there is no act of seeing, just as fire does not burn when there is no fuel and light does not illuminate when nothing is to be illuminated. As it is said: “The seer’s seeing does not perish, because it is imperishable. But there is no second thing, separate from it, that it might see”; and, “When everything has become nothing but the Self...” Liberation characterized by the cessation of special qualities such as cognition is no different from the doctrine of annihilation. The complete absence of seeing, even for something that exists, is no different from nonexistence. And who would desire the nonexistence of the Self, the dearest of all? Liberation would then be no human good. Someone may reply that a person might seek the extinction of the Self because it would end many forms of suffering; we see people stricken with terrible diseases and sins striving for their own extinction. That is true of those whose suffering has become so overwhelming that they embody misery itself. But worldly beings also enjoy the varied pleasures of the gods and others. Just as the ending of varied sufferings makes something a human good, the ending of varied pleasures makes it no human good. Only for the one whose suffering has been completely removed, and whose state is the experience of supreme bliss, is it unquestionably the highest human good. Enough of this digression.

The word “imperishable” indicates the nature of sound: the general is defined by a specific mark. Or it means “unchanging,” by excluding transformation, in which a previous quality perishes. How can it mean the nature of sound? Because scripture says, “The higher and lower Brahman is Om,” and the like. This does not depend on the object denoted by the sound: the ending “-kāra” refers to the sound itself. Even after vowels have combined into a sequence of letters, one finds “the particle eva,” or “the particle ca,” with the ending “-kāra” used to refer to the sound.

Some explain this differently: since Brahman, which transcends every distinction, cannot be meditated upon, this is an instruction to worship Brahman through a symbol. Brahman is to be meditated upon using Om as its support. Just as one who cannot worship a deity directly performs worship before its mark, a piece of wood or stone, with the thought of the deity, so the deity being meditated upon is pleased. Or the deity is to be meditated upon by means of this name, since Om names it. The reply is that this is how one should read a passage where a practice of yoga is prescribed, such as “Meditate upon the Self as Om” or “Join yourself to Om.” But where no word like “join” or “meditate” occurs, the sentence ends in identity, as in “Om is Brahman” and “Om is all this.” Here, by showing that Om follows all speech and cannot be left behind by any word, the text shows that Om is the essence of speech; because the world of forms cannot be left behind as the form of speech, it concludes, “Om alone is all this.”

Even the statement, “By this alone one should meditate upon the supreme person,” is preceded by teaching that everything is the Self. It is not reasonable to say that the identity with all is merely figurative praise, since accepting its primary meaning creates no contradiction. This form of reality, which cannot be established by perception and the other ordinary means, is established by scripture alone; the fact that it is not known through another means of knowledge does not remove it from the subject matter of scripture. The instruction “therefore, the knower...” is addressed only to the one who knows the Self as all, not to someone else. The immediately preceding sentence therefore ends in identity, and the meditation is then prescribed for one who has understood identity with all.

Alternatively, the identity of speech with all is heard in statements such as, “Speech alone gave birth to all the worlds; speech alone enjoyed this; speech spoke.” The hymn to Speech also shows that Speech is the Self of all and their sovereign: “I move with the Rudras and the Vasus,” and so on. When Vāmadeva awakened to the Self, he said, “I was Manu and the Sun.” Moreover, transformations are associated with their material cause, and the world is associated with speech. Therefore, the transformation or manifestation of speech...

...is established in that way. How is this connection understood? Because the meaning of a word is experienced through cognition colored by the word. Everyone can see the marked difference between understanding “there is fire here” from smoke, where the fire and smoke are located in different places, and understanding a meaning from a word. The relation between a noun and its qualifier in “blue lotus” belongs to the object itself; otherwise, understanding a third thing from two mutually distinct objects—for example, “there is a tree because a crow is perched above”—would be the same sort of relation. Moreover, if words served as means of knowledge in the same way smoke does, our certainty would not take the form of the word. But certainty of fire from another means of knowledge does not imitate the form of smoke. By contrast, certainty about objects that arises even from another means of knowledge reflects the word-form. Seeing this, we conclude that understanding from words also takes that form; it is not an error caused merely by one cognition immediately following another.

Even children’s actions toward the breast and other things, in which they exclude alternatives, cannot occur without their having determined, “This is it.” One does not act on the basis of something uncertain, as when one is unsure whether a shape is a post or a person. And their certainty is not free of association with words: because they possess impressions of words from former lives, their cognition is colored by the form of speech. We therefore understand that the world, supported by speech, is a manifestation of speech.

Some things are practically real whose nature consists in nothing other than the manifestation of speech. These include injunctions and prohibitions such as “one should do it” and “one should not do it”; the meaning of a sentence; a collection; and even nonexistent things such as a whirling firebrand, a hare’s horn, and the like. An injunction or prohibition is not an action or non-action in the past, present, or future, since that would fail to distinguish “he cooked,” “he cooks,” and “he will cook.” If it is said to concern an effect, an effect cannot be defined apart from the three times. The injunction and prohibition, then, are only unreal appearances that encourage action or restraint. Yet an appearance cannot be objectless, because cognition is by nature directed toward something, and it cannot be detached from reflection on the form of words. Therefore the very nature of speech appears in different ways, in forms that accord with action and restraint. The same applies to the meaning of a sentence. A relation is not some entity apart from the things related, nor is it an entity different from relation and non-relation. Cognition is not without something known, and conceptual cognition is not free of the overlay of speech. It is thus reasonable that speech itself appears in different ways. The same explanation applies to a collection such as a forest, and to nonexistent things such as a whirling firebrand.

Even if there is cognition of musical notes, cows, and other things before a word is applied, it is not the same as the cognition that occurs afterward. Before the name is given, cognition is indistinct; afterward it is clearer and discriminating. This is why cowherds and others assign names to things, so that knowledge may become discriminating. Since understanding of an object becomes more distinct when it is touched by a word—and since, when the word is withdrawn, those who had noticed it treat even grass and other things along the road as though they had not noticed them—consciousness itself depends on the form of speech. Or, some say, consciousness is the power of speech; when that is withdrawn, the power of speech remains subtle. In every respect, cognition of objects depends on speech, so every knowable thing is understood to be associated with speech; it is a transformation or manifestation of speech. Objects are like pots arising from clay, or moons appearing as reflections in rippling water.

Others infer from the clay analogy and the like that Brahman truly transforms. This is refuted by the word “imperishable.” Why? Scripture calls it “stable,” “eternal,” and so on. One may object that even during transformation its reality is not destroyed, and so its eternity is not contradicted, as it is said, “What does not lose its reality even while undergoing change is also eternal.” That may be so; nevertheless, if the pure nature of the Self were transformed in every respect, it would not be eternal. If only part of it were transformed, it would have parts, which contradicts both eternality and oneness. Brahman’s purity, eternality, and oneness are possible, like space. Space can be imagined as bounded and also be unbounded, where no such boundary is imagined. If a partial transformation is only imagined, it was rightly said to be “imperishable.”

Some have taken Brahman to be the Self of everything because scripture says, “It is all scents, all tastes,” and so on. Then it would make sense that objects can be enjoyed: the objects’ luminosity and the Self’s nature as light would make them shine. If the objects were other than the Self, it would be difficult to explain how unconscious things could be illuminated. The author answers them with the word “not-all.” Why? Scripture excludes all distinctions when it says, “Not gross, not minute,” and so on. If Brahman were inseparable from every distinction, there could be no liberation: an entity cannot be separated from its own nature, just as fire cannot be separated from heat. Even if it could somehow be separated, the continuous flow of the manifold world would remain, and there would be no separation from it; one would be in worldly existence forever. In every way, hunger...

...would become the Self; and an end to that manifold is not accepted. For those who hold that the Self is one, there would be no liberation; for those who hold many Selves, some would be liberated and some not, explaining the distinction between the liberated and the one still in worldly existence. Therefore, Brahman is not a world made up of manifold things; rather, the manifold is only a play of ignorance. If, then, the play of ignorance is the manifold world, its absence must be ultimate reality, and that absence itself must be Brahman. Scripture teaches Brahman through denial of the manifold: “It is not this, not this,” and “not gross, not minute, not short.”

The answer is “all.” This means that Brahman is not the Self of all things in the sense of being limited to their manifold forms; rather, all things have Brahman as their nature and have form by being Brahman. They are not simply a void, because that would entail that all are eternally liberated and that instruction aimed at liberation is pointless. Someone may say that worldly existence is caused by ignorance even though all are eternally liberated. But if ignorance is non-apprehension, how can it cause worldly existence? Non-apprehension is the same in liberation, and, on that account, nothing at all would shine forth. If ignorance is incorrect apprehension, then everything is not empty. Scripture says, “All this is filled by the person,” and “The Self alone is all this”; it teaches the Self as present in everything. It also denies emptiness itself: “How could being arise from nonbeing?” For a real thing that does not shine as it is may shine with an unreal form superimposed upon it. But if everything were empty, what could serve as the basis of superimposition, and what could appear? There would be no basis at all. Since scripture teaches a positive nature in statements such as “consciousness and bliss,” Brahman is not merely the absence of everything; it is the Self of all.

Some hold that there is no state of happiness completely free from contact with suffering, because no living being is observed as entirely happy or entirely unhappy. Rather, happiness remains happiness only for someone who is also suffering; the touch of sandalwood is pleasant only for one who is overheated. The author answers them with the word “fearless.” The state of Brahman is free from every fear, and there is not even the slightest suffering in it, as scripture repeatedly says “fearless,” including “Brahman is indeed fearlessness.” There is no natural fear in Brahman, since that would conflict with its nature as bliss. Nor can fear be caused by something that arrives later, because there is no second thing. As it is said, “Fear arises from a second.” Happiness is not the mere removal of suffering either; that has already been explained in detail.

Another account is this: some think that even those who regard themselves as liberated may return. They offer different possibilities. Conscious Selves may be distinct from Brahman or not distinct; Brahman itself may divide them for the sake of experience, play, or displaying its power, or they may be divided by nature; their division may be caused by ignorance; or only the conscious Selves themselves may be what is called Brahman, with nothing else as Brahman. Their worldly existence may be caused by action and ignorance, or by a mutual fitness between seer and seen. If their return is based on that fitness, the fear of return is unavoidable, since the fitness itself cannot be removed. If they say there is no return because the purpose has been fulfilled, then, after an object such as sound has been experienced once, it should never be experienced again. If they say that material nature, with its endless transformations, ceases when everything has been experienced, but then resumes in order to display its untransformed forms, the capacity for endless experience means that complete experience of everything can never occur. Even someone who has realized the difference between qualities and persons would then be liable to return.

If worldly existence is rooted in ignorance and prior actions, a beginningless succession of actions is endless, and the time at which each action ripens is uncertain. Even after the cosmic dissolution that follows creation, the fear of return from liberation would not be removed. If ignorance is the cause, it is without cause and operates without purpose; what could prevent it from operating again and again in the same way? One sees the same return from reaching Brahman in deep sleep.

If the individual Selves are distinct from independent Brahman, or if they were once undivided and are divided for the sake of enjoyment, no reason is given why they should not again be divided into distinct bodies and senses through enjoyment and similar causes. A sovereign Brahman could bind them again by its free play, by displaying its sovereignty, or by its own nature, just as an ordinary ruler acts freely. If, on the other hand, Brahman depends on action, then action is not under its control. Even so, because actions are endless and the time of their fruition is not fixed, actions whose time has come could cause renewed bondage even after hundreds of cosmic cycles. The stock of action is not limited to a single life; death alone is not what reveals it, since place, time, and other conditions also reveal it. Indeed, even in one body, the results of actions are experienced in succession, while actions that would result in births of incompatible kinds cannot ripen together. If there were no actions causing conception, death, and the like, liberation would follow for everyone. The answer begins: “Fearlessness...”

This is called “fearlessness.” It is heard as the highest attainment of safety; there is no fear of returning to worldly existence in it. Return is not caused by action: knowledge destroys even countless actions whose results have not yet been experienced, just as an expiation destroys them. It is said, “The fire of knowledge burns up all actions,” and, “His actions are exhausted.” Alternatively, when ignorance is removed by knowledge, the division into agent, object, and result of action is dissolved. How could action then arise? Nor can ignorance be the cause, since the basis for its activity is gone. Ignorance is beginningless; for that very reason it does not depend on a cause. Causal activity operates when something is preceded by nonexistence; if there is no prior nonexistence, when could a cause act? A cause has no work to perform on something already existent. But ignorance, once it has been cut off by knowledge, cannot arise again without cause, since it had not existed before.

In deep sleep only the projecting power has ceased; the impression of it and non-apprehension have not ceased. Otherwise, deep sleep would not differ from the fourth state. It is called “attainment of Brahman” only because projection alone is absent. Thus “fearless” was rightly said.

By what means of knowledge is this reality understood? Not by perception, which concerns differences opposite to it; nor by inference, which depends on perception; nor by comparison, which concerns likeness and is based on difference. Presumption concerns the opposite, since no practical activity can be explained without difference; non-difference itself is hard to understand without distinctions such as knower and the rest. Non-apprehension is also not enough to establish a positive reality, nor to establish the absence of the manifold, since perception and the other means of knowledge are present. Nor can a scripture authored by a trustworthy person apply here, because its subject matter is already understood through another means of knowledge. Nor can a scripture be independent of other means of knowledge, since it would then have to take the form of an injunction or prohibition; but once the truth of reality is established, such a form is impossible. Nor can scripture be authoritative solely as a settled description of existing things, independent of injunction: when words report what has happened, they depend on other means of knowledge.

In ordinary life the power of words is learned from speech that directs action. Words are used for objects connected with an action, because that is how they have meaning. Speech that is wholly without action or restraint has no meaning. Furthermore, the relation between words and things is not learned from speech that merely reports what has happened, but from speech that prompts action. From a person’s acting, one infers cognition of the object and recognizes the word’s power to convey it. Thus words are not known to have power for objects unconnected with action. If words had no previously understood power, how could they make an object known when it was stated as something that had happened? If an object is already understood through another means of knowledge, the word is not authoritative about it; if it is not understood, the word is even less authoritative. If words have no meaning, a sentence cannot have a subject matter, because a sentence meaning is made up of words in a particular relation. An object never seen at all and not understood through a word cannot enter into the meaning of a sentence, either as its principal subject or as a qualifying element.

Further, a reality in which every limitation has subsided lies outside the range of cognition. All cognition proceeds by drawing a distinction: “it is so,” “it is not so.” Otherwise, nothing would ever be understood. But if every distinction has come to rest, how could cognition arise? On this point the author says:

“The wise declare its establishment through the Veda,
and its inquiry through the dissolution of the manifold of difference.”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 1 · Brahma — Brahman, bliss, and the authority of Vedānta
units.label: Kāṇḍa 1 · 3
units.deva:
भूतार्थवादित्वे ऽप्यपौरुषेयस्य न सापेक्षत्वमिति वक्ष्यते । न च कार्यनिष्ठान्येव लोके वचांसि । तथा हि प्रियाख्यानानि ‘दिष्ट्या वर्धसे, पुत्रस्ते जातःऽ; इति न प्रवृत्तये निवृत्तये वा, दृश्यन्ते च सुखोत्पादनप्रयोजनानि । न च सुखी भव इति तत्र प्रवृत्तिरुपदिश्यते, वस्तुसामर्थ्यादेव तत्सिद्धेरुपदेशस्यानपेक्षणात् । अथ मतम् --- अस्ति तावत्तत्र प्रवृत्तिविशेषः, वचसश्च तत्र तात्पर्यम् । सत्यम् । उत्पत्त्या तात्पर्यम्, न प्रतिपत्त्या । प्रतिपत्तिस्तु भूतार्थनिष्ठैव । न च भूतार्थपर्यवसितस्यैव शब्दस्य [क्क्स्_24] प्रयोजनवत्त्वे प्रवृत्त्यवधिर्व्यापारः कल्पयितुं शक्यते । अपि चोपाये वाप्रवृत्तः पुरुषः प्रवर्त्यते, अज्ञातोपायत्वाद्वा उपेये प्रागप्रवृत्त उपायप्रज्ञापनद्वारेण तत्र । इह न तावदुपाये पुत्रजन्मनि, तस्य निष्पन्नत्वात् । नोपेये सुखे, तदर्थव्यापारान्तराभावात् । तथा दुर्जनवचनान्यप्रियाख्यानानि विषादप्रयोजनानि न प्रवृत्तिं निवृत्तिं वोपदिशन्ति पूर्वेणैव न्यायेन । तथा रज्जुवेष्टितस्य सर्पवेष्टितमात्मानं मन्यमानस्य भयनिवृत्तये तत्त्वाख्यानं दृश्यते, न तु तत्र ‘मा भैषीःऽ; इति नियोगः । तत्र हि नियोगो भवति, यत्र नियोगार्थं प्रतिबुध्य पुरुषो बुद्धिपूर्वं नियोगसामर्थ्यादिच्छया वा पुनः प्रवर्तते निवर्तते वा । इह तु तत्त्वप्रतिपत्तिमात्रान्नियोगेच्छानपेक्षस्य हेत्वभावादेव तस्य भयनिवृत्तिः । न च भयनिवृत्तौ पुरुषार्थत्वात्स्वयंप्रवृत्तः पुरुषो नियोज्यः, नापि तदुपाये तत्त्वप्रतिपत्तौ, ‘रज्जुः, न सर्पःऽ; इति शब्दादेव तदुत्पत्तेः, शब्दार्थप्रतिपत्त्युत्तरकालस्य च व्यापारस्य विधिनिबन्धनत्वात् । तथा दूरदेशवृत्तान्ताख्यानानि पृष्टवतां कुतूहलिनामौत्सुक्यनिवृत्त्यर्थानि भूतार्थपर्यवसितानि न हानायोपादानाय वा । यत्रापि (अपि च यत्रापि एदितिओन्) भूतार्थप्रतिपत्तौ हानमुपादानं वा संभवति, ‘एष प्रतिरोधकवानध्वा, निधिमानेष भूभागःऽ; इति । तत्रापि हानोपादानयोः शब्दो व्याप्रियते, भूतार्थोपक्षयात् । शब्दाद्भूतमर्थं प्रतिपद्य तस्य प्रमाणान्तरावगतामुपकारहेतुतामपकारहेतुतां वा संस्मृत्य इच्छया प्रवर्तते द्वेषेण निवर्तते वा । ननु प्रयोक्ता बुद्धिपूर्वकारी श्रोतुः प्रवृत्त्यर्थं निवृत्त्यर्थं वा वचनं प्रयुङ्क्ते । तथा च प्रवृत्तिनिवृत्तिपर्यवसितमेव । इदं हि तत्र प्रयोक्तव्यं न प्रयुज्यते ‘न गन्तव्यमनेनाध्वनाऽ; तथा ‘गृहाणेतो निधिम्ऽ; इति । नैतत्सारम् । भूतार्थपर्यवसितस्यापि वचसो भूतार्थावगममुखेन प्रवृत्तिनिवृत्त्यङ्गभावो यतो न व्याहन्यते प्रत्यक्षादीनामिव । भूतार्थप्रमापरिसमाप्तव्यापृतयः प्रत्यक्षादयो मात्रयाप्यगोचरीकृतप्रवृत्तिनिवृत्तयो न प्रवृत्तिनिवृत्त्यङ्गभावं [क्क्स्_25] जहति, तथा शब्दो ऽपीति न किञ्चित्प्रदुष्यति । प्रयोक्त्रभिसंहिते प्रवृत्तिनिवृत्ती इति चेत्, न प्रयोक्त्रभिसंधानाच्छब्दार्थत्वमपि तु सामर्थ्यात् । अन्यथा निधिप्राप्तिद्वारिका नानाविधपुरुषार्थावाप्तिरपि तस्याभिसंहितेति शब्दार्थः स्यात् । यदा च प्रवृत्तिं निवृत्तिं वाभिसंधाय किञ्चित्प्रत्यक्षादिभिर्जिज्ञास्यते, तदाभिसंहिते अपि प्रवृत्तिनिवृत्ती न प्रत्यक्षादिप्रमेये । तदाभिसंहिते अपि प्रवृत्तिनिवृत्ती न शब्दार्थौ । इतश्चैतदेवम् (इतश्च तदेवम् -- एदितिओन्) --- यत्कस्यचिदुपादानबुद्धिः, अन्यस्योपेक्षा । शब्दार्थत्वे हि सर्वेषामुपादानबुद्धिरेव स्यात् । न च प्रवर्तकवाक्यव्यवहारादेव सम्बन्धावगमः, येन प्रवृत्तिपरतैवावगम्येत । अन्यथापि दर्शनात् । ‘देवदत्तः काष्ठैः स्थाल्यामोदनं पचतिऽइत्यव्युत्पन्नकाष्ठशब्दार्थो व्युत्पन्नेतरपदार्थो व्युत्पन्नविभक्त्यर्थश्च यत्पचत्यर्थे करणं पश्यति तस्य काष्ठप्रातिपदिकार्थतां प्रतिपद्यते । तथा हर्षविषादाश्वासप्रयोजनेभ्यः तत्त्वाख्यानेभ्यो हर्षादिनिमित्तेषु भवति व्युत्पत्तिः । यथैव हि प्रवृत्तिविशेषदर्शनाद्विशिष्टप्रवृत्तिप्रत्ययस्तन्निमित्तप्रत्ययो वानुमीयते, हेत्वन्तराभावाच्छब्दानन्तर्याच्छब्दस्य तत्र सामर्थ्यं कल्प्यते, तथा हर्षाद्युपलब्धेः हर्षादिनिमित्तप्रत्ययानुमानम्, शब्दानन्तर्याच्च शब्दस्य तत्र सामर्थ्यकल्पना । प्रमाणान्तरेण च पुत्रजन्मनो हर्षनिमित्तस्य तस्यावगतत्वादन्यस्याभावात् ‘पुत्रस्ते जातःऽइतीदं वाक्यमाप्तेन तत्र पुत्रजन्मनि प्रयुक्तमिति प्रतिपद्यते । पुत्रजन्मैव चास्माद्वाक्यादनेन प्रतीतमित्यवधारयति । तदेवं प्रयोगप्रत्ययाभ्यामस्मिन्नर्थे वाक्यस्य सामर्थ्यं प्रतिपद्यते । भवतु वा लोके सर्ववचसां प्रवर्तकता, ततश्च सम्बन्धावगमः । तथापीदं विचार्यम् --- किं विधायकपदव्यतिरेकिणां पदानां स्वार्थमात्रपरता, आहोस्वित्कार्यार्थसंसर्गपरता, उत पदार्थमात्रसंसर्गपरतेति । तत्र स्वार्थमात्रपर्यवसाने वाक्यार्थप्रत्ययाभावः प्रयोगवैयर्थ्यं च स्यात् । तस्मादन्यार्थव्यतिषङ्गपरता । [क्क्स्_26] तावता प्रयोगप्रत्यययोरुपपत्तौ न विशेषव्यतिषङ्गे प्रमाणमस्ति । यो हि विशेषव्यतिषङ्गं कल्पयति, कल्पयत्यसावर्थान्तरव्यतिषङ्गम् । तथा च विनापि कार्येण पदार्थानां परस्परसंसर्गाद्विशिष्टभूतार्थप्रत्ययसिद्धिः । अवश्यं चैतदेवं विज्ञेयम् । अन्यथा लोके विवक्षापरत्वात्पदार्थान्वयस्य, तदभावाद्वेदे वेदार्थप्रतीतिर्न स्यात् । अपि च सर्वेषां कार्यान्वयित्वे परस्परं पदार्थानामनभिसम्बन्धः । तत्र न विशिष्टपदार्थविषयो नियोगः प्रतीयेत । एकपदार्थसाध्य एव स्यात् । अथ न विनियोगप्रत्यर्थी नियोगः, विशिष्टविषयत्वात् । पूर्वस्तर्हि विनियोगः, पश्चान्नियोगः । किमतः? अस्ति नियोगातिरिक्तार्थान्वये ऽपि पदस्य सामर्थ्यं नियोगानपेक्षं च, परस्परान्वितानां इयोगान्वयात् । न च नियोगाकाङ्क्षानिबन्धनः संसर्ग इति प्रतिपादयिष्यते । अनधिगतमपि रमाणान्तरेणानधिगतसम्बन्धं च स्वशब्देन शक्यं शब्देन निरूपयितुं विशेषप्रतिषेधमुखेन, विशेषशब्दानां नञश्च यथायथमर्थैर्विदितसङ्गतित्वात् । तथा चेत्थमेव तदुपदिश्यते ‘अस्थूलम्ऽइति सर्वविशेषातिगम् । एतत्कथयति --- भेदप्रपञ्चविलयद्वारेणेति । एतच्च वक्ष्यत इति । अन्यो ऽर्थः । यदुक्तम् --- प्रत्यस्तमितसकलविशेषं तत्त्वं प्रतिपत्तेरेवाविषय इति, तत्रोच्यते --- विशेषनिवृत्त्यैव तच्छब्देन बुद्धौ निधीयते, सुवर्णतत्त्ववत् । न हि सुवर्णतत्त्वं पिण्डरुचकादिसंस्थानभेदोपप्लवरहितं दृश्यते । न च त एव सुवर्णतत्त्वम्, तत्परित्यागे ऽपि भावात्संस्थानान्तरे । अथ चादृष्टसंस्थानभेदोपप्लवविवेकमपि बुद्ध्या भेदापोहद्वारेण स्वयं प्रतीयते, परस्मै च प्रतिपाद्यते । स एष प्रतिपत्तिक्रमः श्रुत्यैव दर्शितः --- ‘स एष नेति नेतिऽ; इति । तथान्यैः --- ‘सत्यमाकृतिसंहारे यदन्ते व्यवतिष्ठतेऽ; । तथापरैः --- ‘अध्यारोपापवादाभ्यां निष्प्रपञ्चं प्रपञ्च्यतेऽ; इति । इदमिदानीं विचार्यते --- किं कृत्स्न आम्नायो भेदप्रपञ्चविलयमुखेन ब्रह्म निरूपयति, आहोस्वित्कश्चिदस्यैकदेशः? तत्र केचिदाहुः --- सर्वत्रैवाम्नाये [क्क्स्_27] क्वचित्कस्यचिद्भेदस्य प्रविलयो गम्यते, यथा ‘स्वर्गकामो यजेतऽ; इति शरीरात्मभावस्य प्रविलयः । अत्र हि देहव्यतिरिक्तस्वर्गोपभोगसमर्थो ऽधिकारी गम्यते, तेन देहात्मभावप्रविलयः । तथा ‘गोदोहनेन पशुकामस्य प्रणयेत्ऽइत्यधिकृताधिकारादधिकारिभेदप्रविलयः । तथा विधिनिषेधचोदनास्वपि नैसर्गिकीणां रागादिनिबन्धनानां प्रवृत्तीनां प्रविलयः । निषेधेषु साक्षात्, विधिषु प्रवृत्त्यन्तर्नियोगेन । लोके ऽप्यनभिप्रेतात्पथः साक्षाद्वा निवारणम्, पथ्यन्तरोपदेशेन वा । एवं च रागादिनिबन्धननैसर्गिकप्रवृत्तिभेदविलयद्वारेण दृष्टेनैव कर्मविधय आत्मज्ञानाधिकारोपयोगिनः । तथा हि --- शान्तस्य दान्तस्य समाहितस्य चात्मनि दर्शनमुपदिश्यते । शक्यं च । न हि विषयैराकृष्यमाणस्तदुपायप्रवृत्तिकृतचेताः शक्नोत्यात्मनि समाधातुम् । नैसर्गिकीभ्यस्तु प्रवृत्तिभ्य उपरतो नियतमानस आत्मदर्शनेनाधिक्रियते, सामर्थ्यात् । अन्ये (म्स् अ; अन्ये तु एदितिओन्) मन्यन्ते --- अनवाप्तकामः कामोपहतमना न परमाद्वैतदर्शनयोग्यः । कर्मभिस्तु कृतकामनिबर्हणः सहस्रसंवत्सरपर्यन्तैः प्राजापत्यात्पदात्परमाद्वैतमात्मानं प्रतिपद्यत इति । उभयोरपि पक्षयोरनयोः कृत्स्न आम्नाय आत्मज्ञानैकपर्यवसायी । अन्येषां दर्शनम् --- पृथक्कार्या एव सन्तः कर्मविधय आत्मज्ञानाधिकारमवतारयन्ति पुरुषम्, अनपाकृतर्णत्रयस्य तत्रानधिकारात् --- ‘ऋणानि त्रीण्यपाकृत्य मनो मोक्षे निवेशयेत्ऽ; इति । अन्ये तु संयोगपृथक्त्वेन सर्वकर्मणामेवात्मज्ञानाधिकारानुप्रवेशमाहुः ‘विविदिषन्ति यज्ञेनऽइति श्रुतेः, ‘येन केनचन यजेतापि दर्वीहोमेनानुपहतमना एव भवतिऽ; इति च । [क्क्स्_28] अन्ये तु पुरुषसंस्कारतयात्मज्ञानाधिकारसंस्पर्शं कर्मणां वर्णयन्ति --- ‘महायज्ञैश्च यज्ञैश्च ब्राह्मीयं क्रियते तनुःऽ, ‘यस्यैते चत्वारिंशत्संस्कारा अष्टावात्मगुणाःऽ; इति च । अन्ये त्वेतदेव विपरीतं वर्णयन्ति, आत्मज्ञानमेव कर्तृसंस्कारतया कर्माधिकारानुप्रवेशीति । अन्ये तु परस्परविरोधिनोः कर्मात्मज्ञानयोः द्वैताद्वैतविषयत्वेनासंबन्ध एवेति मन्यन्ते । तत्र न तावत्प्रथमः कल्पः । न हि कर्मादिविधयः स्ववाक्यसमधिगतस्वर्गादिकार्याः कार्यान्तरमपेक्षन्ते । नाप्यात्मज्ञानविधिर्यथोदितब्रह्मचर्यादिसाधननिराकाङ्क्षः कर्मविधीनपेक्षते । तत्र कुत एकाधिकारत्वम् । यदि मन्येतानवगतकार्या (अथ अनवगत@ -- एदितिओन्) एव कर्मादिविधयः, स्वर्गादीनां गुणत्वेन संबन्धादिति, स्वर्गकामाधिकरणमस्मै व्याचक्षीत । अपि च सर्वविधिनिषेधानां नामरूपप्रविलयकार्यापवर्गित्वे जन्तूनामभ्युदयविनिपाता अकर्मनिमित्ता आकस्मिकाः स्युः । तथापवर्गो ऽपि स्यादिति वैयर्थ्यं शास्त्रस्यापि । अथ स्वर्गादिकार्यद्वारेण कर्मविधीनां ज्ञानाधिकारानुप्रवेशिता मार्गग्रामगमनोपदेशानामिवाभिमतनगरगमनोपदेशानुप्रवेशित्वम् । तदसत् । युक्तं मार्गग्रामप्राप्तेरनभिमतदेशप्राप्त्युपदेशानुप्रवेशित्वम् । न हि मार्गग्रामोपदेशेषु पुरुषार्थप्राप्तिः । अतः साकाङ्क्षत्वाद्यत्र पुरुषार्थप्राप्तिः, तमनुप्रविशन्ति । न त्वेवं कर्मविधिषु पुरुषार्थस्यालाभः, स्वर्गादीनां पुरुषेणार्थ्यमानत्वात् । तत्र च नैराकाङ्क्ष्ये कथमन्यानुप्रवेशः? अथ मतम् --- यदोपच्छन्द्य नीयत उत्तरोत्तरग्रामगुणोपदर्शनेनाभिप्रेतं देशम्, तदा पूर्वग्रामोपदेशाः प्राप्ताभिमतकार्या उपदेशान्तरानुप्रवेशिनश्चेति । युक्तं तत्रापि प्रमाणान्तरेण वक्तुरभिप्रायाधिगमात् । प्रमाणान्तरेण हि तत्रेदमधिगतम् --- एतद्देशप्राप्ताविदमस्य समीहितं वक्तुः संपद्यते, तस्मादिदमस्य विवक्षितमिति । न तु शब्दवृत्तिमात्रानुसारेण (शब्दप्रवृत्तिमात्रा@ म्स् अ; शब्दवृत्तमात्रा@ -- एदितिओन्) । इतश्चैतदेवम् --- [क्क्स्_29] यत्प्रतिग्रामं वक्तुः श्रोतुश्च सत्यामर्थप्राप्तौ प्रमाणान्तरेणानधिगते परदेशप्राप्त्यभिप्राये पूर्वोपदेशान् पूर्वार्थानेव पार्श्वस्थाः प्रतिपत्तारः प्रतिपद्यन्ते, परदेशोपदेशं च स्वार्थनिष्ठम् । यद्यपि वस्तुस्थित्या पूर्वोपदेशार्थाः परोपकारिणः, तथापि न शब्दस्य तात्पर्यम्, द्रव्यार्जनादिविधेरिव क्रतुविध्यर्थोपकारे ऽपि । शब्दवृत्तानुसारेण चेह तात्पर्यम्, प्रमाणान्तराभावादिति । अपि चाध्वग्रामोपदेशानां तत्परत्वाध्यवसायेनैव तत्र गमनमर्थप्राप्तिश्च । तत्र परदेशप्राप्तिपरतायां तु न नियोगतस्तत्र गमनम् । मार्गान्तरेणापि तत्प्राप्तेर्विवक्षितत्वाद्गच्छेत् । न च नियोगतो ऽर्थप्राप्तिः, अन्यपरेषु प्रयोजनश्रुतेरप्यर्थवादत्वात् । तदिह यदि विधिनिषेधाः कार्यान्तरपराः, न स्वर्गादिकार्याः । न खलु स्वर्गादिकार्यं प्रयाजादिकार्यतुल्यम्, येन कार्यान्तरमनुपतेत् । कथं च दृष्टेनैवात्मज्ञानाधिकारोपकारिण इति वक्तव्यम् । यदि तावद्रागाद्याक्षिप्तदृष्टार्थप्रवृत्तिनिरोधेन, भवतु प्रतिषेधानामेवंभावः । कर्मविधयस्तु कथं निरुन्धन्तीति वाच्यम् । नहि ते परिसंख्यायकाः, न च नियामकाः, अत्यन्तमप्राप्तार्थत्वात् । प्राप्तार्थो हि विधिरन्यनिवृत्तिफलो विज्ञायते । न च तुल्यकार्यत्वेन विरोधेन निवृत्तिः । अनियतकालफला हि नैयोगिक्यः प्रवृत्तयो ऽदृष्टार्थाः । दृष्टार्थास्तु रागाद्याक्षिप्ताः स्वाभाविक्यः । न च साङ्ग्रहण्याः सेवायाश्च ग्रामोपायत्वे कश्चिद्विरोधः, एतावति प्रमाणत्वाच्छास्त्रस्य । तत्र युगपत्क्रमेण वा फलभूमार्थिनः सेवासाङ्ग्रहण्यावनुतिष्ठतः को विरोधः? अपि च सकलदृष्टार्थप्रवृत्तिनिरोधे नियोगनिष्ठा अपि प्रवृत्तयो निरुध्येरन्, अनार्जितधनस्य साधनविकलस्य तासामसम्भवात् । अपि च तुल्ये कामोपायत्वे दृष्टादृष्टार्थप्रवृत्त्योर्न न विशेषो रागाद्याक्षिप्तत्वे । तथा हि --- ‘स्वर्गकामःऽइति रागाद्याक्षिप्तप्रवृत्त्यनुवादेन विशेषविधानम् । तथा च प्रपञ्चाभिनिवेशे तुल्ये केन विशेषेण एकात्मानुगुण्यं भजते, तद्विरोधिन्यपरा? कामाक्षेपो ह्यविशिष्टो मनसः । अथ कामोपायत्वमेव न मन्येत, वर्णितमाकस्मिकत्वम्, उक्तश्च न्यायः प्रत्युद्ध्रियेत । तुल्यकार्यनिबन्धनत्वाच्च विरोधाद्या [क्क्स्_30] निरोधाशङ्का सा दूरतो निरस्तावकाशा स्यात् । अथ कामप्राप्त्या कर्मविधयः कामान् प्रविलापयन्तो ज्ञानाधिकारानुगुणाः । यथोक्तम् ---

ऽयदा सर्वे प्रमुच्यते कामा ये ऽस्य हृदि श्रिताः । अथ मर्त्यो ऽमृतो भवत्यत्र ब्रह्म समश्नुतेऽ; ॥ इति । तदप्यसत् । यतो न कामप्राप्त्या कामप्रविलयः, अपि तु दोषपरिभावनाभुवा प्रसङ्ख्यानेन । कलयापि चेत्कामैर्मनः संस्पृश्यते ह्रियत एव हारिभिः । उक्तं हि --- ‘न जातु कामः कामानामुपभोगेन शाम्यतिऽ, ‘भोगाभ्यासमनु विवर्धन्ते रागाः कौशलानि चेन्द्रियाणाम्ऽ; इति च । अनुपायत्वादपि तावदयं कामेभ्यो विनिवर्तेत । निखिलक्लेशोपशमरूपं चात्मज्ञानं संश्रयेत । कर्मविधिनिदर्शितविविधोपायस्तु तानेव प्रकृतहारिणो भोगानभिनिविशेत । तत्प्रविलयरूपाचात्मज्ञानादुद्विजेत । श्रुतो ऽपि ह्यात्मन्यानन्दो ऽननुभूतो नानुभूतविषयनिबन्धनानन्दाभिलाषं मन्दीकर्तुमप्युत्सहते, प्रागेवोच्छेत्तुम् । तस्मात्प्रसंख्यानमेवैकः कामनिबर्हणोपायः, कर्मविधयस्तु विपर्ययहेतवः । यदपि --- सर्वत्रैवाम्नाये क्वचित्कस्यचिद्भेदस्य विलयः, यथा ‘स्वर्गकामो यजेतऽ; इति शरीरात्मत्वप्रविलय इति । तदप्यसत्, अनिदंपरत्वात् । न हीदं वचनं देहव्यतिरिक्तात्मतत्त्वावबोधपरम् । अथान्यपरादप्यर्थादेवमवसीयत इति, तदपि हस्तिनि दृष्टे तत्पदेन तस्यानुमानमिव । साक्षाद्धि ‘अस्थूलम्ऽइत्युपक्रम्य देहेन्द्रियविलयो दर्शितः, अर्थाच्च कामादिग्रन्थेः काठिन्यं वैदिकं स्यादिति । द्वितीयो ऽपि कल्पो वर्णितादेव कामानां कामनिबर्हणसामर्थ्याभावात्स्वकार्यनिराकाङ्क्षाणां चान्यानुप्रवेशे प्रमाणभावादसमञ्जसः । एकाधिकारत्वे तु समुच्चयः सर्वकर्मणां स्यात् । स चाशक्य इति । [क्क्स्_31] ये ऽपि विपर्ययेण ज्ञानकर्मणोरेकाधिकारत्वमाहुः, तैरपि ज्ञानस्य कर्मसम्बन्धे प्रमाणं वक्तव्यम् । न तावत् ‘ब्रीहीन् प्रोक्षतिऽ; इति यथा । तत्र हि प्रकरणात्प्रकृतकर्मापूर्वलक्षणापरो ब्रीहिशब्दः स्वस्वरूप आनर्थक्यात्प्रकृतापूर्वसम्बन्धं बोधयति । नापि यथा ‘यस्य पर्णमयी जुहूर्भवतिऽ; इति । तत्र हि जुह्वाद्यव्यभिचरितकर्मसम्बन्धमसत्यपि प्रकरणे कर्मोपस्थापयति । तत्र वाक्येनैव सम्बन्धः । आत्मज्ञानं तु न प्रकरणे श्रुतम् । नाप्यात्माव्यभिचरितकर्मसम्बन्धः । तेनास्य कर्मसम्बन्धो दुर्वचः । तथा चाज्ञाते पारार्थ्ये या नाम फलश्रुतिर्न सार्थवादिनी भवतीति पृथगधिकारत्वम् । अथ मतम् --- वर्तमानापदेशात् ‘न स (च --एदितिओन्) पुनरावर्ततेऽइति कामोपबन्धाभावात्फलं विपरिणमय्य कल्पयितव्यम् । तच्च तदाकाङ्क्षायां सत्याम् । न तु दृष्टे सति तदाकाङ्क्षा । अस्ति चात्मज्ञानविधेर्दृष्टफलं देहान्तरोपभोग्यफलेषु कर्मसु प्रवृत्तिः । तस्मात्स्वाध्यायाध्ययनविधिवदात्मज्ञानविधिः । स्वाध्यायाध्ययनविधिर्हि दृष्टकर्मावबोधनिराकाङ्क्षो नार्थवादतः फलं प्रार्थयते, तथात्मज्ञानविधिरपीति नाधिकारान्तरम् । तदप्यसत् । यतो ऽयमन्य एवौपनिषदः पुरुषो वेदान्तेषु जिज्ञास्यते । न च तज्ज्ञानं कर्मप्रवृत्तिहेतुः । न हि तस्य कर्तृत्वभोक्तृत्वे । एवं ह्याह --- ‘न तदश्नाति किञ्चनऽ; ‘अनश्नन्नन्यो ऽभिचाकशीतिऽ; इति । यस्तु कर्मणां कर्ता भोक्ता च, स एव सर्वप्रत्यक्षसिद्धः । न शब्दप्रमेयः । ननु जीवपरमात्मनोरेकत्वमेव । एवं ह्याह --- ‘अनेन जीवेनात्मनाऽ; इति । सत्यम् । तस्यैव तु जीवस्यैवमविद्यानुबन्धं प्रत्यक्षावसेयं रूपम्, तच्च कर्मप्रवृत्तिहेतुः । न च तच्छब्दमपेक्षते । यत्तु स्वयंप्रकाशं सर्वविभागशून्यं तच्छब्दाज्ज्ञातुमिष्यते । तच्च कर्मप्रवृत्तिविरोधि । तज्ज्ञानस्य कथं कर्मप्रवृत्तिर्दृष्टं प्रयोजनं स्यात्? तथा हि --- ब्रह्मानन्दमेकमद्वयमात्मानं विजानतः किमर्थं कथं वा प्रवृत्तिः स्यात्, आप्तकामत्वात्साधनाद्युपायाभावाच्च? स्यादेतत् --- औपनिषदपुरुषज्ञानमेव कर्माङ्गत्वेन चोदितम् ‘यदेव विद्यया करोति श्रद्धयोपनिषदा [क्क्स्_32] तदेव वीर्यवत्तरं भवतिऽ; इति । तथा ‘यो वा एतदक्षरं गार्ग्यविदित्वास्मिंल्लोके जुहोतिऽइत्युपक्रम्य यागादिफलस्यान्तवत्तादर्शनेन ब्रह्मविद्यायास्तादर्थ्यं दर्शितम् । ‘तं विद्याकर्मणी समन्वारभेतेऽ; इति च विद्याकर्मणोः साहित्यं दर्शितम् । पूर्वं तावत्प्रकृतोद्गीथविषयम्, ‘ओमित्येतदक्षरमुद्गीथम्ऽ; इत्युपक्रमात् । परेणापि कर्मनिन्दयाक्षरज्ञानस्तुतिः । विद्याकर्मणोश्च समन्वारम्भो भेदेन --- विद्यावन्तं विद्यान्वारभते कर्मवन्तं कर्मेति । तस्मादेवमपि न कर्मज्ञानयोरेकाधिकारत्वमिति । ये ऽपि विरोधादसम्बन्ध एव कर्मज्ञानयोः ‘द्वैतविषयं कर्म, अद्वैतविषयं ज्ञानम्ऽइति मन्यन्ते, तेषामनुत्पाद एवाद्वैतज्ञानस्य प्रसज्यते, प्रमाणादिविभागाद्वैतप्रतिपत्त्योर्विरोधात् । अथोपायोपेययोरयौगपद्यादविरोधः, प्रलीयत एवाद्वैतप्रतिपत्तौ सर्वो विभागः । न च विरोधो ऽनुपायत्वं वा, उपायस्य पूर्वकालत्वात्, तदा च तस्याप्रलीनत्वात् । भेद एव चाभेदप्रतिपत्तावुपायः । न तर्हि कर्मभिरपि विरोधः, उपायत्वादेव । स्यादेतत् --- असाध्यत्वाद्ब्रह्मणो न कर्मणामुपयोगो विद्यते । श्रूयते च --- ‘नास्त्यकृतः कृतेनऽ; इति । न च ज्ञानोत्पत्तावुपयोगः, ज्ञानस्य प्रमाणाधीनत्वात् । न च ज्ञानसहकारीणि कर्माणि, ज्ञानस्य साध्यान्तराभावात् । न तस्य मोक्षः साध्यः, अनित्यत्वप्रसङ्गात् । अथ बन्धहेतुविच्छेदः साध्य इति तस्मिन् विच्छिन्ने तदभावान्मुच्यते । कः पुनर्बन्धहेतुः? अनाद्यविद्या, न तर्हि पृथक्तद्विच्छेदः साध्यः, यतो विद्योदय एवाविद्याव्यावृत्तिः । स्यादेतत् --- भवत्वग्रहणलक्षणाविद्याव्यावृत्तिर्विद्योत्पादः, यतो भाव एवाभावव्यावृत्तिः । न च विद्योत्पाद एव विपर्यासज्ञानव्यावृत्तिः । न खलु भावान्तरं भावान्तरव्यावृत्तिः । न च परस्पराभावात्मानो भावाः, अभावत्वप्रसङ्गात् । यदि मन्येत --- तत्त्वाग्रहणनिमित्तो विपर्यासो निमित्तनिवृत्तौ स्वयमेव निवर्तिष्यते, तच्च न । न खल्वग्रहणमभावः कस्यचिन्निमित्तम्, मूर्च्छादिषु [क्क्स्_33] प्रसङ्गात् । किं तर्हि निमित्तम्? ‘अनादिरप्रयोजना चाविद्याऽ; इत्युक्तम् । तत्र च हेत्वनुयोगो निरवकाशः । विपर्यासतत्संस्कारयोश्च परस्परहेतुफलभावेन व्यवस्थानान्न दोषः । अतो विपर्ययज्ञानस्य निवृत्तिर्विद्यया साध्येति तत्र ज्ञानस्य सहकार्यपेक्षा स्यात् । एतच्च वार्तम् । न खलु शुक्तिकादिषु विपर्यासपुरस्सरं समुपजातसम्यग्ज्ञानास्तन्निवृत्तये पृथक् प्रयतन्ते, सहकारि वान्यदपेक्षन्ते । यतो विरोधिभावान्तरोत्पाद एव पूर्वप्रध्वंसः, न शून्यम् । अन्यथा न प्रध्वंसो हेतुमान् स्यात् । विरोधिनी च विद्या विपर्ययज्ञानस्य । तदुत्पत्तौ विपर्यासो नष्ट एव भवति । अथोच्येत --- कर्माणि बन्धहेतवः । तत्क्षयो ज्ञानात्सहकारिसव्यपेक्षादिति । तच्च प्रमृष्टाशेषविशेषविशुद्धज्ञानोदये कुतः सम्भवः? तथा च विपर्याससंशयाभ्यां तुल्यवत्प्रसंख्यातानि कर्माणि ---

ऽभिद्यन्ते हृदयग्रन्थिश्छिद्यन्ते सर्वसंशयाः । क्षीयन्ते चास्य कर्माणि तस्मिन् दृष्टे परावरेऽ; ॥ इति । अथ विज्ञानवैमल्यायान्यापेक्षा । सापि मुधा, संशयविपर्यासयोर्ज्ञानमलयोः प्रमाणोत्थविज्ञाने ऽसंभवात् । अथ मतम् --- शाब्दज्ञानादन्यदपि प्रत्यक्षं ज्ञानमिष्यते विगलितविभागोद्ग्राहं सर्वविकल्पातीतम् । तस्य हि ब्रह्म गोचरः, न शाब्दस्य विभक्तपदार्थसंसर्गोद्ग्राहिणः । तदुत्पत्तौ कर्मोपासनाद्यपेक्षेति । कः पुनरस्य विशेषः, येन तदर्थ्यते? स्पष्टाभत्वम्, न तस्योपयोगः । ज्ञानं हि ज्ञेयाभिव्याप्तये, शाब्दज्ञाने चोत्पन्न आप्तमेव ज्ञेयम् । प्रमितेः प्रत्यक्षपरत्वात्तत्र च नैराकाङ्क्ष्यात्तदर्थ्यत इति चेत्, एतदधिगते प्रमेये किमन्यदाकाङ्क्ष्येत? प्रमाणान्तरमिति चेन्न, प्रमेयसिद्ध्यर्थत्वात्तदाकाङ्क्षायाः । पुनः सिद्ध्यर्थमिति चेन्न, पूर्वस्मादप्यसकृत्तत्सिद्धेः । सिद्धस्य च सिद्ध्यपेक्षायां न हेतुरस्ति । उपायान्तरसद्भावश्चेत्, उपायान्तरं तर्ह्यपेक्षेत । प्रमेये तु नैराकाङ्क्ष्यमेव । प्रीतिविशेषश्चेत्, स पूर्वप्रमाणजादपि [क्क्स्_34] दर्शनात्सिध्यति । न तत्सिद्ध्यर्थं प्रमाणान्तरम् । प्रत्यक्षदृष्टमपीतरैस्तत्सम्भवाज्जिज्ञास्येत, विशेषाभावात् । निश्चायकत्वमितरेषामपि, प्रमाणभावात् । हानादियोग्यविषयं प्रत्यक्षम्, सन्निकृष्टार्थत्वात्, नेतराणीति चेत् । सन्निकर्षहेतुस्तर्ह्यपेक्ष्यताम् । न प्रमाणम्, सिद्धत्वात्प्रमायाः । प्रकृते च प्रमेये नैष विशेषो ऽस्ति । सामान्यविषयाः शब्दादयः, विशेषविषयं प्रत्यक्षमिति चेत् । अनधिगत एव तर्हि शब्देन प्रत्यक्षस्य विषयः । बाढम् । उक्तमेतत् --- न शाब्दस्य ज्ञानस्य विषयो ब्रह्मेति । यदि तर्हि न शब्देनाधिगतं ब्रह्म, कथं तस्मिन्नुपासना प्रवर्तताम्? न चान्यस्मिन्नुपास्यमाने ऽन्यत्साक्षाद्भवति । कस्य च रूपस्य साक्षात्करणाय यज्ञादिविधानम्? शब्दोपदर्शितनिरतिशयानन्दापहतपाप्मादिरूपब्रह्मस्वभावस्यात्मनः साक्षात्करणाय यज्ञादिविधिरुपपद्यते । अविदितपुरुषार्थरूपे तद्विपरीतरूपे निर्विचिकित्सात्प्रमाणात्प्रकटतां प्राप्ते नापरमपेक्ष्यमस्ति । नन्ववगते ऽपि ‘तत्त्वमसिऽ; इति शब्दाद्ब्रह्मात्मभावे प्रागिव सांसारिकधर्मदर्शात्तन्निवृत्तये भवत्यन्यापेक्षा । नैतत्सारम् । कथं खल्ववगतब्रह्मात्मभावो विदितात्मयाथातथ्यो मिथ्यादर्शननिमित्तैर्धर्मैर्युज्यते? श्रूयते च --- ‘ब्रह्म वेद ब्रह्मैव भवतिऽ; इति । न च ब्रह्मण्यपहतपाप्मनि तेषामवकाशः । तथा ---

‘आत्मानं चेद्विजानीयादयमस्मीति पूरुषः । किमिच्छन् कस्य कामाय शरीरमनुसञ्ज्वरेत्ऽ; ॥ तथा ‘अशरीरं वाव सन्तं न प्रियाप्रिये स्पृशतःऽ; इति । मिथ्याभिमाननिमित्तः शरीरसम्बन्धः । तस्मिन्याथातथ्यदर्शनान्निवृत्ते ऽशरीरत्वम् । तत्र प्रियाप्रिययोरसम्बन्ध आख्यायते । तस्मान्नावगतब्रह्मात्मभावः प्रागिव सांसारिकधर्मभाक् । यस्तु तथा, नासाववगतब्रह्मात्मभाव इति । [क्क्स्_35] अत्रोच्यते --- निश्चिते ऽपि प्रमाणात्तत्त्वे सर्वत्र मिथ्यावभासा निवर्तन्ते, हेतुविशेषादनुवर्तन्ते ऽपि । यथा द्विचन्द्रदिग्विपर्यासादय आप्तवचनविनिश्चितदिक्चन्द्रतत्त्वानाम् । तथा निर्विचिकित्सादाम्नायादवगतात्मतत्त्वस्यानादिमिथ्यादर्शनाभ्यासोपचितबलवत्संस्कारसामर्थ्यान्मिथ्यावभासानुवृत्तिः । तन्निवृत्तये ऽस्त्यन्यदपेक्ष्यम् । तच्च तत्त्वदर्शनाभ्यासो लोकसिद्धः, यज्ञादयश्च शब्दप्रमाणकाः । अभ्यासो हि संस्कारं द्रढयन् पूर्वसंस्कारं प्रतिबध्य स्वकार्यं सन्तनोति । यज्ञादयश्च केनाप्यदृष्टेन प्रकारेण । श्रेयःपरिपन्थिकलुषनिबर्हणद्वारेणेत्यन्ये, नित्यानां कर्मणां दुरितक्षयार्थत्वात् । स्यादेतत् --- अनुवर्तन्तां मिथ्यावभासाः । प्रमाणात्तु निश्चयः । यथातत्त्वं यथानिश्चयं च व्यवहारः । तस्मानावगतात्मतत्त्वस्य काचन शुभाशुभा वा प्रवृत्तिरुपपद्यते । उच्यते --- जाते ऽपि तत्त्वदर्शने, अनाहिते च पटौ संस्कारे, द्रढियसि च मिथ्यादर्शनजे संस्कारे निश्चया अपि मिथ्यार्था भवन्ति । यथा दिङ्मूढस्याननुसंहिताप्तवचसः, प्रागिव प्रवृत्तिदर्शनात् । तथा प्रमितरज्जुभावाया अपि रज्ज्वाः प्रमाणाननुसन्धाने सर्पभ्रान्त्या भयदर्शनम् । तस्माज्जाते ऽपि प्रमाणात्तत्त्वदर्शने अनादिमिथ्यादर्शनाभ्यासपरिनिष्पन्नस्य द्रढीयसः संस्कारस्याभिभवायोच्छेदाय वा तत्त्वदर्शनाभ्यासं मन्यन्ते । तथा च ‘मन्तव्यो निदिध्यासितव्यःऽ; इत्युच्यते । शमदमब्रह्मचर्ययज्ञादिसाधनविधानं च । अन्यथा कस्तदुपदेशार्थः? स्यादेतत् --- ब्रह्मचर्यादिसाधनकरणादेवाम्नायात्तत्त्वविज्ञानम् । तदसत् । शब्दमात्रात्प्रतिपत्तेरुत्पत्तेः । न हि प्राक् साधनविशेषेभ्यस्तत्त्वप्रतिपत्तिपर आम्नायो ऽवाचकः, नाप्यनिश्चायकः, अशेषाशङ्कानिर्मोक्षात् । अन्यथा तदुपदिष्टेषु साधनेष्वपि दुर्लभा प्रतिपत्तिः । अपि चान्यथानिश्चये ऽपि रङ्गगता भरतादयो मिथ्यावभासेन शोकभयादिहेतवः । निश्चिते ऽपि गुडस्य माधुर्ये तत्र मिथ्यातिक्तावभासो ऽवितथ इव दुःखयति, अवितथस्येव तस्यापि धूत्कृत्य त्यागात् । तस्मात्तन्निवृत्तये विनिश्चितब्रह्मात्मभावेनापि साधनान्यपेक्ष्याणि । [क्क्स्_36] यथैव प्रमाणात्तत्त्वाभिव्यक्तौ न मुक्तेः कार्यता, तथाभिव्यक्तिविशेषे ऽपि साधनेभ्यः । श्रुतयस्त्वभ्यासपरिनिष्पत्त्यवस्थाविषयाः शब्दसाधनज्ञानापेक्षा वा भवन्तु, तद्धेतुत्वादुत्तरस्य --- इत्यलमतिविस्तरेण । यदपि पृथक्कार्या एव कर्मविधयो ज्ञानाधिकारमवतारयन्ति, अपाकृतर्णत्रयस्य तत्राधिकारात् --- तदपि न नियोगतः, आश्रमविकल्पस्य स्मरणात् --- ‘तस्स्याश्रमविकल्पमेकेऽ; ‘यमिच्छेत्तमवसेद्ऽ; इति, ‘यदि वेतरथा ब्रह्मचर्यादेव प्रव्रजेद्ऽ; इति श्रवणात् । ‘एतद्ध स्म वै तत्पूर्वे विद्वांसो ऽग्निहोत्रं न जुहवाञ्चक्रिरेऽ; तथा ‘किं प्रजया करिष्यामःऽ; तथा ‘किमर्था वयमध्येष्यामहे किमर्था वयं यक्ष्यामहेऽ; इति कर्मत्यागदर्शनात् । प्रतिपन्नगार्हस्थ्यस्यात्मविद्ययैव कृतकृत्यतां मन्वानस्य ऋणापाकरणं प्रत्यनादृतस्य विहिताकरणनिमित्तस्य पाप्मनो विद्योदयप्रतिबन्धृत्वं दर्शयति --- ‘ऋणानि त्रीण्यपाकृत्यऽ; इति । इदं तु युक्तम् --- कार्यान्तरनिराकाङ्क्षाणामपि कर्मणां संयोगपृथक्त्वात् ‘तमेतं वेदानुवचनेन ब्राह्मणा विविदिषन्ति यज्ञेनऽ; इति विद्याङ्गभावः । सो ऽप्युत्पत्त्यर्थतया, न प्रयाजादिवत्कायोपयोगेन । विद्यायाः कार्यान्तराभावात् । संस्कारपक्षो वा, स्मृतेः । संस्कृतस्य हि विद्योत्पत्तेः । तदुक्तम् --- ‘विहितत्वाच्चाश्रमकर्मापिऽ; इति । ननु दृष्टोत्पाय एव विद्योत्पादः । तत्र दृष्टैवेतिकर्तव्यतापेक्ष्यतां शमदमादिसाधनविशेषश्चित्तविक्षेपस्य विहन्त्री, समहितचित्तस्याभसतो ज्ञानप्रसादोत्पत्तेः । न तु यज्ञादयः, तैर्विनाप्यभ्यासेन तत्सम्भवात् । सत्यम् । तथा चोर्ध्वरेतसां चाश्रमिणां विनापि तैर्विशुद्धविद्योदय इष्यते । किं तु कालकृतो विशेषः । साधनविशेषाद्धि सा क्षिप्रं क्षिप्रतरं च व्यज्यते । तदभावे चिरेण चिरतरेण च । तदुक्तम् --- ‘सर्वापेक्षा च यज्ञादिश्रुतेरश्ववत्ऽ;
