। [क्क्स्_37] एषो ऽर्थः --- ‘यज्ञेन दानेनऽइति श्रवणात्कर्माण्यपेक्ष्यन्ते विद्यायामभ्यासलभ्यायामपि, यथान्तरेणाप्यश्वं ग्रामप्राप्तौ सिद्द्यन्त्यां शैघ्र्यायाक्लेशाय वाश्वो ऽपेक्ष्यते । ननु विद्यारूपं ब्रह्मैव । न विद्या ब्रह्मणो ऽन्या । तच्च नित्यमकार्यम् । तत्र कथं किञ्चिदपेक्ष्येत? उच्यते --- यथोपधानतिरोहितरूपस्फटिकमणिरुपधावकर्षणं स्वरूपाभिव्यक्तये ऽपेक्षते तथेहापि द्रष्टव्यम् । न हि स्फटिकमणेः पूर्वरूपं विनष्टमुपधानसन्निधेः, तदपगमे वान्यदुत्पन्नम् । न ह्यकस्मादनेकविसभागक्षणव्यवहितस्य पूर्वसभागक्षणस्योत्पत्तिः सम्भवति । न ह्यग्निविगमे ऽङ्गारेभ्यः पुनः काष्ठसन्ततिप्रवृत्तिः । तस्माद्यथैवाकार्यं स्फटिकरूपमुपधानावकर्षणमपेक्षते तथात्मरूपमपि । स्यदेतत् --- ज्ञानं तत्र सापेक्षम् । तच्च स्फटिकाद्भिन्नं कार्यम् । पुरुषप्रयत्नो हि तत्र ज्ञानार्थः । किं पुनर्ज्ञानं स्वरूपेणैवार्थितम्, आहोस्विदर्थस्वभावसिद्धये? न तावत्स्वरूपेण, अर्थेन व्यवहारत् । न विज्ञानमात्रनिबन्धनो व्यवहारः, मिथ्याज्ञानेनापि प्रसङ्गात् । अथार्थस्वभाय ज्ञानमर्थ्येत, तदर्थो व्यापारस्तेनार्थितो भवति । न च ज्ञानादर्थे कश्चिद्विकारः, तयोरसंबन्धात् । योग्यदेशतायाः सर्वत्र भावात् । सर्वप्रतिपत्तृणां च विदितत्वप्रसङ्गात् । ध्वस्तानागतेषु च तदसंभवात् । तस्माद्यथातिरोहितमपि तिरोहितमिवाभिव्यज्यत इव प्रयत्नापेक्षम्, तथात्मतत्त्वमप्यतिरोहितं तिरोहितमिव प्रयत्नादभिव्यज्यत इवेति पुष्कलम् । संहृताखिलभेदो ऽतः सामान्यात्मा स वर्णितः । हेमेव पारिहार्यादिभेदसंहारसूचितम्

bhūtārthavāditve 'pyapauruṣeyasya na sāpekṣatvamiti vakṣyate / na ca kāryaniṣṭhānyeva loke vacāṃsi / tathā hi priyākhyānāni ‘diṣṭyā vardhase, putraste jātaḥ'; iti na pravṛttaye nivṛttaye vā, dṛśyante ca sukhotpādanaprayojanāni / na ca sukhī bhava iti tatra pravṛttirupadiśyate, vastusāmarthyādeva tatsiddherupadeśasyānapekṣaṇāt / atha matam --- asti tāvattatra pravṛttiviśeṣaḥ, vacasaśca tatra tātparyam / satyam / utpattyā tātparyam, na pratipattyā / pratipattistu bhūtārthaniṣṭhaiva / na ca bhūtārthaparyavasitasyaiva śabdasya [kks_24] prayojanavattve pravṛttyavadhirvyāpāraḥ kalpayituṃ śakyate / api copāye vāpravṛttaḥ puruṣaḥ pravartyate, ajñātopāyatvādvā upeye prāgapravṛtta upāyaprajñāpanadvāreṇa tatra / iha na tāvadupāye putrajanmani, tasya niṣpannatvāt / nopeye sukhe, tadarthavyāpārāntarābhāvāt / tathā durjanavacanānyapriyākhyānāni viṣādaprayojanāni na pravṛttiṃ nivṛttiṃ vopadiśanti pūrveṇaiva nyāyena / tathā rajjuveṣṭitasya sarpaveṣṭitamātmānaṃ manyamānasya bhayanivṛttaye tattvākhyānaṃ dṛśyate, na tu tatra ‘mā bhaiṣīḥ'; iti niyogaḥ / tatra hi niyogo bhavati, yatra niyogārthaṃ pratibudhya puruṣo buddhipūrvaṃ niyogasāmarthyādicchayā vā punaḥ pravartate nivartate vā / iha tu tattvapratipattimātrānniyogecchānapekṣasya hetvabhāvādeva tasya bhayanivṛttiḥ / na ca bhayanivṛttau puruṣārthatvātsvayaṃpravṛttaḥ puruṣo niyojyaḥ, nāpi tadupāye tattvapratipattau, ‘rajjuḥ, na sarpaḥ'; iti śabdādeva tadutpatteḥ, śabdārthapratipattyuttarakālasya ca vyāpārasya vidhinibandhanatvāt / tathā dūradeśavṛttāntākhyānāni pṛṣṭavatāṃ kutūhalināmautsukyanivṛttyarthāni bhūtārthaparyavasitāni na hānāyopādānāya vā /

yatrāpi (api ca yatrāpi edition) bhūtārthapratipattau hānamupādānaṃ vā saṃbhavati, ‘eṣa pratirodhakavānadhvā, nidhimāneṣa bhūbhāgaḥ'; iti / tatrāpi hānopādānayoḥ śabdo vyāpriyate, bhūtārthopakṣayāt / śabdādbhūtamarthaṃ pratipadya tasya pramāṇāntarāvagatāmupakārahetutāmapakārahetutāṃ vā saṃsmṛtya icchayā pravartate dveṣeṇa nivartate vā / nanu prayoktā buddhipūrvakārī śrotuḥ pravṛttyarthaṃ nivṛttyarthaṃ vā vacanaṃ prayuṅkte / tathā ca pravṛttinivṛttiparyavasitameva / idaṃ hi tatra prayoktavyaṃ na prayujyate ‘na gantavyamanenādhvanā'; tathā ‘gṛhāṇeto nidhim'; iti / naitatsāram / bhūtārthaparyavasitasyāpi vacaso bhūtārthāvagamamukhena pravṛttinivṛttyaṅgabhāvo yato na vyāhanyate pratyakṣādīnāmiva / bhūtārthapramāparisamāptavyāpṛtayaḥ pratyakṣādayo mātrayāpyagocarīkṛtapravṛttinivṛttayo na pravṛttinivṛttyaṅgabhāvaṃ [kks_25] jahati, tathā śabdo 'pīti na kiñcitpraduṣyati / prayoktrabhisaṃhite pravṛttinivṛttī iti cet, na prayoktrabhisaṃdhānācchabdārthatvamapi tu sāmarthyāt / anyathā nidhiprāptidvārikā nānāvidhapuruṣārthāvāptirapi tasyābhisaṃhiteti śabdārthaḥ syāt / yadā ca pravṛttiṃ nivṛttiṃ vābhisaṃdhāya kiñcitpratyakṣādibhirjijñāsyate, tadābhisaṃhite api pravṛttinivṛttī na pratyakṣādiprameye / tadābhisaṃhite api pravṛttinivṛttī na śabdārthau / itaścaitadevam (itaśca tadevam -- edition) --- yatkasyacidupādānabuddhiḥ, anyasyopekṣā / śabdārthatve hi sarveṣāmupādānabuddhireva syāt /

na ca pravartakavākyavyavahārādeva sambandhāvagamaḥ, yena pravṛttiparataivāvagamyeta / anyathāpi darśanāt / ‘devadattaḥ kāṣṭhaiḥ sthālyāmodanaṃ pacati'ityavyutpannakāṣṭhaśabdārtho vyutpannetarapadārtho vyutpannavibhaktyarthaśca yatpacatyarthe karaṇaṃ paśyati tasya kāṣṭhaprātipadikārthatāṃ pratipadyate / tathā harṣaviṣādāśvāsaprayojanebhyaḥ tattvākhyānebhyo harṣādinimitteṣu bhavati vyutpattiḥ / yathaiva hi pravṛttiviśeṣadarśanādviśiṣṭapravṛttipratyayastannimittapratyayo vānumīyate, hetvantarābhāvācchabdānantaryācchabdasya tatra sāmarthyaṃ kalpyate, tathā harṣādyupalabdheḥ harṣādinimittapratyayānumānam, śabdānantaryācca śabdasya tatra sāmarthyakalpanā / pramāṇāntareṇa ca putrajanmano harṣanimittasya tasyāvagatatvādanyasyābhāvāt ‘putraste jātaḥ'itīdaṃ vākyamāptena tatra putrajanmani prayuktamiti pratipadyate / putrajanmaiva cāsmādvākyādanena pratītamityavadhārayati / tadevaṃ prayogapratyayābhyāmasminnarthe vākyasya sāmarthyaṃ pratipadyate /

bhavatu vā loke sarvavacasāṃ pravartakatā, tataśca sambandhāvagamaḥ / tathāpīdaṃ vicāryam --- kiṃ vidhāyakapadavyatirekiṇāṃ padānāṃ svārthamātraparatā, āhosvitkāryārthasaṃsargaparatā, uta padārthamātrasaṃsargaparateti / tatra svārthamātraparyavasāne vākyārthapratyayābhāvaḥ prayogavaiyarthyaṃ ca syāt / tasmādanyārthavyatiṣaṅgaparatā / [kks_26] tāvatā prayogapratyayayorupapattau na viśeṣavyatiṣaṅge pramāṇamasti / yo hi viśeṣavyatiṣaṅgaṃ kalpayati, kalpayatyasāvarthāntaravyatiṣaṅgam / tathā ca vināpi kāryeṇa padārthānāṃ parasparasaṃsargādviśiṣṭabhūtārthapratyayasiddhiḥ / avaśyaṃ caitadevaṃ vijñeyam / anyathā loke vivakṣāparatvātpadārthānvayasya, tadabhāvādvede vedārthapratītirna syāt / api ca sarveṣāṃ kāryānvayitve parasparaṃ padārthānāmanabhisambandhaḥ / tatra na viśiṣṭapadārthaviṣayo niyogaḥ pratīyeta / ekapadārthasādhya eva syāt / atha na viniyogapratyarthī niyogaḥ, viśiṣṭaviṣayatvāt / pūrvastarhi viniyogaḥ, paścānniyogaḥ / kimataḥ? asti niyogātiriktārthānvaye 'pi padasya sāmarthyaṃ niyogānapekṣaṃ ca, parasparānvitānāṃ iyogānvayāt / na ca niyogākāṅkṣānibandhanaḥ saṃsarga iti pratipādayiṣyate / anadhigatamapi ramāṇāntareṇānadhigatasambandhaṃ ca svaśabdena śakyaṃ śabdena nirūpayituṃ viśeṣapratiṣedhamukhena, viśeṣaśabdānāṃ nañaśca yathāyathamarthairviditasaṅgatitvāt / tathā cetthameva tadupadiśyate ‘asthūlam'iti sarvaviśeṣātigam / etatkathayati --- bhedaprapañcavilayadvāreṇeti / etacca vakṣyata iti /

anyo 'rthaḥ / yaduktam --- pratyastamitasakalaviśeṣaṃ tattvaṃ pratipatterevāviṣaya iti, tatrocyate --- viśeṣanivṛttyaiva tacchabdena buddhau nidhīyate, suvarṇatattvavat / na hi suvarṇatattvaṃ piṇḍarucakādisaṃsthānabhedopaplavarahitaṃ dṛśyate / na ca ta eva suvarṇatattvam, tatparityāge 'pi bhāvātsaṃsthānāntare / atha cādṛṣṭasaṃsthānabhedopaplavavivekamapi buddhyā bhedāpohadvāreṇa svayaṃ pratīyate, parasmai ca pratipādyate / sa eṣa pratipattikramaḥ śrutyaiva darśitaḥ --- ‘sa eṣa neti neti'; iti / tathānyaiḥ --- ‘satyamākṛtisaṃhāre yadante vyavatiṣṭhate'; / tathāparaiḥ --- ‘adhyāropāpavādābhyāṃ niṣprapañcaṃ prapañcyate'; iti /

idamidānīṃ vicāryate --- kiṃ kṛtsna āmnāyo bhedaprapañcavilayamukhena brahma nirūpayati, āhosvitkaścidasyaikadeśaḥ? tatra kecidāhuḥ --- sarvatraivāmnāye [kks_27] kvacitkasyacidbhedasya pravilayo gamyate, yathā ‘svargakāmo yajeta'; iti śarīrātmabhāvasya pravilayaḥ / atra hi dehavyatiriktasvargopabhogasamartho 'dhikārī gamyate, tena dehātmabhāvapravilayaḥ / tathā ‘godohanena paśukāmasya praṇayet'ityadhikṛtādhikārādadhikāribhedapravilayaḥ / tathā vidhiniṣedhacodanāsvapi naisargikīṇāṃ rāgādinibandhanānāṃ pravṛttīnāṃ pravilayaḥ / niṣedheṣu sākṣāt, vidhiṣu pravṛttyantarniyogena / loke 'pyanabhipretātpathaḥ sākṣādvā nivāraṇam, pathyantaropadeśena vā / evaṃ ca rāgādinibandhananaisargikapravṛttibhedavilayadvāreṇa dṛṣṭenaiva karmavidhaya ātmajñānādhikāropayoginaḥ / tathā hi --- śāntasya dāntasya samāhitasya cātmani darśanamupadiśyate / śakyaṃ ca / na hi viṣayairākṛṣyamāṇastadupāyapravṛttikṛtacetāḥ śaknotyātmani samādhātum / naisargikībhyastu pravṛttibhya uparato niyatamānasa ātmadarśanenādhikriyate, sāmarthyāt /

anye (ms a; anye tu edition) manyante --- anavāptakāmaḥ kāmopahatamanā na paramādvaitadarśanayogyaḥ / karmabhistu kṛtakāmanibarhaṇaḥ sahasrasaṃvatsaraparyantaiḥ prājāpatyātpadātparamādvaitamātmānaṃ pratipadyata iti / ubhayorapi pakṣayoranayoḥ kṛtsna āmnāya ātmajñānaikaparyavasāyī / anyeṣāṃ darśanam --- pṛthakkāryā eva santaḥ karmavidhaya ātmajñānādhikāramavatārayanti puruṣam, anapākṛtarṇatrayasya tatrānadhikārāt --- ‘ṛṇāni trīṇyapākṛtya mano mokṣe niveśayet'; iti / anye tu saṃyogapṛthaktvena sarvakarmaṇāmevātmajñānādhikārānupraveśamāhuḥ ‘vividiṣanti yajñena'iti śruteḥ, ‘yena kenacana yajetāpi darvīhomenānupahatamanā eva bhavati'; iti ca / [kks_28] anye tu puruṣasaṃskāratayātmajñānādhikārasaṃsparśaṃ karmaṇāṃ varṇayanti --- ‘mahāyajñaiśca yajñaiśca brāhmīyaṃ kriyate tanuḥ', ‘yasyaite catvāriṃśatsaṃskārā aṣṭāvātmaguṇāḥ'; iti ca / anye tvetadeva viparītaṃ varṇayanti, ātmajñānameva kartṛsaṃskāratayā karmādhikārānupraveśīti / anye tu parasparavirodhinoḥ karmātmajñānayoḥ dvaitādvaitaviṣayatvenāsaṃbandha eveti manyante /

tatra na tāvatprathamaḥ kalpaḥ / na hi karmādividhayaḥ svavākyasamadhigatasvargādikāryāḥ kāryāntaramapekṣante / nāpyātmajñānavidhiryathoditabrahmacaryādisādhananirākāṅkṣaḥ karmavidhīnapekṣate / tatra kuta ekādhikāratvam / yadi manyetānavagatakāryā (atha anavagata@ -- edition) eva karmādividhayaḥ, svargādīnāṃ guṇatvena saṃbandhāditi, svargakāmādhikaraṇamasmai vyācakṣīta / api ca sarvavidhiniṣedhānāṃ nāmarūpapravilayakāryāpavargitve jantūnāmabhyudayavinipātā akarmanimittā ākasmikāḥ syuḥ / tathāpavargo 'pi syāditi vaiyarthyaṃ śāstrasyāpi / atha svargādikāryadvāreṇa karmavidhīnāṃ jñānādhikārānupraveśitā mārgagrāmagamanopadeśānāmivābhimatanagaragamanopadeśānupraveśitvam / tadasat / yuktaṃ mārgagrāmaprāpteranabhimatadeśaprāptyupadeśānupraveśitvam / na hi mārgagrāmopadeśeṣu puruṣārthaprāptiḥ / ataḥ sākāṅkṣatvādyatra puruṣārthaprāptiḥ, tamanupraviśanti / na tvevaṃ karmavidhiṣu puruṣārthasyālābhaḥ, svargādīnāṃ puruṣeṇārthyamānatvāt / tatra ca nairākāṅkṣye kathamanyānupraveśaḥ? atha matam --- yadopacchandya nīyata uttarottaragrāmaguṇopadarśanenābhipretaṃ deśam, tadā pūrvagrāmopadeśāḥ prāptābhimatakāryā upadeśāntarānupraveśinaśceti / yuktaṃ tatrāpi pramāṇāntareṇa vakturabhiprāyādhigamāt / pramāṇāntareṇa hi tatredamadhigatam --- etaddeśaprāptāvidamasya samīhitaṃ vaktuḥ saṃpadyate, tasmādidamasya vivakṣitamiti / na tu śabdavṛttimātrānusāreṇa (śabdapravṛttimātrā@ ms a; śabdavṛttamātrā@ -- edition) / itaścaitadevam --- [kks_29] yatpratigrāmaṃ vaktuḥ śrotuśca satyāmarthaprāptau pramāṇāntareṇānadhigate paradeśaprāptyabhiprāye pūrvopadeśān pūrvārthāneva pārśvasthāḥ pratipattāraḥ pratipadyante, paradeśopadeśaṃ ca svārthaniṣṭham / yadyapi vastusthityā pūrvopadeśārthāḥ paropakāriṇaḥ, tathāpi na śabdasya tātparyam, dravyārjanādividheriva kratuvidhyarthopakāre 'pi / śabdavṛttānusāreṇa ceha tātparyam, pramāṇāntarābhāvāditi /

api cādhvagrāmopadeśānāṃ tatparatvādhyavasāyenaiva tatra gamanamarthaprāptiśca / tatra paradeśaprāptiparatāyāṃ tu na niyogatastatra gamanam / mārgāntareṇāpi tatprāptervivakṣitatvādgacchet / na ca niyogato 'rthaprāptiḥ, anyapareṣu prayojanaśruterapyarthavādatvāt / tadiha yadi vidhiniṣedhāḥ kāryāntaraparāḥ, na svargādikāryāḥ / na khalu svargādikāryaṃ prayājādikāryatulyam, yena kāryāntaramanupatet / kathaṃ ca dṛṣṭenaivātmajñānādhikāropakāriṇa iti vaktavyam / yadi tāvadrāgādyākṣiptadṛṣṭārthapravṛttinirodhena, bhavatu pratiṣedhānāmevaṃbhāvaḥ / karmavidhayastu kathaṃ nirundhantīti vācyam / nahi te parisaṃkhyāyakāḥ, na ca niyāmakāḥ, atyantamaprāptārthatvāt / prāptārtho hi vidhiranyanivṛttiphalo vijñāyate / na ca tulyakāryatvena virodhena nivṛttiḥ / aniyatakālaphalā hi naiyogikyaḥ pravṛttayo 'dṛṣṭārthāḥ / dṛṣṭārthāstu rāgādyākṣiptāḥ svābhāvikyaḥ / na ca sāṅgrahaṇyāḥ sevāyāśca grāmopāyatve kaścidvirodhaḥ, etāvati pramāṇatvācchāstrasya / tatra yugapatkrameṇa vā phalabhūmārthinaḥ sevāsāṅgrahaṇyāvanutiṣṭhataḥ ko virodhaḥ? api ca sakaladṛṣṭārthapravṛttinirodhe niyoganiṣṭhā api pravṛttayo nirudhyeran, anārjitadhanasya sādhanavikalasya tāsāmasambhavāt / api ca tulye kāmopāyatve dṛṣṭādṛṣṭārthapravṛttyorna na viśeṣo rāgādyākṣiptatve / tathā hi --- ‘svargakāmaḥ'iti rāgādyākṣiptapravṛttyanuvādena viśeṣavidhānam / tathā ca prapañcābhiniveśe tulye kena viśeṣeṇa ekātmānuguṇyaṃ bhajate, tadvirodhinyaparā? kāmākṣepo hyaviśiṣṭo manasaḥ / atha kāmopāyatvameva na manyeta, varṇitamākasmikatvam, uktaśca nyāyaḥ pratyuddhriyeta / tulyakāryanibandhanatvācca virodhādyā [kks_30] nirodhāśaṅkā sā dūrato nirastāvakāśā syāt / atha kāmaprāptyā karmavidhayaḥ kāmān pravilāpayanto jñānādhikārānuguṇāḥ / yathoktam ---

'yadā sarve pramucyate kāmā ye 'sya hṛdi śritāḥ /
atha martyo 'mṛto bhavatyatra brahma samaśnute'; //

iti /

tadapyasat / yato na kāmaprāptyā kāmapravilayaḥ, api tu doṣaparibhāvanābhuvā prasaṅkhyānena / kalayāpi cetkāmairmanaḥ saṃspṛśyate hriyata eva hāribhiḥ / uktaṃ hi --- ‘na jātu kāmaḥ kāmānāmupabhogena śāmyati', ‘bhogābhyāsamanu vivardhante rāgāḥ kauśalāni cendriyāṇām'; iti ca / anupāyatvādapi tāvadayaṃ kāmebhyo vinivarteta / nikhilakleśopaśamarūpaṃ cātmajñānaṃ saṃśrayeta / karmavidhinidarśitavividhopāyastu tāneva prakṛtahāriṇo bhogānabhiniviśeta / tatpravilayarūpācātmajñānādudvijeta / śruto 'pi hyātmanyānando 'nanubhūto nānubhūtaviṣayanibandhanānandābhilāṣaṃ mandīkartumapyutsahate, prāgevocchettum / tasmātprasaṃkhyānamevaikaḥ kāmanibarhaṇopāyaḥ, karmavidhayastu viparyayahetavaḥ / yadapi --- sarvatraivāmnāye kvacitkasyacidbhedasya vilayaḥ, yathā ‘svargakāmo yajeta'; iti śarīrātmatvapravilaya iti / tadapyasat, anidaṃparatvāt / na hīdaṃ vacanaṃ dehavyatiriktātmatattvāvabodhaparam / athānyaparādapyarthādevamavasīyata iti, tadapi hastini dṛṣṭe tatpadena tasyānumānamiva / sākṣāddhi ‘asthūlam'ityupakramya dehendriyavilayo darśitaḥ, arthācca kāmādigrantheḥ kāṭhinyaṃ vaidikaṃ syāditi /

dvitīyo 'pi kalpo varṇitādeva kāmānāṃ kāmanibarhaṇasāmarthyābhāvātsvakāryanirākāṅkṣāṇāṃ cānyānupraveśe pramāṇabhāvādasamañjasaḥ /

ekādhikāratve tu samuccayaḥ sarvakarmaṇāṃ syāt / sa cāśakya iti / [kks_31] ye 'pi viparyayeṇa jñānakarmaṇorekādhikāratvamāhuḥ, tairapi jñānasya karmasambandhe pramāṇaṃ vaktavyam / na tāvat ‘brīhīn prokṣati'; iti yathā / tatra hi prakaraṇātprakṛtakarmāpūrvalakṣaṇāparo brīhiśabdaḥ svasvarūpa ānarthakyātprakṛtāpūrvasambandhaṃ bodhayati / nāpi yathā ‘yasya parṇamayī juhūrbhavati'; iti / tatra hi juhvādyavyabhicaritakarmasambandhamasatyapi prakaraṇe karmopasthāpayati / tatra vākyenaiva sambandhaḥ / ātmajñānaṃ tu na prakaraṇe śrutam / nāpyātmāvyabhicaritakarmasambandhaḥ / tenāsya karmasambandho durvacaḥ / tathā cājñāte pārārthye yā nāma phalaśrutirna sārthavādinī bhavatīti pṛthagadhikāratvam / atha matam --- vartamānāpadeśāt ‘na sa (ca --edition) punarāvartate'iti kāmopabandhābhāvātphalaṃ vipariṇamayya kalpayitavyam / tacca tadākāṅkṣāyāṃ satyām / na tu dṛṣṭe sati tadākāṅkṣā / asti cātmajñānavidherdṛṣṭaphalaṃ dehāntaropabhogyaphaleṣu karmasu pravṛttiḥ / tasmātsvādhyāyādhyayanavidhivadātmajñānavidhiḥ / svādhyāyādhyayanavidhirhi dṛṣṭakarmāvabodhanirākāṅkṣo nārthavādataḥ phalaṃ prārthayate, tathātmajñānavidhirapīti nādhikārāntaram / tadapyasat / yato 'yamanya evaupaniṣadaḥ puruṣo vedānteṣu jijñāsyate / na ca tajjñānaṃ karmapravṛttihetuḥ / na hi tasya kartṛtvabhoktṛtve / evaṃ hyāha --- ‘na tadaśnāti kiñcana'; ‘anaśnannanyo 'bhicākaśīti'; iti / yastu karmaṇāṃ kartā bhoktā ca, sa eva sarvapratyakṣasiddhaḥ / na śabdaprameyaḥ / nanu jīvaparamātmanorekatvameva / evaṃ hyāha --- ‘anena jīvenātmanā'; iti / satyam / tasyaiva tu jīvasyaivamavidyānubandhaṃ pratyakṣāvaseyaṃ rūpam, tacca karmapravṛttihetuḥ / na ca tacchabdamapekṣate / yattu svayaṃprakāśaṃ sarvavibhāgaśūnyaṃ tacchabdājjñātumiṣyate / tacca karmapravṛttivirodhi / tajjñānasya kathaṃ karmapravṛttirdṛṣṭaṃ prayojanaṃ syāt? tathā hi --- brahmānandamekamadvayamātmānaṃ vijānataḥ kimarthaṃ kathaṃ vā pravṛttiḥ syāt, āptakāmatvātsādhanādyupāyābhāvācca? syādetat --- aupaniṣadapuruṣajñānameva karmāṅgatvena coditam ‘yadeva vidyayā karoti śraddhayopaniṣadā [kks_32] tadeva vīryavattaraṃ bhavati'; iti / tathā ‘yo vā etadakṣaraṃ gārgyaviditvāsmiṃlloke juhoti'ityupakramya yāgādiphalasyāntavattādarśanena brahmavidyāyāstādarthyaṃ darśitam / ‘taṃ vidyākarmaṇī samanvārabhete'; iti ca vidyākarmaṇoḥ sāhityaṃ darśitam / pūrvaṃ tāvatprakṛtodgīthaviṣayam, ‘omityetadakṣaramudgītham'; ityupakramāt / pareṇāpi karmanindayākṣarajñānastutiḥ / vidyākarmaṇośca samanvārambho bhedena --- vidyāvantaṃ vidyānvārabhate karmavantaṃ karmeti / tasmādevamapi na karmajñānayorekādhikāratvamiti /

ye 'pi virodhādasambandha eva karmajñānayoḥ ‘dvaitaviṣayaṃ karma, advaitaviṣayaṃ jñānam'iti manyante, teṣāmanutpāda evādvaitajñānasya prasajyate, pramāṇādivibhāgādvaitapratipattyorvirodhāt / athopāyopeyayorayaugapadyādavirodhaḥ, pralīyata evādvaitapratipattau sarvo vibhāgaḥ / na ca virodho 'nupāyatvaṃ vā, upāyasya pūrvakālatvāt, tadā ca tasyāpralīnatvāt / bheda eva cābhedapratipattāvupāyaḥ / na tarhi karmabhirapi virodhaḥ, upāyatvādeva / syādetat --- asādhyatvādbrahmaṇo na karmaṇāmupayogo vidyate / śrūyate ca --- ‘nāstyakṛtaḥ kṛtena'; iti / na ca jñānotpattāvupayogaḥ, jñānasya pramāṇādhīnatvāt / na ca jñānasahakārīṇi karmāṇi, jñānasya sādhyāntarābhāvāt / na tasya mokṣaḥ sādhyaḥ, anityatvaprasaṅgāt / atha bandhahetuvicchedaḥ sādhya iti tasmin vicchinne tadabhāvānmucyate / kaḥ punarbandhahetuḥ? anādyavidyā, na tarhi pṛthaktadvicchedaḥ sādhyaḥ, yato vidyodaya evāvidyāvyāvṛttiḥ / syādetat --- bhavatvagrahaṇalakṣaṇāvidyāvyāvṛttirvidyotpādaḥ, yato bhāva evābhāvavyāvṛttiḥ / na ca vidyotpāda eva viparyāsajñānavyāvṛttiḥ / na khalu bhāvāntaraṃ bhāvāntaravyāvṛttiḥ / na ca parasparābhāvātmāno bhāvāḥ, abhāvatvaprasaṅgāt / yadi manyeta --- tattvāgrahaṇanimitto viparyāso nimittanivṛttau svayameva nivartiṣyate, tacca na / na khalvagrahaṇamabhāvaḥ kasyacinnimittam, mūrcchādiṣu [kks_33] prasaṅgāt / kiṃ tarhi nimittam? ‘anādiraprayojanā cāvidyā'; ityuktam / tatra ca hetvanuyogo niravakāśaḥ / viparyāsatatsaṃskārayośca parasparahetuphalabhāvena vyavasthānānna doṣaḥ / ato viparyayajñānasya nivṛttirvidyayā sādhyeti tatra jñānasya sahakāryapekṣā syāt / etacca vārtam / na khalu śuktikādiṣu viparyāsapurassaraṃ samupajātasamyagjñānāstannivṛttaye pṛthak prayatante, sahakāri vānyadapekṣante / yato virodhibhāvāntarotpāda eva pūrvapradhvaṃsaḥ, na śūnyam / anyathā na pradhvaṃso hetumān syāt / virodhinī ca vidyā viparyayajñānasya / tadutpattau viparyāso naṣṭa eva bhavati / athocyeta --- karmāṇi bandhahetavaḥ / tatkṣayo jñānātsahakārisavyapekṣāditi / tacca pramṛṣṭāśeṣaviśeṣaviśuddhajñānodaye kutaḥ sambhavaḥ? tathā ca viparyāsasaṃśayābhyāṃ tulyavatprasaṃkhyātāni karmāṇi ---

'bhidyante hṛdayagranthiśchidyante sarvasaṃśayāḥ /

kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare'; //

iti /

atha vijñānavaimalyāyānyāpekṣā / sāpi mudhā, saṃśayaviparyāsayorjñānamalayoḥ pramāṇotthavijñāne 'saṃbhavāt / atha matam --- śābdajñānādanyadapi pratyakṣaṃ jñānamiṣyate vigalitavibhāgodgrāhaṃ sarvavikalpātītam / tasya hi brahma gocaraḥ, na śābdasya vibhaktapadārthasaṃsargodgrāhiṇaḥ / tadutpattau karmopāsanādyapekṣeti / kaḥ punarasya viśeṣaḥ, yena tadarthyate? spaṣṭābhatvam, na tasyopayogaḥ / jñānaṃ hi jñeyābhivyāptaye, śābdajñāne cotpanna āptameva jñeyam / pramiteḥ pratyakṣaparatvāttatra ca nairākāṅkṣyāttadarthyata iti cet, etadadhigate prameye kimanyadākāṅkṣyeta? pramāṇāntaramiti cenna, prameyasiddhyarthatvāttadākāṅkṣāyāḥ / punaḥ siddhyarthamiti cenna, pūrvasmādapyasakṛttatsiddheḥ / siddhasya ca siddhyapekṣāyāṃ na heturasti / upāyāntarasadbhāvaścet, upāyāntaraṃ tarhyapekṣeta / prameye tu nairākāṅkṣyameva / prītiviśeṣaścet, sa pūrvapramāṇajādapi [kks_34] darśanātsidhyati / na tatsiddhyarthaṃ pramāṇāntaram / pratyakṣadṛṣṭamapītaraistatsambhavājjijñāsyeta, viśeṣābhāvāt / niścāyakatvamitareṣāmapi, pramāṇabhāvāt / hānādiyogyaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣam, sannikṛṣṭārthatvāt, netarāṇīti cet / sannikarṣahetustarhyapekṣyatām / na pramāṇam, siddhatvātpramāyāḥ / prakṛte ca prameye naiṣa viśeṣo 'sti / sāmānyaviṣayāḥ śabdādayaḥ, viśeṣaviṣayaṃ pratyakṣamiti cet / anadhigata eva tarhi śabdena pratyakṣasya viṣayaḥ / bāḍham / uktametat --- na śābdasya jñānasya viṣayo brahmeti / yadi tarhi na śabdenādhigataṃ brahma, kathaṃ tasminnupāsanā pravartatām? na cānyasminnupāsyamāne 'nyatsākṣādbhavati / kasya ca rūpasya sākṣātkaraṇāya yajñādividhānam? śabdopadarśitaniratiśayānandāpahatapāpmādirūpabrahmasvabhāvasyātmanaḥ sākṣātkaraṇāya yajñādividhirupapadyate / aviditapuruṣārtharūpe tadviparītarūpe nirvicikitsātpramāṇātprakaṭatāṃ prāpte nāparamapekṣyamasti / nanvavagate 'pi ‘tattvamasi'; iti śabdādbrahmātmabhāve prāgiva sāṃsārikadharmadarśāttannivṛttaye bhavatyanyāpekṣā / naitatsāram / kathaṃ khalvavagatabrahmātmabhāvo viditātmayāthātathyo mithyādarśananimittairdharmairyujyate? śrūyate ca --- ‘brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati'; iti / na ca brahmaṇyapahatapāpmani teṣāmavakāśaḥ / tathā ---

‘ātmānaṃ cedvijānīyādayamasmīti pūruṣaḥ /

kimicchan kasya kāmāya śarīramanusañjvaret'; //

tathā ‘aśarīraṃ vāva santaṃ na priyāpriye spṛśataḥ'; iti /

mithyābhimānanimittaḥ śarīrasambandhaḥ / tasminyāthātathyadarśanānnivṛtte 'śarīratvam / tatra priyāpriyayorasambandha ākhyāyate / tasmānnāvagatabrahmātmabhāvaḥ prāgiva sāṃsārikadharmabhāk / yastu tathā, nāsāvavagatabrahmātmabhāva iti / [kks_35] atrocyate --- niścite 'pi pramāṇāttattve sarvatra mithyāvabhāsā nivartante, hetuviśeṣādanuvartante 'pi / yathā dvicandradigviparyāsādaya āptavacanaviniścitadikcandratattvānām / tathā nirvicikitsādāmnāyādavagatātmatattvasyānādimithyādarśanābhyāsopacitabalavatsaṃskārasāmarthyānmithyāvabhāsānuvṛttiḥ / tannivṛttaye 'styanyadapekṣyam / tacca tattvadarśanābhyāso lokasiddhaḥ, yajñādayaśca śabdapramāṇakāḥ / abhyāso hi saṃskāraṃ draḍhayan pūrvasaṃskāraṃ pratibadhya svakāryaṃ santanoti / yajñādayaśca kenāpyadṛṣṭena prakāreṇa / śreyaḥparipanthikaluṣanibarhaṇadvāreṇetyanye, nityānāṃ karmaṇāṃ duritakṣayārthatvāt / syādetat --- anuvartantāṃ mithyāvabhāsāḥ / pramāṇāttu niścayaḥ / yathātattvaṃ yathāniścayaṃ ca vyavahāraḥ / tasmānāvagatātmatattvasya kācana śubhāśubhā vā pravṛttirupapadyate / ucyate --- jāte 'pi tattvadarśane, anāhite ca paṭau saṃskāre, draḍhiyasi ca mithyādarśanaje saṃskāre niścayā api mithyārthā bhavanti / yathā diṅmūḍhasyānanusaṃhitāptavacasaḥ, prāgiva pravṛttidarśanāt / tathā pramitarajjubhāvāyā api rajjvāḥ pramāṇānanusandhāne sarpabhrāntyā bhayadarśanam / tasmājjāte 'pi pramāṇāttattvadarśane anādimithyādarśanābhyāsapariniṣpannasya draḍhīyasaḥ saṃskārasyābhibhavāyocchedāya vā tattvadarśanābhyāsaṃ manyante / tathā ca ‘mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ'; ityucyate / śamadamabrahmacaryayajñādisādhanavidhānaṃ ca / anyathā kastadupadeśārthaḥ? syādetat --- brahmacaryādisādhanakaraṇādevāmnāyāttattvavijñānam / tadasat / śabdamātrātpratipatterutpatteḥ / na hi prāk sādhanaviśeṣebhyastattvapratipattipara āmnāyo 'vācakaḥ, nāpyaniścāyakaḥ, aśeṣāśaṅkānirmokṣāt / anyathā tadupadiṣṭeṣu sādhaneṣvapi durlabhā pratipattiḥ / api cānyathāniścaye 'pi raṅgagatā bharatādayo mithyāvabhāsena śokabhayādihetavaḥ / niścite 'pi guḍasya mādhurye tatra mithyātiktāvabhāso 'vitatha iva duḥkhayati, avitathasyeva tasyāpi dhūtkṛtya tyāgāt / tasmāttannivṛttaye viniścitabrahmātmabhāvenāpi sādhanānyapekṣyāṇi / [kks_36] yathaiva pramāṇāttattvābhivyaktau na mukteḥ kāryatā, tathābhivyaktiviśeṣe 'pi sādhanebhyaḥ / śrutayastvabhyāsapariniṣpattyavasthāviṣayāḥ śabdasādhanajñānāpekṣā vā bhavantu, taddhetutvāduttarasya --- ityalamativistareṇa /

yadapi pṛthakkāryā eva karmavidhayo jñānādhikāramavatārayanti, apākṛtarṇatrayasya tatrādhikārāt --- tadapi na niyogataḥ, āśramavikalpasya smaraṇāt --- ‘tassyāśramavikalpameke'; ‘yamicchettamavased'; iti, ‘yadi vetarathā brahmacaryādeva pravrajed'; iti śravaṇāt / ‘etaddha sma vai tatpūrve vidvāṃso 'gnihotraṃ na juhavāñcakrire'; tathā ‘kiṃ prajayā kariṣyāmaḥ'; tathā ‘kimarthā vayamadhyeṣyāmahe kimarthā vayaṃ yakṣyāmahe'; iti karmatyāgadarśanāt / pratipannagārhasthyasyātmavidyayaiva kṛtakṛtyatāṃ manvānasya ṛṇāpākaraṇaṃ pratyanādṛtasya vihitākaraṇanimittasya pāpmano vidyodayapratibandhṛtvaṃ darśayati --- ‘ṛṇāni trīṇyapākṛtya'; iti /

idaṃ tu yuktam --- kāryāntaranirākāṅkṣāṇāmapi karmaṇāṃ saṃyogapṛthaktvāt ‘tametaṃ vedānuvacanena brāhmaṇā vividiṣanti yajñena'; iti vidyāṅgabhāvaḥ / so 'pyutpattyarthatayā, na prayājādivatkāyopayogena / vidyāyāḥ kāryāntarābhāvāt / saṃskārapakṣo vā, smṛteḥ / saṃskṛtasya hi vidyotpatteḥ / taduktam --- ‘vihitatvāccāśramakarmāpi'; iti /

nanu dṛṣṭotpāya eva vidyotpādaḥ / tatra dṛṣṭaivetikartavyatāpekṣyatāṃ śamadamādisādhanaviśeṣaścittavikṣepasya vihantrī, samahitacittasyābhasato jñānaprasādotpatteḥ / na tu yajñādayaḥ, tairvināpyabhyāsena tatsambhavāt / satyam / tathā cordhvaretasāṃ cāśramiṇāṃ vināpi tairviśuddhavidyodaya iṣyate / kiṃ tu kālakṛto viśeṣaḥ / sādhanaviśeṣāddhi sā kṣipraṃ kṣiprataraṃ ca vyajyate / tadabhāve cireṇa ciratareṇa ca / taduktam --- ‘sarvāpekṣā ca yajñādiśruteraśvavat'; / [kks_37] eṣo 'rthaḥ --- ‘yajñena dānena'iti śravaṇātkarmāṇyapekṣyante vidyāyāmabhyāsalabhyāyāmapi, yathāntareṇāpyaśvaṃ grāmaprāptau siddyantyāṃ śaighryāyākleśāya vāśvo 'pekṣyate /

nanu vidyārūpaṃ brahmaiva / na vidyā brahmaṇo 'nyā / tacca nityamakāryam / tatra kathaṃ kiñcidapekṣyeta? ucyate --- yathopadhānatirohitarūpasphaṭikamaṇirupadhāvakarṣaṇaṃ svarūpābhivyaktaye 'pekṣate tathehāpi draṣṭavyam / na hi sphaṭikamaṇeḥ pūrvarūpaṃ vinaṣṭamupadhānasannidheḥ, tadapagame vānyadutpannam / na hyakasmādanekavisabhāgakṣaṇavyavahitasya pūrvasabhāgakṣaṇasyotpattiḥ sambhavati / na hyagnivigame 'ṅgārebhyaḥ punaḥ kāṣṭhasantatipravṛttiḥ / tasmādyathaivākāryaṃ sphaṭikarūpamupadhānāvakarṣaṇamapekṣate tathātmarūpamapi / syadetat --- jñānaṃ tatra sāpekṣam / tacca sphaṭikādbhinnaṃ kāryam / puruṣaprayatno hi tatra jñānārthaḥ / kiṃ punarjñānaṃ svarūpeṇaivārthitam, āhosvidarthasvabhāvasiddhaye? na tāvatsvarūpeṇa, arthena vyavahārat / na vijñānamātranibandhano vyavahāraḥ, mithyājñānenāpi prasaṅgāt / athārthasvabhāya jñānamarthyeta, tadartho vyāpārastenārthito bhavati / na ca jñānādarthe kaścidvikāraḥ, tayorasaṃbandhāt / yogyadeśatāyāḥ sarvatra bhāvāt / sarvapratipattṛṇāṃ ca viditatvaprasaṅgāt / dhvastānāgateṣu ca tadasaṃbhavāt / tasmādyathātirohitamapi tirohitamivābhivyajyata iva prayatnāpekṣam, tathātmatattvamapyatirohitaṃ tirohitamiva prayatnādabhivyajyata iveti puṣkalam /

saṃhṛtākhilabhedo 'taḥ sāmānyātmā sa varṇitaḥ /
hemeva pārihāryādibhedasaṃhārasūcitam
units.translation:
Although the Veda reports facts, it is not dependent on some other authority, since it has no human author; this will be explained. Nor are all statements in ordinary life directed toward an action. Consider good news such as, “How fortunate you are—your child has been born!” It does not tell anyone to act or refrain from acting, yet it plainly serves to produce happiness. It does not instruct the listener, “Be happy,” because happiness follows from the fact itself, and no instruction is needed.

Someone may say that such a statement does have a particular effect, and that the speaker’s purpose lies there. That is true: its purpose lies in producing the utterance, not in producing an act of understanding. The understanding itself rests on the fact being reported. If the statement’s only purpose were to give a factual understanding, it would not be possible to imagine that the word’s operation must culminate in an injunction in order for the statement to be useful. Further, a person is prompted to act only toward a means or an end that has not yet been pursued: either the person does not know the means, or has not yet pursued the end, and is prompted by an explanation of the means. Here the report does not prompt the listener toward the means, the birth of the child, since that has already occurred; nor toward the end, happiness, since no further action is needed to obtain it. In the same way, unpleasant reports by a bad person, whose purpose is to cause sorrow, do not instruct the listener to act or refrain from acting; the same reasoning applies.

Likewise, someone who has been wrapped in a rope and thinks a snake is coiled around him is told the truth so that his fear will cease. No injunction such as “Do not be afraid” is given. An injunction is present only when someone, understanding what is enjoined, acts or refrains again through the force of the injunction or from desire. Here fear ceases merely from understanding what is true, without any need to want or follow an injunction. Since the person acts spontaneously because the fear has ended, there is no reason to enjoin him to stop being afraid, even though ending fear is a human good. Nor need he be enjoined to understand the means to that end, since the understanding “It is a rope, not a snake” arises from the words themselves. Activity that follows the understanding of a word’s meaning may be governed by an injunction, but not the understanding itself.

Reports of events in distant places likewise answer the curiosity of people who have asked a question and remove their uncertainty. They convey facts, not instructions to take or abandon something. Even where understanding a fact can lead to taking or avoiding something—for example, “This road has robbers,” or “This place contains treasure”—the words function in those actions only after the fact is understood. The listener first understands the fact from the words, then recalls, from another means of knowledge, that it is helpful or harmful, and then acts from desire or refrains from aversion.

Someone may object that the speaker deliberately uses a statement to make the hearer act or refrain, and that therefore the statement must culminate in action or restraint. This is not sound. A statement that reports a fact can serve as a part of an action or restraint through the understanding of that fact, just as perception and other means of knowledge can serve them, without having those aims as their own subject matter. The speaker’s intention does not make action or restraint the meaning of the words; their meaning is determined by their power to convey. Otherwise, because the speaker intends the hearer to obtain the treasure and all the many human goods that follow from it, all those results would become the meaning of the sentence. And when someone asks about a matter with the intention of acting or refraining, even though perception and other means of knowledge may establish it, the intended action or restraint is not itself what those means establish. Nor is it the meaning of the words, even when the speaker intends it.

There is another reason. One person may understand an object as something to take, while another treats it with indifference. If action or restraint were the meaning of the words, everyone would have to understand the object as something to take. Nor is the relation between words and things learned only from the use of sentences that prompt action, as will be shown: it is also seen in other kinds of statements. A person who does not know the meaning of “wood,” but knows the other words and grammatical forms in “Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with wood,” sees the wood serving as an instrument in the act of cooking and thereby understands that “wood” names its object. In the same way, a person learns the relation between a factual statement and its words from accounts that produce happiness, sorrow, or reassurance. When one hears true news of a child’s birth, for instance, one understands that the reliable speaker used “your child has been born” to report that birth, and that this is what the sentence has conveyed. By seeing the use and the resulting understanding, one learns the sentence’s power to convey that fact.

Even if one grants that every statement in ordinary life prompts action, and that this is how the relation between words and their meanings is learned, a further question remains. Do words other than those that express an injunction each convey only their separate meanings? Do they convey those meanings in relation to an action? Or do they convey the meanings in relation to one another? If they culminate only in their individual meanings, there would be no understanding of the sentence, and its use would be pointless. They must therefore connect with other meanings. But if such a connection is enough to explain how the sentence is understood, there is no evidence requiring a special relation to an action. Anyone who supposes a special relation to an action must also accept a connection between the words’ meanings, and that alone suffices for the understanding of a factual statement, without an injunction. This must be admitted. Otherwise, because in ordinary language the words all connect only with action, their meanings would not connect with one another, and no sentence meaning would be understood. An injunction concerns a connected, qualified object, not just one isolated object-word. If the relation among objects is first established by applying the words to an injunction, then the words must already have the capacity to relate meanings apart from an injunction, since the injunction depends on the meanings being related. It will be shown that their connection does not depend on an injunction being expected.

Even something not previously known and whose relation is not previously understood can be conveyed by a word through the denial of particular qualities, since words that exclude a specific quality are understood in relation to their corresponding objects. This is how the teaching “not gross” conveys what transcends every distinction. This is what is meant by “through the dissolution of the manifold of difference,” and it will be explained.

Another interpretation begins from the claim that all determinate cognition ceases when every field and division of cognition has subsided...

...is outside the range of cognition. The reply is that it is placed in the mind through the very removal of distinctions, as with the nature of gold. The nature of gold is never seen apart from the confusing differences of shape—lump, ornament, and so forth. Yet those shapes themselves are not the nature of gold, since the gold remains even after one form is discarded and another shape is present. The mind can recognize and communicate to another the nature of gold even without confusing it with the differences of shape, by excluding those differences. Scripture itself shows this sequence of understanding in “It is not this, not this.” Other authorities say, “When forms are destroyed, what remains at the end is reality”; still others say, “The unmanifest, free from the manifold, is taught by first superimposing and then retracting.” The question now is whether the entire Veda describes Brahman by dissolving the manifold of difference, or only one part of it.

Some say that throughout the Veda one finds the dissolution of some particular difference. For example, “One who desires heaven should sacrifice” dissolves the identification of the Self with the body, since it presents an eligible person capable of enjoying heaven apart from the body. Likewise, “For one who desires cattle, he should offer with the milking vessel” dissolves distinctions between qualified persons in relation to the office. In injunctions and prohibitions too, natural actions based on desire and the like are dissolved: directly in prohibitions and indirectly in injunctions, by requiring another action. In ordinary life also, one is directly prevented from taking an unintended road or redirected by being shown another route. In this way, they say, ritual injunctions serve the qualification for knowledge of the Self through the visible removal of the divisions in natural actions driven by desire and the like. Scripture teaches that the Self is seen by one who is calm, controlled, and concentrated. That is possible: a person whose mind is drawn away by objects and occupied with the activities that obtain them cannot concentrate on the Self. One who has withdrawn from natural impulses and steadied the mind is qualified for the vision of the Self.

Others say that a person whose desires remain unfulfilled and whose mind is overcome by desire is not fit for the realization of supreme nonduality. But through ritual actions that fulfill desires, extending even over a thousand years, the desires are exhausted; starting from the state of Prajāpati, the person comes to realize the supreme nondual Self. On either of these two views, they say, the entire Veda ultimately culminates in knowledge of the Self.

Another view is that ritual injunctions, while serving their own distinct purposes, bring a person to the qualification for knowledge of the Self, since one who has not discharged the three debts is not qualified for it. As scripture says, “Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation.” Others say that all ritual acts enter into qualification for knowledge of the Self through a special connection, on the authority of “They desire to know by means of sacrifice,” and also, “Even if one sacrifices in any manner whatsoever, even with a ladle offering, one’s mind remains undisturbed.” Still others explain that ritual acts touch the qualification for knowledge of the Self as a refinement of the person: “Through the great rites and sacrifices this body is made fit for Brahman”; and, “One who has these forty sacraments and the eight qualities of the Self...” Others explain the reverse: knowledge of the Self itself enters into qualification for ritual action by refining the agent. Still others hold that ritual action and knowledge of the Self are opposed to one another, and are unrelated because they concern duality and nonduality, respectively.

Of these, the first account is not tenable. The ritual injunctions do not depend on some other result: their own sentences establish heaven and other results as ends. Nor does an injunction to know the Self, which does not depend on the means already mentioned, need the ritual injunctions; it has its own means, such as the disciplines of celibacy. Why, then, should there be a single qualification for both? If someone says that ritual injunctions have no known result of their own because heaven and the like are only qualifiers of the action, this is the subject of the discussion concerning a person who desires heaven. Moreover, if every injunction and prohibition aimed at dissolving names and forms and thereby at liberation, the rise and fall of living beings would not be caused by action but would be accidental; liberation too would be accidental, and the scriptures would be pointless.

Someone may reply that ritual injunctions enter into qualification for knowledge of the Self through the result of heaven, as directions to a village on the way enter into directions for reaching a desired city. That is unsound. Directions to a village on the route can enter into directions for reaching an undesired place because the person has no human goal in reaching the village itself; they are pursued only because the goal is elsewhere. Thus, when an instruction is dependent on another one, it is because it is not independently sufficient and the desired end is reached only through the latter. Ritual injunctions, however, do yield a human goal: heaven and the like are desired by people. Once their result is sufficient in itself, how can they depend on another injunction?

One might say that the route to the desired city is taught by pointing out one village after another, each with its particular advantages, and so instructions to reach the earlier villages achieve their own goals yet enter into later instructions. That is reasonable only because the speaker’s intention is understood through another means of knowledge: the person learns that reaching this place is what the speaker wants to bring about. It is not understood merely from the words themselves. So, too, the person standing to one side understands the direction to each village as concerning that village, and the final direction as concerning its own goal, even though, as a matter of fact, the earlier directions are helpful for reaching the later destination. The word’s intention is not inferred from that incidental usefulness, just as a rule for acquiring materials may help a sacrifice without being directed at the purpose of the ritual injunction.

Furthermore, one travels and reaches the destination only after deciding that the directions about the villages lead to the desired destination. If the instructions were intended to direct one to the distant place, it would not be necessary to travel there by that precise route; the speaker’s intention might be fulfilled by another route. Reaching the desired result is not compulsory merely because one has been enjoined to reach it. Even when the stated purpose of a sentence that is directed elsewhere is to produce some result, that purpose is treated only as praise of the action.

Thus, if injunctions and prohibitions are directed to some further result, ritual injunctions cannot have heaven and the like as their own result. The result of a ritual act is not like the result of the preliminary acts. How, then, can ritual acts alone be said to help qualify a person for knowledge of the Self? If the proposal is that they prevent natural actions directed toward visible ends and prompted by desire, this may describe prohibitions. But one must explain how positive ritual injunctions prevent such actions. They are neither exclusions nor restrictions, because they concern actions and objects not previously undertaken. An injunction is understood to yield the exclusion of another option when its object is already something one would otherwise pursue; that does not apply here. Nor do they restrain action by being opposed in purpose: ritual actions have results that occur at an uncertain time and are undertaken under injunction, whereas natural actions prompted by desire are directed toward visible ends. There is no contradiction in both a Saṅgrahaṇī rite and service being means of reaching a village. Therefore, at this point...

...what contradiction would there be if someone seeking the goal of a field undertook both service and the Saṅgrahaṇī rite, either together or in sequence? Moreover, if all activity aimed at visible results were suppressed, then activities rooted in injunctions would also be stopped, since they would be impossible for a person who had acquired no wealth and lacked the means. If ritual actions and ordinary visible actions are both means to desires, there is no difference between them in their being prompted by attachment. The injunction “one who desires heaven” specifically presupposes action prompted by desire; it does not remove that desire. If people are equally attached to the manifold world, why should one action be especially suited to oneness while another is opposed to it? Desire affects the mind without distinction. If one denies that ritual is itself a means to desire, then the problem of its accidental results, already described, returns. And since ordinary and ritual acts have similar results, the concern that the two would conflict and suppress one another has no room to arise in the first place.

If someone says that ritual injunctions qualify a person for knowledge of the Self by fulfilling desires and thereby dissolving them, they cite the verse:

“When all the desires lodged in the heart are released,
then the mortal becomes immortal and here attains Brahman.”

That is unsound. Desires are not dissolved by attaining what they desire; they are dissolved by sustained discernment that comes from reflecting on their defects. Even if the mind is touched by desire to the slightest degree, it is carried away by what attracts it. It is said, “Desire never comes to an end through enjoying the things desired,” and also, “Passions grow with repeated enjoyment, while the senses become more adept.” A person should therefore turn away from desires because they are no means to the goal, and take up knowledge of the Self, which is the cessation of all suffering. By contrast, ritual injunctions display many means of obtaining the objects of desire, and a person becomes attached to precisely the enjoyments that already carry him away. The person would recoil from knowledge of the Self, which dissolves those desires. Even bliss in the Self, though heard about, has not been experienced; it cannot be expected to weaken even a little the desire for objects whose pleasure has been experienced, much less to remove that desire completely. Therefore, only sustained discernment is a means to end desire; ritual injunctions are causes of the opposite.

The claim that somewhere in the Veda a particular difference is dissolved—for instance, the difference between the body and the Self in “one who desires heaven should sacrifice”—is also unsound, because that is not the passage’s subject. That sentence is not directed toward understanding a Self distinct from the body. To infer that meaning from it would be like inferring an elephant from the word “that” after seeing an elephant. The text explicitly begins with “not gross,” and so on, and shows the dissolution of body, senses, and the rest; it is not necessary to infer that meaning from a sentence directed elsewhere. And if one argues that a meaning can be inferred from a passage directed to something else, one might just as well infer any desired meaning from an unrelated sight.

The second proposal is also incoherent: desires are not dissolved by the fulfillment of desire, as has been explained, and there is no evidence that actions that have no further need of their own result enter into another injunction. If all actions shared a single qualification, then all actions would have to be combined, which is impossible. Those who reverse the proposal and say that the knowledge of the Self qualifies one for action must also state what proves that knowledge is connected with ritual action. It is not like the statement “He sprinkles the rice,” where context makes the word “rice” refer to the unseen result of the ritual being discussed, since the ordinary meaning of the word would otherwise be pointless. Nor is it like “One whose ladle is made from palāśa wood,” where the ladle’s connection with a ritual brings the ritual to mind even without the surrounding context. In that case the connection is established by the sentence itself. But knowledge of the Self is not stated in the context of ritual, nor is it something invariably connected with ritual. It is therefore difficult to explain any connection between knowledge of the Self and ritual action. And if the promised result is not known to be secondary to something else, then a statement of its fruit is not mere praise; the two matters have distinct qualifications.

One may say that because scripture says, “He does not return,” the result must be reinterpreted since it is not connected with desire. That is so only when the result is something one still expects to have explained. Here, however, knowledge of the Self has a result visible in this life: it stops action directed at results to be enjoyed in another life. The injunction to know the Self is therefore like the injunction to study one’s Veda. That study does not depend on a fruit mentioned in praise, because it already has the visible result of understanding the actions one should perform. The injunction to know the Self is like this, and so it does not share a qualification with ritual action.

That too is unsound, because a different person—the person taught in the Upaniṣads—is what the Vedānta texts seek to know. Knowing that person does not prompt ritual action, for that person is neither an agent nor an experiencer. Scripture says, “It eats nothing,” and, “The other watches without eating.” The agent and experiencer of action is the one established by everyone’s perception, not the subject matter of words. Someone may object that the individual Self and supreme Self are one, as scripture says, “Having entered with this living Self.” That is true; but the individual Self in its present form, bound by ignorance and known through perception, is the cause of ritual action and does not depend on words. What one seeks to know from words is the self-illuminating reality free from every division. Knowing that is opposed to action. How could knowledge of it have a result consisting in ritual action visible in this life? What action or means could there be for one who knows the one, nondual Self, which is the bliss of Brahman, since all desires are fulfilled and there is no need for means or actions?

Someone may object that the knowledge of the person taught in the Upaniṣads is itself enjoined as a part of ritual action, citing, “Whatever one does with knowledge, faith, and the Upaniṣad becomes more powerful.” They also cite the passage that begins, “Whoever, without knowing this imperishable, offers sacrifice in this world,” which shows that the results of sacrifice and the like are limited, and thereby shows that knowledge of Brahman is for that purpose. The statement, “Knowledge and action follow after him,” is said to show that knowledge and action go together.

The first statement, however, concerns the Udgītha, since it begins, “This syllable Om is the Udgītha.” The later statement praises knowledge of the imperishable by censuring ritual action. Knowledge and action follow after a person in different ways: knowledge follows the one who has knowledge, and action follows the one who performs actions. Therefore, even on this account, knowledge and ritual action do not share one qualification.

Those who say that knowledge and ritual action are simply unrelated because they conflict—action concerning duality and knowledge concerning nonduality—would make the arising of knowledge of nonduality impossible, since the divisions among means of knowledge and their objects conflict with the understanding of nonduality. If one says there is no conflict because means and ends do not occur at the same time, then every division ceases precisely when nonduality is understood. The means come earlier, when the distinctions have not yet ceased. And if difference is a means to understanding non-difference, ritual actions do not conflict with knowledge either; they are also means.

Someone may object that action is of no use because Brahman is not something to be produced. Scripture says, “There is no unmade result through what is made.” Nor do ritual actions help knowledge arise, since knowledge depends on its means of knowledge. Nor do actions assist knowledge, because knowledge has no further result to produce; liberation is not something produced, since that would make it impermanent. If, instead, the goal is to cut off the cause of bondage, the cause of bondage is beginningless ignorance; but...

...and it is not a separate destruction of it that must be brought about. The arising of knowledge is itself the removal of ignorance. Someone may say that ignorance as non-apprehension is indeed removed when knowledge arises, since something existent is removed by the arising of something existent. But the arising of knowledge is not itself the removal of erroneous cognition: one positive thing is not the removal of another positive thing, and entities are not simply absences of one another. Otherwise they would be unreal.

If one holds that error is caused by not apprehending reality and will disappear on its own when that cause is removed, that is not so. Mere non-apprehension is not a cause of anything; otherwise the same would apply to fainting and similar states. What, then, is the cause? It was said that ignorance is beginningless and without purpose. There is no occasion to ask for its cause. Nor is there a problem in the fact that error and its latent impression stand in a mutual relation of cause and effect. Thus one may say that the removal of erroneous cognition is an end to be brought about by knowledge, and that knowledge therefore needs some auxiliary. This is mistaken. When correct knowledge arises after the mistaken perception of silver in a shell, people make no separate effort or seek another auxiliary to remove the error. The mere arising of an opposing state already destroys what came before; destruction is not a void. Otherwise destruction could not have a cause. Knowledge is opposed to erroneous cognition, and when knowledge arises, the error is already gone.

Someone may say that actions are the causes of bondage, and that knowledge destroys them only with the help of an auxiliary. How could that be possible when knowledge arises as purified awareness, free from every particular distinction? Scripture says that the same actions are destroyed as erroneous and doubtful cognition: “When the higher and lower are seen, the knot of the heart is cut, all doubts are severed, and his actions are exhausted.” If something else were needed to purify knowledge, that would be pointless too, since neither doubt nor error can be present in knowledge that arises from a means of knowledge.

Someone may argue that, besides knowledge from words, one needs direct cognition: a distinct knowledge that grasps reality without divisions and transcends every conceptual distinction. Brahman is the object of this direct cognition, not of verbal knowledge, which grasps meanings in relation to one another; ritual and meditation are required for its arising. What special feature makes it necessary? Greater clarity? That is of no use. Knowledge is for making its object manifest, and once verbal knowledge has arisen, the object has already been fully established. If perception is supposed to supersede it, what further object could one seek after the object has been known? Perhaps another means of knowledge is needed to establish it. No: the need for another means arises only when the object has not been established. If a further means is required to establish it again, the first establishment would have to be repeated without end; there is no reason to seek another establishment for what is already established. If another means is said to exist, then one should simply seek that other means. But there is no such further expectation concerning the object itself.

Perhaps direct cognition yields a special pleasure. That too can be established from the seeing produced by the first means of knowledge; no second means is needed to establish it. Even something seen through perception may be investigated by another person, since there is no difference in that respect. Other means of knowledge can also establish certainty, since they are means of knowledge. Perhaps perception alone concerns an object fit to be accepted or rejected because it is in direct contact with it, unlike the other means. Then the cause of that contact should be sought; perception is not itself the means at issue, because the cognition is already established. There is no such distinction in the matter under discussion. Someone may say that words and the other means concern general features, while perception concerns particular features. In that case, Brahman’s particular features would remain unknown through words. Certainly; it has already been said that Brahman is not the object of verbal cognition.

If Brahman is not known from words, how could a meditation on it begin? And what is meditated upon does not directly become something else. What form is produced by injunctions concerning sacrifices and the like? They make direct the Self whose nature is Brahman: the word-revealed Brahman is unsurpassed bliss, free from sin, and so on. Once this has been clearly established by a means of knowledge that admits no doubt, there is nothing more to expect. Someone may object that even after words such as “You are that” have established that Brahman is the Self, the qualities of worldly existence are still seen as before, so something else is needed to remove them. That is not sound. How could someone who has understood identity with Brahman and the true nature of the Self continue to be joined to qualities caused by a false view? Scripture says, “One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman.” Those qualities have no place in Brahman, which is free from sin. It also says:

“If a person knew the Self as, ‘I am this,’
desiring what, and for whose sake, would he torment the body?”

And, “When one is bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch one.” The connection with the body is caused by false identification; seeing the truth removes it. Therefore one who has understood identity with Brahman does not continue to bear the qualities of worldly existence as before.

The reply is this: even when reality has been settled by a means of knowledge, false appearances may persist everywhere because of a particular cause. A person who knows from reliable testimony what the moon and the directions truly are may still see two moons or mistake the direction. Likewise, even when the truth of the Self has been known without doubt from the Veda, false appearances may persist through the force of impressions strengthened by beginningless practice of false seeing. Something else is needed to remove them. That is repeated practice in seeing the truth, which is well known in ordinary life, together with ritual actions and other disciplines established by scripture. Repeated practice strengthens the impression of truth, restrains the earlier impression, and extends the effect of the new one. Ritual actions remove impurities by some unseen means; others say that obligatory rites destroy wrongdoing, and so on.

Someone may object that false appearances can remain, while certainty from a means of knowledge guides action in accordance with what is true; so no further discipline is necessary. The answer is that even after reality has been seen, if no firm impression of truth has been established and the false impression produced by long practice is stronger, one’s certainty too may result in false conduct. This is like a person who is disoriented about the directions and does not bring to mind reliable testimony: the same mistaken action continues. In the same way, a person who has learned that something is a rope may still be afraid of a snake if the knowledge is not recalled. Thus, even after reality has been known through a means of knowledge, repeated practice in seeing the truth is accepted to overcome and destroy the stronger impression developed through beginningless practice of false perception. Scripture accordingly says, “It should be reflected upon and meditated upon.” It also prescribes means such as tranquility, self-restraint, celibacy, and ritual. Otherwise, what purpose would those instructions serve?

One may say that knowledge of reality arises from the Veda precisely through the performance of disciplines such as celibacy. That is unsound, because understanding arises from the words alone. It is not the case that understanding reality does not arise before those particular disciplines...

The Veda is neither non-denotative nor indecisive, since it removes every doubt. Otherwise even the means it teaches would be difficult to understand. Moreover, even after something has been understood correctly, false appearances can still cause sorrow, fear, and the like, as when actors such as Bharata on a stage produce grief or fear through their performance. Even when one is certain that molasses is sweet, the false appearance of bitterness can cause distress as though it were real, because one recoils from it and rejects it as if it were real. Thus, even after the identity of Brahman and the Self is known with certainty, disciplines are needed to remove such appearances.

Just as liberation is not something produced when reality is made manifest by a means of knowledge, it is not produced by a special degree of manifestation that results from disciplines. Scriptural statements may concern the stage in which repeated practice is complete, or the knowledge that depends on words may be a cause of what follows, and so on. Enough of this extended discussion.

The claim that ritual injunctions, each having its own separate result, bring a person to qualification for knowledge because the person must first discharge the three debts is also not a necessary rule. Scripture and tradition allow different life-stages: “Some prescribe this order of life,” “One may live in whichever stage one chooses,” and, “If one wishes, one may renounce from the stage of celibacy itself.” We also see that people of earlier times who possessed knowledge did not perform the Agnihotra, and ask, “What shall we do with children?” and “For what reason should we study, for what reason should we sacrifice?”—all indicating the giving up of ritual action. The passage “Having discharged the three debts...” teaches a person already established in household life, who thinks the knowledge of the Self alone has fulfilled the purpose of life, that neglecting the prescribed discharge of the debts gives rise to wrongdoing that can obstruct the arising of knowledge.

This much, however, is reasonable: all rituals, even if they have no need of another result of their own, can be connected with knowledge of the Self because of the conjunction of different practices, as scripture says, “Brahmins seek to know this Self through the recitation of the Veda and through sacrifice.” Even so, their role is to help knowledge arise, not to produce a bodily result as the preliminary rites do, since knowledge has no further result to produce. Or their role may be to refine the person, as tradition teaches: “Through the great rites and sacrifices this body is made fit for Brahman.” For knowledge arises in one who has been refined in this way. It is said, “Rites of the life-stages are also enjoined.”

One may object that knowledge arises through a directly visible cause. Only the practical steps should be needed, such as tranquility and self-control, which remove distraction of mind; knowledge arises as the clear understanding of a concentrated mind. Sacrifices and the like are not needed, since this is possible through repeated practice even without them. The reply is: that is true. Knowledge is accepted to arise in ascetics who have abandoned ritual while practicing, without those rites. But there is a difference in the time it takes. Specific disciplines make knowledge manifest sooner and sooner; without them, it becomes manifest after a longer time. As scripture says, “Everything is required, because scripture says so, as in the case of a horse.” This means that, because scripture says that knowledge depends on sacrifices and gifts, these acts are required even when knowledge is gained through practice—just as one can reach a village without a horse, but uses a horse to reach it more quickly and with less effort.

Someone may object: Brahman is itself the nature of knowledge, and knowledge is not different from Brahman. Brahman is eternal and not produced, so how could it depend on anything? The answer is that it should be understood like a crystal whose nature is hidden by something placed beside it: the crystal depends on the removal of that covering for its own nature to become manifest. Likewise here, the Self’s nature has not been destroyed by the presence of a limiting condition, and nothing new is produced when that condition is removed. A likeness of it would not suddenly arise after being separated by many moments of a wholly different kind; when the fire has died, a succession of logs does not begin again from the embers. Thus the unproduced nature of a crystal can depend on removal of what covers it, and so too can the nature of the Self.

One may object that it is knowledge, which depends on something, that is being discussed, and that knowledge is an effect different from the crystal. What is human effort for in relation to knowledge? Is knowledge desired for its own sake or to establish the real nature of its object? It is not desired solely for itself, since practical conduct depends on the real object. Conduct is not based merely on cognition, or else false cognition would produce it too. If knowledge is desired to establish the nature of its object, the activity aims at the object itself. But knowledge causes no change in the object, because the two are unrelated; the object is equally accessible everywhere. If it did, everyone who perceives would know it. And if knowledge were to change past or future objects, that would not be possible. Therefore, just as a crystal whose nature is covered appears to become manifest through effort when the covering is removed, though neither covering nor new production truly affects its nature, so the nature of the Self, though never truly concealed, appears as if concealed and becomes manifest through effort.

The verse says:

“Therefore the universal Self has been described with every distinction withdrawn,
its nature indicated by the removal of differences, like gold when ornaments are put aside.”

यतश्च विशेषप्रत्यस्तमुखेन तन्निरूपणम्, अतो ऽन्यैर्ब्रह्मविद्याभियुक्तैः सामान्यरूपं ब्रह्म निरूपितम् --- ‘स एव महानज आत्मा सत्तालक्षणःऽ; तथा ‘सत्तैव सर्वभेदयोनिः प्रकृतिः पराऽ; इति । यथा सुवर्णतत्त्वं कटकाङ्गुलीयादिविशेषोपसंहारेण निरूप्यमाणं तत्सामान्यमिति । ये वा --- [क्क्स्_38] ‘निर्विशेषं न सामान्यं भवेच्छशविषाणवत्ऽइत्यभावमाहुः, तान् प्रत्युच्यते --- संहृताखिलभेद इति । यदि तावदसामान्यत्वं साध्यते सिद्धसाधनम् । विशेषाणामभावे केषां तत्सामन्यम्? सामन्यं तूक्तं ब्रह्मवादिभिर्विशेषप्रत्यस्तमुखेन निरूपणादुपचारतः । अथाभाव एव साध्यः, विशेषैरेवास्य निर्विशेषैर्व्यभिचार इति । [इति श्रीमन्मण्डनमिश्रविरचितायां ब्रह्मसिद्धौ ब्रह्मकाण्डः समाप्तः । -- एदितिओन्; ओरिगिनल्ल्य् ब्रह्म- अन्द् तर्क-काण्डस् wएरे तोगेथेर्; वचस्पति दोएस् नोत् क्नोw थिस् दिविसिओन्.]

[क्क्स्_39]

[ ॥ तर्ककाण्डः ॥ ]

ननु प्रत्यक्षादिभिर्व्यावृत्तानां भावस्वभावानामवगमान्नैकस्मिन्नद्वये शब्दः प्रमाणम्, प्रत्यक्षादिविरोधात्, ग्रावप्लवनाद्यर्थवचोवत् । उच्यते ---

आहुर्विधातृ प्रत्यक्षं न निषेद्धृ विपश्चितः । नैकत्व आगमस्तेन प्रत्यक्षेण विरुध्यते
units.iast:
yataśca viśeṣapratyastamukhena tannirūpaṇam, ato 'nyairbrahmavidyābhiyuktaiḥ sāmānyarūpaṃ brahma nirūpitam --- ‘sa eva mahānaja ātmā sattālakṣaṇaḥ'; tathā ‘sattaiva sarvabhedayoniḥ prakṛtiḥ parā'; iti / yathā suvarṇatattvaṃ kaṭakāṅgulīyādiviśeṣopasaṃhāreṇa nirūpyamāṇaṃ tatsāmānyamiti / ye vā --- [kks_38] ‘nirviśeṣaṃ na sāmānyaṃ bhavecchaśaviṣāṇavat'ityabhāvamāhuḥ, tān pratyucyate --- saṃhṛtākhilabheda iti / yadi tāvadasāmānyatvaṃ sādhyate siddhasādhanam / viśeṣāṇāmabhāve keṣāṃ tatsāmanyam? sāmanyaṃ tūktaṃ brahmavādibhirviśeṣapratyastamukhena nirūpaṇādupacārataḥ / athābhāva eva sādhyaḥ, viśeṣairevāsya nirviśeṣairvyabhicāra iti /

[iti śrīmanmaṇḍanamiśraviracitāyāṃ brahmasiddhau brahmakāṇḍaḥ samāptaḥ / -- edition; originally brahma- and tarka-kāṇḍas were together; vacaspati does not know this division.]

[kks_39]

[//tarkakāṇḍaḥ //]

nanu pratyakṣādibhirvyāvṛttānāṃ bhāvasvabhāvānāmavagamānnaikasminnadvaye śabdaḥ pramāṇam, pratyakṣādivirodhāt, grāvaplavanādyarthavacovat / ucyate ---

āhurvidhātṛ pratyakṣaṃ na niṣeddhṛ vipaścitaḥ /
naikatva āgamastena pratyakṣeṇa virudhyate
units.translation:
Since Brahman is described by turning away from every particular feature, other thinkers devoted to the knowledge of Brahman have described it in a general form: “That great, unborn Self is existence itself,” and “Existence alone, the supreme source of nature, is the source of every distinction.” This is like describing the nature of gold, after setting aside the particular forms of bracelets, rings, and the like, as their common substance.

This also answers those who say, “What has no distinguishing features cannot be a general property; it would be like a hare’s horn,” and thus assert sheer nonexistence. Brahman is said to be “that in which all distinctions have been gathered up.” If the claim to be established is simply that it is not a general property, that is already established: without particular things, what could it be general to? But those who speak of Brahman do describe it figuratively as a general reality, by turning away from particular features. If instead sheer nonexistence is what is to be established, then it is contradicted by the particular things themselves, which are not nonexistent.

[Here the Brahma section of the Brahmasiddhi, composed by the revered Maṇḍana Miśra, concludes. The editor notes: the Brahma and Logic sections were originally together; Vācaspati does not appear to know of this division.]

## Logic Section

Someone may object: when real things are known as excluded by perception and other means of knowledge, words cannot be a means of knowledge about a single nondual reality, since this conflicts with perception, like a statement about stones floating. We reply:

“The learned say that perception affirms, not denies. Therefore scripture does not conflict with perception when it teaches unity.”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 1 · Tarka — reasoning about perception, difference, and nonduality
units.label: Kāṇḍa 1 · 5
units.deva:
ननु प्रमाणान्तरपरतन्त्राणां पुरुषवचसां तद्विरोधाद्युक्तमप्रमाणत्वम् । स्वतन्त्रस्य त्वाम्नायस्यानपेक्षितप्रमाणान्तरप्रवृत्तेस्तद्विरोधे ऽपि कस्मादप्रमाणत्वम्? आम्नायविरोधादेव तु प्रत्यक्षादीनि प्रमाणतायाः किमिति न च्यवन्ते? तुल्ये ऽनपेक्षत्वे न विशेषहेतुरस्ति । तत्र वृथा प्रमाणान्तरविरोधपरिहारपरिश्रम इति । तत्र केचिदाहुः --- प्रत्यक्षादिविरोधे आम्नायस्य दौर्बल्यम्, सापेक्षत्वत् । तथा हि स्वरूपसिद्ध्यर्थमेव तावत्प्रत्यक्षादीन्याम्नायो ऽपेक्षते । तथा च तेषां प्रामाण्यमनुमन्तव्यम्, तदपबाधने स्वरूपस्यैव तावदसिद्धेः । न त्वेवमाम्नाये प्रत्यक्षादीनां काचिदपेक्षा । दृष्टव्यभिचारत्वाच्च शब्दस्य, प्रत्यक्षस्य चादृष्टव्यभिचारात् । अपि च सावकाशानवकाशयोरनवकाशं बलवत् । अनवकाशाश्च प्रत्यक्षादयः, सावकाशस्तु शब्दो गौणेनार्थेन । तथा हि --- शक्यमेकत्वमभेदश्रुतीनामुपचरितमवकाशो वर्णयितुम् । अविवक्षितार्थानां वा वेदान्तानां जपोपयोगो ऽवकाशः । उपनिषदो वेदान्ता इति वर्णितम् । किं च व्याकुलत्वादाम्नायस्याव्याकुलत्वात्प्रत्यक्षादीनाम् । कर्मविधयो हि भेदाश्रया अभेदाश्रयाश्च वेदान्ताः परस्परपराहता असत्यपि प्रमाणान्तरविरोधे दुर्लभप्रामाण्याः । किं पुनरव्याहतप्रतिष्ठितप्रामाण्यादिविरोधे । तस्मादिदमविरोधाय प्रयत्यत इति । मुख्यत्वाच्च । मुख्या हि प्रत्यक्षादयः । जातस्य जन्तोरपरकाल आम्नायः । स तैः प्रतिष्ठितार्थैरपहृतविषयः कल्पनीयार्थो बाध्यते, तदनुसारेण वार्थकल्पनामर्हति । अर्थतो ऽपि च मुख्यता प्रत्यक्षादीनाम् । पदपदार्थविभागाधीन आम्नायार्थपरिच्छेदः, स च प्रत्यक्षादिष्वापतते । अतो ऽविरोधाय प्रयत्यत इति । [क्क्स्_40] अन्ये मन्यन्ते --- तुल्यबलत्वे ऽपि प्रत्यक्षादीनामाम्नायस्य च वस्तुनि विकल्पानुपपत्तेर्विरोधे संशयः स्यात् । तेनाविरोध उपपाद्यत इति । अन्यद्दर्शनम् --- आम्नाय एव बलवांस्तद्विरोधे । ‘पौर्वापर्ये पूर्वदौर्बल्यं प्रकृतिवत्ऽ; । ‘पूर्वाबाधेन नोत्पत्तिरुत्तरस्य हि सिध्यतिऽ; इति । तथा हि --- सर्वस्य निसर्गजः प्रत्यक्षादिनिबन्धनः किल विभक्तवस्तुपरिच्छेदः । तदपेक्षस्तु तत्पूर्वको ऽनिसर्गजः कस्यचिदेवागन्तुरद्वैतावगमः । स पूर्वमनुपमृद्योदेतुमशक्नुवंस्तदपबाधात्मोदीयते । इतश्च --- संभवद्विचित्रविभ्रमहेतुत्वात्प्रत्यक्षादीनाम्, विगलितनिखिलदोषाशङ्कत्वाच्चाम्नायस्य । पुरुषाश्रयाणां हि दोषाणां शब्दे पुरुषाभावे ऽसंभवात् । शक्यो ह्याम्नायादेवानादिरविद्यासंस्कारो विभ्रमहेतुः प्रत्यक्षादिषु संभावयितुं निश्चेतुं च देहात्माभिमान इव । न त्वेवमपौरुषेये शब्दे काचिद्दोषाशङ्का । सत्यां वा प्रमाणमेव न स्यात् । प्रत्यक्षादीनां तु व्यावहारिकं प्रामाण्यम्, अविद्यासंस्कार्स्य स्थेम्ना व्यवहारविपर्ययाभावात् । यत्र च व्यवहारविपर्ययो न तत्र प्रामाण्यम् । शब्दे तु संभावितदोषे न तत्त्वावेदनेन प्रामाण्यम् । न व्यवहाराविपर्ययेण । अदृष्टार्थत्वाद्दोषेभ्यो व्यवहारविसंवादिज्ञानदर्शनाच्च । प्रत्यक्षादीनां तु व्यवहारे संवादान्न शक्यते व्यवहारविसंवादिज्ञानहेतुर्दोषः कल्पयितुम् । व्यवहारविपर्ययाद्धि स कल्प्येत । तत्त्वदर्शनस्य तु वेदान्तजन्मनः प्रतिपक्षत्वात्तत्त्वप्रतिहतिमात्रहेतुरेवानादिरविद्यानुबन्धः कल्प्यते । ततो दोषानुबन्धः प्रामाण्यं चेति न विरोधः । शब्दस्तु संभावितदोषो दुर्लभप्रामाण्य एव स्यात् । दृश्यते हि दोषेभ्यो व्यवहारविसंवादिज्ञानोत्पत्तिः । तत्र दोषाशङ्कया व्यवहारविसंवादस्य शङ्कितत्वात्तत्त्वप्रतिघातस्य च, न तत्त्वावेदनलक्षणं प्रामाण्यम्, न व्यवहाराविसंवादलक्षणमिति । तस्माच्छब्दस्य प्रामाण्याभ्युपगमे प्रमाणान्तरविरोधे ऽपि तस्यैव बलवत्त्वमिति सांप्रतम् । यत्तु प्रत्यक्षाद्यपेक्षणादिति, तत्रोच्यते --- न प्रमितावपेक्षावत्ता शब्दस्य प्रत्यक्षादिषु, किं तु स्वरूपसिद्धौ । अन्यथा प्रमाणमेव न स्यात् । तथा च स्वकार्ये ऽपेक्षत्वान्न प्रत्यक्षादिभ्यो हीयते । प्रत्यक्षादयो पि स्वरूपसिद्धौ नान्यानपेक्षाः । कार्ये हि सापेक्षत्वं [क्क्स्_41] सामर्थ्यमपकर्षतीति । यत्त्वेतेषां प्रामाण्यमनुमातव्यमिति, को वान्यथाह? व्यवहाराविसंवादिलक्षणं तु तत्, न तत्त्वावेदनलक्षणम् । व्यावहारिकप्रामाण्योपेतेभ्यः प्रत्यक्षादिभ्यः सिद्धादाम्नायात्तत्त्वदर्शनम्, तद्विरोधात्तेषु तत्त्वदर्शनांशमेवापबाधते, न व्यवहाराविसंवादांशम् । दृष्टं च हेतुत्वेनापेक्षिताया अपि पूर्वस्याः प्रतिपत्तेः परस्याः प्रतिपत्तेर्बलीयस्त्वम् । यथा दूरस्थेषु वनस्पतिषु हस्तिप्रतिपत्तिभ्यो वनस्पतिप्रतिपत्तेः । अपेक्षिता हि हस्तिप्रतिपत्तयो व्यक्तवनस्पतिप्रतिपत्त्या हेतुत्वेन । न तस्या इन्द्रियार्थसंनिकर्षमात्राज्जन्म, आपाते ऽभावात् । न च देशविशेषात्, तद्देशस्थस्यैवोत्पत्तेः । तस्मात्पुरोवर्तिषु वनस्पतिषु प्रणिहितमनसः प्राच्यविपर्यासानुगतमतिसंस्कारसचिवेन्द्रियादिसंयोगकारिता सेति मन्तव्यम् । एवमेकादिसंख्याबुद्ध्यपाया विंशत्यादिबुद्धयो ऽप्युदाहार्याः । एवं च यदेके वर्णयन्ति --- स्वयमेव व्याहता वेदान्तार्थप्रतिपत्तिः । नाभेदो भेदमन्तरेण शक्यो ऽवसातुम् । भेदोपाया हि तस्य प्रतिपत्तिः । तत्राभेदः समाक्षिप्तभेद एव प्रतायत इति व्याघातः --- तदपास्तम् । यत उपायमाक्षिपति प्रतिपत्तिः । नोपायस्य परमार्थताम्, मिथ्याज्ञानादपि तत्त्वप्रतिपत्तेः । व्यावहारिकं च भेदस्य सत्यत्वमिष्टमेवेति । व्यभिचारदर्शनं च दुष्टहेतुजन्मनोः शब्दप्रत्यक्षयोः समानम् । इतरयोरपि तुल्यमव्यभिचारित्वम् । तथानवकाशत्वमपि । यदि खल्वेकमद्वयं वेदान्तार्थः, कस्तेषामन्यो ऽवकाशः? अथौपचारिकत्वमेकत्वं तदर्थो ऽविवक्षितार्थता वा जपोपयोगिनाम्, तत्र विरोध एव नास्तीति बलाबलचिन्ता नावतरति । तत्कुतः सावकाशत्वेन दौर्बल्यम्? कथं च मुख्यमर्थमतिलङ्घ्योपचरितो ऽवकाशः? कथं वौत्पत्तिके शब्दस्यार्थं प्रति शेषभावे --- ‘दृष्टो हि तस्यार्थः कर्मावबोधनम्ऽ; ‘अविशिष्टस्तु वाक्यार्थःऽइति च अविवक्षितार्थता? प्रमाणान्तरविरोधादिति चेत्, वार्तमेतत् । न प्रमाणस्य प्रमाणान्तरापेक्षं प्रामाण्यम्, येन तद्विरोधे स्वरसं जह्यात् । तदपेक्षत्वे हि तदनुगुणतया वर्तेत । निरपेक्षस्य कः प्रमाणान्तरानुसरणे [क्क्स्_42] हेतुः? लौकिकास्तु शब्दाः प्रमाणान्तरापेक्षं स्वार्थमभिदधतीति युक्ता तेषां तदनुसारिणी वृत्तिः । तुल्ये त्वनपेक्षत्वे किमिति न विपर्ययः, उभयोर्वा व्याघातादप्रामाण्यम्, ‘पौर्वापर्ये पूर्वदौर्बल्यम्ऽइति वा रजतज्ञानस्येव पूर्वस्य बाधः? न खलु रजतज्ञानविरोधाच्छुक्तिज्ञानमन्यविषयमविषयं वा । कथं तर्हि वेदे गुणवादः । यत्र श्रौतैरर्थैः प्रमाणार्थनिष्पत्तेरसम्भवः, तत्र द्वितीयस्या अपि वृत्तेः शब्दानां प्रवृत्तिदर्शनात्तया प्रमाणविषयलाभः । यत्र तु शब्दाः स्वरसेन लभन्ते विषयम्, तत्र न प्रमाणान्तरविरोधादपावर्तन्ते । न ह्येषां प्रमाणान्तरनिबन्धनो ऽर्थो येन तद्वशादपावर्तेरन् । अथ मतम् --- उभयानुग्रहादेवं कल्प्यते । एवं हि शब्दः प्रत्यक्षादयश्चानुगृहीता भवन्ति । अन्यथा प्रत्यक्षादयो ऽत्यन्तमपबाधिताः (म्स् अ; @मेव बाधिताः -- एदितिओन्) स्युः । नैतत्सारम् । प्रमाणसामर्थ्यानुसारेण प्रमेये काचित्कल्पना स्यात् । प्रमाणे तु स्वरससिद्धं परित्यज्य कल्पनायां न निबन्धनमस्ति । तस्मात्प्रमाणानुसारेण विकल्पसमुच्चयव्यवस्थाः कल्प्यन्ते, नोभयानुग्रहात् । नोभयमनुगृहीतव्यमिति प्रमाणमस्ति । ते एव प्रमाणे इति चेत् --- यदि मतम्, न प्रमाणस्य प्रमाणान्तरादनुग्राह्यत्वम्, अपि तु स्वत एव । प्रमाणत्वादेव हि तस्य तेनार्थव्यवस्थापना --- यथा तर्हि ततो ऽर्थो ऽवगम्यते तथा व्यवस्थापनीयः । एवं तदनुगृहीतं भवति । अन्यथा बाधितं स्यात् । अप्रमाणिका चार्थव्यवस्था, ततः स्वरसेनाप्रतीतेः, अन्यस्य चाभावात्, इतरेतराश्रयप्रसङ्गाच्च । प्रामाण्यात्सिद्धादर्थान्तरे प्रतीतिः प्रामाण्यान्यथानुपपत्त्या कल्पनीया, तत्प्रतीतेश्च प्रामाण्यम् । स्वरसलभ्ये त्वर्थे प्रतीतित एव प्रामाण्यमिति नेतरेतराश्रयता । तस्माद्विरोधे बाध एव पूर्वस्य प्रमाणानुसारी, तथा प्रतीतेः । नोत्तरस्य विषयान्तरकल्पना । न खलु रजतज्ञानानुग्रहाय शुक्तिशकलज्ञानस्य गोचरो ऽपरः कल्प्यते । न च प्रत्यक्षादीनामनन्यगतित्वादनवकाशत्वम् । या खलु रजतादिविभ्रमाणां गतिः, सा तेषामपि । यदि तेषामुपचरितः कल्पितो वा विषयः, प्रत्यक्षादीनामपि तथा । अथासत्त्वात्तस्याविषया अविद्यमानार्थाः प्रत्यक्षादयो ऽप्येवम् । तस्मादविवक्षितार्थत्वमुपचरितार्थत्वं [क्क्स्_43] वा गतिरुभयोरविशिष्टा । एतेनेदमपि पराकृतम्, यदाहुः --- शब्दस्य प्रमाणान्तरविरोधे दृष्टमुपचरितार्थत्वमविवक्षितार्थत्वं वा लोके । तस्मात्प्रत्यक्षादिविरोधे वेदान्तानां तथाभाव इति, प्रत्यक्षादिष्वपि तथा दर्शनादिति । यत्तु मुख्यत्वात्प्रतिष्ठितार्थैरपहतविषय आम्नाय इति । अत एव बाधकः, शुक्तिज्ञानवत् । न च तदनुसारेणार्थकल्पनामर्हति, अनपेक्षत्वात् । न, तदधीनमस्य प्रमाणत्वम् । न तैः संभूयकारित्वम्, नाम्नायस्य प्रत्यक्षादीनां चैकवाक्यभावः । परस्परानपेक्षो ह्युभयत्र बुद्ध्युत्पादः । तत्र परबलीयस्त्वं न्याय्यम् । यथोक्तम् ---

‘पूर्वात्परबलीयस्त्वं तत्र नाम प्रतीयताम् । अन्योन्यनिरपेक्षाणां यत्र जन्म धियां भवेत्ऽ; ॥ यत्र त्वेकवाक्यतया संभूयकारित्वं तत्रानुपजातविरोधितया स्वरसवृत्त्या मुख्ये स्थिते, प्रथमया वृत्त्या तदेकवाक्यत्वं प्रतिपत्तुमशक्नुवन्ति तदपेक्षितार्थसमर्पणानुपपत्तेः परपदानि द्वितीयया वृत्त्या पूर्वापेक्षितमर्थं समर्पयन्त्येकवाक्यतासामर्थ्यादिति मुख्यबलीयस्त्वम् । यत्तु व्याकुलत्वादिति, तत्रोच्यते --- स्याद्व्याकुलत्वम्, यदि कर्मविधयो भेदप्रतिपादनपराः स्युः । ते तु सिद्धं भेदमुपाश्रित्य ‘इदमनेनेत्थं साधयेत्ऽ; इति पुरुषहितानुशासनप्रधानाः । स्यादेतत् । असति भेदे ऽंशत्रयप्रत्यस्तमयात्कुतो हितानुशासनम्? उच्यते --- यथा खलु श्येनादिषु ‘न हिंस्यात्सर्वा भूतानिऽ; इति प्रतिषेधात्साध्यांशप्रत्यस्तमये ऽप्यनुशासनम्, एवं सर्वत्र सर्वांशप्रत्यस्तमये ऽपि । तथा हि --- निषिद्धानर्थोदया कथं हिंसा साध्या स्यात्? अथ भवति कस्य चित्तीव्रक्रोधाक्रान्तस्वान्ततया समुद्धतध्वान्ततिरस्कृतविवेकविज्ञानस्यानर्थमप्यर्थत्वेन पश्यतः शास्त्रोपदेशमतिक्रामतः, तथा ज्योतिष्टोमादिषु निसर्गजाविद्योपदर्शिता अप्रतिबुद्धानां त्रयो ऽप्यंशाः, तानुपाश्रित्य तेषामनुशासनम् । प्रतिबुद्धास्तु कर्मविधिभिर्नानुशिष्यन्ते । यथा श्येनादिविधिभिरपजितक्रोधारातयः । तदेवं व्यवहारसिद्धभेदाश्रयेषु कर्मविधिषु यद्यपि भेदप्रतीतिरस्ति [क्क्स्_44], तथापि तेषामतत्परत्वान् न तत्र प्रामाण्यं वृत्तान्तेष्विवार्थवादपदानाम् । तथा च कुतस्तैर्वेदान्तानां पराहतिः, वेदान्तैर्वा तेषाम्? अपि च प्रत्यक्षादिष्वेव पराहतिरुपलभ्यते, बाध्यबाधकभावदर्शनाद्रजतशुक्तिशकलादिज्ञानेषु, भेदाभेदप्रतीतेश्च सर्वत्र । तदेवं बलवत्त्वे ऽप्याम्नायस्य यो नाम मन्दधीर्लौकिकवचसां प्रत्यक्षादिविरोध उपचरितार्थत्वदर्शनाल्लोकवद्वेदे ऽपि शब्दवृत्तमिति मन्यते, यो वा निरूढनिबिडतया भेददर्शनान्धकारस्य प्रत्यक्षादीनामेव बलवत्त्वं मन्यते, लोकवचसां च तैर्बाधदर्शनात्, तत्प्रतिबोधनाय विरोधो निरस्यते, न हि यो नाम मन्दविषेण वृश्चिकेन दष्टो म्रियते, नासौ न चिकित्स्यत इति । तत्र प्रत्यक्षे त्रयः कल्पाः --- वस्तुस्वरूपविधिः वस्त्वन्तरस्य व्यवच्छेदः, उभयं वेत्ति, उभयस्मिन्नपि त्रैविध्यम् --- यौगपद्यम्, व्यवच्छेदपूर्वको विधिः, विधिपूर्वको व्यवच्छेद इति । तत्र वस्त्वन्तरव्यवच्छेदे उभयस्मिन् वा भेदः प्रत्यक्षगोचर इति भवति विरोधः । स्वरूपविधिमात्रे तु कस्यचिद्व्यवच्छेदेन शून्ये न भेदः प्रमाणार्थः, न हि व्यवच्छेदादृते भेदसिद्धिः । विधिमात्रव्यापारं च प्रत्यक्षम्, अतो न विरोधः कथमित्युच्यते ---

लब्धरूपे क्वचित्किञ्चित्तादृग् एव निषिध्यते । विधानमन्तरेणातो न विषेधस्य संभवः
