dāhapākavibhāgena kṛśānurna hi bhedavān /
nārthakriyābhedādbhāvānāṃ parasparāpekṣo rūpabhedaḥ pratīyate, nāpyanumātuṃ śakyate / vyapadeśabhedamātraṃ tu syāt, ekasminnapi vahnau dāhapākādikāryabhedadṛṣṭeḥ / atha matam --- rūpādisamūho vahniḥ / tatra rūpātprakāśaḥ, sparśāddāha iti / [kks_51] kāmam, dāhapākau tu sparśādeva / tau ca loke pratītibhedau satyapi saṃyogidravyavikriyāsāmānye / karma caikaṃ saṃyogavibhāgasaṃskārāṇāṃ hetuḥ, ātmā cecchādīnām, sattvādayaśca pratyekamabhedāllāghavaprakāśādīnām, rūpādayo jñānaviśeṣāṇāṃ sajātīyakṣaṇānāṃ cetyutprekṣitavyam / nanu nārthakriyābhedamātrādbhedaṃ brūmaḥ, api tu tatrāsaṃbhāvinyā adṛṣṭāyāḥ / yathā cakṣuṣi satyapyadṛṣṭāyāśca badhire tatrāsaṃbhāvinyāḥ śabdabuddherindriyabhedaḥ / parasparāsaṃbhavikāryāśca prāyeṇa bhāvāḥ, anyakāryasyānyatrādarśanāt / atha kāryāsaṃbhavaḥ kathaṃ pratyetavyaḥ? nanūktaṃ tatrādarśanāt / na tarhyasaṃbhavaḥ / yasya khalvadvayaṃ jagattasya kāryajātamekatraiva dṛśyata iti kathamadarśanam? tatra siddhe bhede tatrādarśanam, tatrādarśanācca bhedasiddhiritītaretarāśrayānna bhedānumānam / atha matam --- adṛṣṭasya darśanāditi / tadasat, ekasmādapi kramavatāṃ kāryāṇāṃ darśanāt / syādetat --- ekāntato 'bhede kāryadarśanādarśane na yukte, viśeṣābhāvāt / na tarhi kāryabhedo 'bhedamapabādhate / tadanupamardena viśeṣamātrānumānaṃ syāt / tacca kalpanāviṣayaṃ naivāvajānīmahe, vastusatastasyāyogāt, tattvānyatvayorasaṃbhavāt / yastu kṣaṇikavādī tattvameva viśeṣasya na manyate, tasyāsati kāraṇasvabhāvābhede kathaṃ tulyasvabhāvakāryotpādaḥ / atha niranvayavināśānāmapi kalpanāviṣayādabhedātkāryasya tulyatā / hanta! tarhi bhedādeva kalpanāviṣayātkāryabhedasiddhermudhā kāraṇabhedakalpanā / atha kāryābhede na (atha na kāryābhedena -- edition) kāraṇasvabhāvābhedo 'pekṣyeta, bhinnasvabhāvebhyaḥ sahakāribhya ekakāryotpatteḥ, yathā cakṣurādibhyo rūpavijñānasya (rūpādijñānasya ms a, ms c; rūpādijñānasya -- edition) / yathā tarhi kāryasvabhāvābhedāya na kāraṇasvabhāvābhedo 'pekṣyate, tathā tadbhedāya kāraṇabhedo 'pi nāpekṣitavyaḥ / api cānekakāraṇajanye 'pyekasmin kārye kāraṇavyāpāraviṣayabhedastenaiva varṇitaḥ, yathā rūpajñānasya --- cakṣuṣo rūpagrahaṇaniyamaḥ, samanantarajñānādupalambhātmatā, viṣayāttadākārateti / yadi ca kāryatulyatvaṃ na hetusāmyakṛtam, na kāryāddhetvanumānaṃ syāt, bhinnajātīyādapi tulyajātīyotpattisaṃbhavāt / hetvabhedaścenna [kks_52] kāryābheda upayujyate, kastulyajātīyādvijātīyasya janma nivārayet? tatra yathā vyāvahārikādabhedātkāryābhedastathā vyāvahārikādbhedātkāryabheda iti na viśeṣaḥ / syādetat --- kalpitaścedbhedaḥ kāryabhedāya prabhuḥ, na tarhi kalpitaḥ / na hyanyatparamārthasato lakṣaṇamarthakriyāsāmarthyāt / tulyamidamabhede 'pi /

yo 'pi manyate --- yugapadviruddhārthakriyādarśanādbhedāvagatiḥ / tathā hi --- jananamaraṇavṛddhikṣayasthānagamanaśokaharṣādivividhaviruddhadharmasamupetamekadā viśvamupalabhyate / tadbhedavaditi gamyate / tasyāpīdamevottaramāvṛttyā --- dāhapākavibhāgeneti / katham? idaṃ tāvadayaṃ praṣṭavyaḥ --- ko viruddhārthaḥ? yadyekatrāsaṃbhavaḥ, so 'siddhaḥ / atha parasparavyavacchinnātmatā, jananādayaśca paraspararūpanivṛttyātmāna iti / na tarhyato bhedasiddhiḥ / ekasminnapi vahnau dagdhṛtvapaktṛtvadarśanāt / na hi parasparavyavacchedamantareṇa nānātvaṃ dharmāṇām / tataścedbhedaḥ, nānekadharmakamekaṃ kiñcitsyāt / atha parasparābhāvātmataiva virodhaḥ --- naikasmin sa eva bhavati, na ca bhavatīti / tato bhedāvasāyaḥ / tadasat / na hyevaṃ dharmāveva, kutastayorvirodhādbhedāvagatiḥ / khapuṣpādiṣu cobhayābhāvādubhayaprasaṅgaḥ / atha vadhyaghātakabhāvo (vadhyaghātuka@ -- edition) virodhaḥ --- harṣaḥ śokaṃ hanti śokaśca tam, evamitareṣvapi / tatrāpi nājāta eko 'nyaṃ nāśayati, nānyādhikaraṇam / tasmādekādhikaraṇo bhūtvā nāśayatīti vācyam / evaṃ ca tayorekādhikaraṇatvadarśanānna taddarśanenādhikaraṇabhedānumānamavyabhicāram / atha bhāvarūpatadvyavacchedātmāno dharmā virodhinaḥ --- nityatvānityatvamūrtatvāmūrtatvādayaḥ / tatsaṃbandhādbhedagatiḥ / tadapi na / yato nāvaśyam, yo yatra bhavati, sa taṃ vyāpnoti / na hi rathādayastatsaṃyogādayo vā nabho vyaśnuvate, anyān vā saṃyoginaḥ pṛthivyādīn, avacchinnatvāt / evamavacchinnā [kks_53] dharmā anavacchinnamanantamarthamāśrayanto 'pi na vyaśnuvate / ato naikasminnapi bhāvābhāvavirodhaḥ / yastu manyeta --- arthakriyābhedo 'rthakriyāvyavasthā / tato bhedādhigamaḥ / ekatve hi na vyavasthā yujyate / tathā ca payaso 'pi tailaṃ tilebhyaśca dadhi syāt / tathaikasmiñjāyamāne sarvaṃ jāyeta, naśyati ca naśyet / anyathā bheda eva śabdāntareṇoktaḥ syāt / taduktam --- sahotpattivināśau sarvaṃ ca sarvatropayujyeta iti / tasyāpīdamevottaram --- dāhapākavibhāgeneti / yadi kāryanānātvaṃ vyavasthā, na tayā tilānāṃ payasaśca bhedaṃ pratipadyate / atha payaso dadhno janma, nānyata iti vyavasthā / nānyatvaṃ siddhayā vyavasthayā pramitsitaṃ tallakṣaṇamanupraveṣṭumarhati, tasyā asiddhiprasaṅgāt / tasmāddadhijananaśaktistadabhāvaśca vyavasthā / tato bhedaḥ / na hyekaviṣaya ekasya śaktyaśaktī yujyete iti --- sa cāyaṃ virodhidharmayogo bhedaheturanantarameva nirāsi / yathā khalu dīrghakālāḥ padārthā mitakālairdharmaiḥ saṃbadhyamānāstaddharmāṇo 'taddharmāṇaśca na virodhapadabhājaḥ, tathā parimitadeśairvipuladeśā anantāśca / kathamanantasyāntavān dharma iti cet, vyatireke 'nivarcanīyatve vā nāstyasaṃbhāvanāvakāśaḥ / avyatireke 'pi dīrghakālasyeva mitakālaḥ / yo 'pi dīrghakālamarthaṃ na pratipadyate taṃ pratīdaṃ punaḥ paṭhitavyam --- dāhapākavibhāgeneti / eko 'pi vahniḥ kiñcideva dahati pacati ca / tathā ca dāhakaścādāhakaśca na bhidyate / tathā na dāhāntarāṇi pākāntarāṇi vā karoti tasminneva dāhye pākye ca / tathā bījādayaḥ pratyekaṃ samarthā api nāṅkurāntarāṇi janayanti, nāpi sāmagrī / tathā ca janakatvamajanakatvamiti / athaikasminneva janakaśaktiḥ, anyaṃ pradhvastamāgāminaṃ vaikaṃ kiṃ na janayati / atha tatraivaiṣāṃ sāmarthyam, nānyatra tulyajātīye 'pi / kutaḥ? tasyaivotpatteḥ, kāryagamyatvācca sāmarthyasya / tathā ca na śaktiraśaktiśceti virodhaḥ / abhede 'pi tarhi payasastilānāṃ dadhno 'nutpattau na virodhaḥ / tathā hi --- yasya tāvaddadhnaḥ payaso janma na tasya tilebhyo 'nutpattiḥ, yena śaktyaśaktivirodhād [kks_54] bhedaḥ syāt / kutaḥ? tilānāṃ payaso 'bhedāt / atha dadhyantarasyānutpattervirodhaḥ / tacca na, anyatrāśaktestatraiva śakterbījādīnāmiva / na hi samarthamityeva kāraṇaṃ sarvaṃ tulyajātīyaṃ janayati, ekasmādeva sarvatulyajātīyakāryotpattiprasaṅgāt / atha matam --- arthakriyāsu bhedena viniyogādbhedamadhyavasyāmaḥ / dadhne hi payo viniyujyate, na sikateti / tadapyanaikāntikam, ekatve 'pi bhedena viniyogadarśanāt / tadevārthavastu sahakārisametaṃ viniyujyate, na kevalam / atha matam --- bhinnameva tat, sahakārisannidhānopādhibhedāt / aupādhikastarhi pratyayamātraniveśī bhedaḥ, na paramārthataḥ / tathābhūtaśca bhāvabhedo hyanujñāyata eva / yo 'pi kṣaṇikatvena bhedamāha, tasyāpi bhedasya tulyatvātsarvaṃ sarvatra viniyujyate, na vā kiñcitkvacit, adṛṣṭasāmarthyatvāt / atha kalpanāviṣayādabhedāttatsiddhiḥ, parasyāpi tādṛśādbhedāditi na viśeṣa ityuktam / yo 'pyekasyobhayaṃ pratijānīte --- bhedamabhedaṃ ca, tenaikatrāpi viruddhadharmāveśamabhyupayatā durlabha eva dadhno janakatvājanakatvābhyāṃ tilapayasorvibhāga iti /

tadevam ---
ekasyaivaiṣa mahimā bhedasaṃpādanāsahaḥ
units.translation:
Fire is not divided into distinct entities merely because it burns and cooks in different ways. A difference in what things do does not establish that their natures depend on one another or differ; nor can such a difference be inferred. At most, there may be a difference in how one names them, since even one fire is observed to perform different functions, such as burning and cooking. Someone may say that fire is a collection of qualities: light comes from its form, and burning from touch. Granted; cooking and burning are both understood through touch. Yet the world recognizes the difference between the two even though both arise from a common interaction with an object. A single action is the cause of conjunction, separation, and the impression of movement; the Self is the cause of desire and the like; the qualities of lucidity and so forth each account for lightness, clarity, and the like; form and other qualities are causes of particular cognitions and successive moments of the same kind. One might accordingly suppose that these different functions arise from different qualities.

A critic may say that we do not infer difference merely from a difference in function, but from seeing that a particular function, which could not occur there, is absent. The difference between the senses, for example, is inferred because the cognition of sound cannot occur through the eye, despite the eye being present. Things generally have effects that cannot occur through one another, since an effect produced by one thing is not seen elsewhere. But how can we know that an effect is impossible in a different thing? It was said: because it is not seen there. Then it is not impossible. For one who holds that the world is nondual, every kind of effect is seen in the one reality; how could there be absence? First the difference would have to be established, and only then could one say that the effect is not seen in one thing. If absence of an effect establishes difference, while difference is needed to establish its absence, the reasoning is circular and proves nothing.

One may reply that something is seen where one thing is absent. That does not work, since effects that arise successively can be seen in the same thing. Someone might say that if things were absolutely identical, it would be unreasonable to see one effect and not another, since there would be no difference. But then a mere particular distinction could be inferred without disturbing the identity of the thing. We do not deny such a distinction in a conceptual account; it is not possible for it to be real in the thing, since a real thing cannot be both identical with and different from another.

A momentary-cognition theorist does not accept a real nature at all for a specific feature. If there is no identity in the cause’s nature, how could effects of the same kind arise from it? One might say that even effects arising from unrelated destruction appear alike because their sameness is conceptual. Then one could just as well say that effects differ because the difference is conceptual; there would be no point in imagining a real difference in causes. Or one may say that, even when effects are the same, the nature of their causes need not be the same, because a single effect can arise from different auxiliary causes, as visual cognition of color arises from the eye and other conditions. In that case, just as the cause’s nature need not be the same when the effect’s nature is the same, a cause need not be different when the effects are different. The critic himself explains the different roles of causes even when they produce one effect, as in cognition of color: the eye is specifically for seeing color, a preceding cognition gives the cognition its character as an awareness, and the object gives it its form. If a common kind of effect were not due to a shared cause, it would not be possible to infer a cause from an effect, because a cause of an entirely different kind could produce the same kind of effect. And if a difference in effect does not require a difference in the cause, what would prevent an effect of a different kind from arising from a cause of the same kind? Just as the practical identity of things can account for practical identity in their effects, practical difference can account for practical differences in effects; there is no distinction.

Someone may object that imagined difference must be effective because we observe different results, so it cannot be merely imagined; nothing is ultimately real apart from its capacity to produce effects. The same applies to identity as well. Another says that difference is understood from seeing opposed effects at the same time. The world is observed to possess at once many opposing properties—birth and death, growth and decline, standing and movement, grief and joy, and so forth—and therefore things must be different. The reply is again the same: fire performs burning and cooking, as was said. The objector must first say what the opposition is. If it means that both properties cannot occur in one thing, that has not been established. If it means that each is the absence of the other, then birth, death, and the other properties are not established as differences, since one fire is observed both to burn and to cook. Properties are not many without being mutually exclusive. If difference is established through that mutual exclusion, then nothing could be one thing with many properties.

If opposition means that each property is the absence of the other—one thing both is and is not—then difference is inferred from that. This too is unsound: these are not even established as properties; how can opposition between them establish difference? In the case of a hare’s horn and similar things, both sides are absent, which would entail both outcomes. Or one might define opposition as the relation of killer and killed: joy destroys sorrow, and sorrow destroys joy, and so on for the rest. Even there, one thing does not destroy another that has never arisen, nor something in another location. Therefore, being based in one and the same thing...

...one must explain whether they are based in one and the same thing. Since both are observed in a single basis, they do not reliably establish a difference in the basis. One may say that the opposed qualities are positive properties that exclude one another, such as permanence and impermanence, or form and formlessness; their relation establishes difference. That is not so. It is not necessary that a quality extend everywhere that its bearer exists. Chariots and other things, or the conjunctions they have, do not extend through space or through other things conjoined with them, such as earth, because they are limited. In the same way, limited qualities can belong to an unlimited, infinite thing without extending through it. Thus there is no opposition between positive and negative qualities in one thing.

Someone may say that we establish difference from the ordered distribution of causal functions: if things were one, that order would not make sense. Milk would produce oil, sesame seeds would produce curds, and whenever one thing arose, everything would arise or perish with it. Otherwise, as it is said, everything would arise and perish together, and anything could serve any purpose anywhere. The answer is again the difference between burning and cooking. If the variety of effects is the order, it does not establish a difference between milk and sesame. If the order is instead defined by milk producing curd and sesame not producing it, then one is relying on the producing and non-producing capacities to establish the order. But the order cannot be used to establish a difference whose very definition depends on the order; that would be circular. The claim that a power to produce and a lack of power cannot belong to the same thing is precisely the argument from opposed properties that was just refuted.

Long-lasting things can be associated with qualities that last only a short time without contradiction; likewise, things that occupy a limited region can be associated with qualities that cover a wide or even unlimited region. If someone says that an unlimited thing cannot have a quality that is limited, that is not impossible: either the quality is different from the thing, or their relation is indeterminable. Even if they are not different, the relation can be like that of a long-lasting object to a temporary quality. For one who does not understand this, the example of burning and cooking should be repeated. Even a single fire burns or cooks only particular things; the one that burns is not different from the one that does not burn, nor does it make separate kinds of burning and cooking in the very same thing. Seeds and other causes, though each capable of producing something, do not produce different sprouts; nor does an entire collection of materials produce every possible effect. Someone may ask why a cause with the power to produce one thing should not also produce something else that is already destroyed or has yet to arise. The answer is that its power is specific to just that effect, not to another, even one of the same kind. How is this known? That effect alone arises, and causal capacity is inferred from the result. Thus having and not having a particular power are not incompatible properties.

Even if things are non-different, then, it is no contradiction that milk does not produce what sesame seeds produce, or vice versa. For the curd that arises from milk does not fail to arise from sesame because of a contradiction in the cause’s capacity; sesame is not different from milk. Someone may say that the non-production of a different curd is the contradiction. That is not so: a cause can be incapable in one case and capable in another, as with seeds and their particular effects. Being capable does not mean that a cause produces every effect of the same kind; otherwise the same cause would produce all effects of that kind.

Someone may say that we establish difference because things are put to different uses: milk is used for curd, not sand. That too is inconclusive, since the same thing may be used differently. The very same material thing is used in conjunction with an auxiliary condition, not by itself. Someone may reply that it is then different because the auxiliary condition is present, and so there is a difference in its limiting condition. In that case the difference is only contextual, entering into a cognition; it is not ultimately real. A practical difference of just that kind is admitted. Even the momentarist who claims that difference follows from momentariness faces the same issue: unless there is an observable capacity, everything could be used for everything, or nothing could be used for anything. It was already said that conceptual identity can account for this just as well as conceptual difference.

Even someone who accepts both difference and non-difference in one thing—allowing opposed qualities in a single basis—will have difficulty accounting for the distinction between milk and sesame by their capacity and incapacity to produce curd. Thus:

“This is the glory of the one alone: it does not admit the production of difference.”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 1 · Tarka — reasoning about perception, difference, and nonduality

units.deva:
वह्नेरिव यदा भावभेदकल्पस्तदा मुधा । एकत्र क्रियाभेदोपलब्धेः, असंभवस्य चासिद्धेः, अदृष्टदर्शनस्य चाभेदबाधने सामर्थ्याभावात्, विशेषमात्रहेतुत्वात्तस्य च तत्त्वान्यत्वाभ्यामनिर्वाच्यस्य कल्पनास्पदत्वात्, अभेदादिव च तादृशात् कार्याभेदस्य भेदादपि तद्विधाद्भेदस्योपपत्तेः, विरोधस्य चानैकान्तिकत्वादसिद्धत्वाद्वा व्यवस्थायाश्च, विनियोगभेदस्य चानैकान्तिकत्वात्, अभेदादिव च कल्पिताद्भेदात्तत्सिद्धेः, भेदाभेदयोश्चैकत्र समवाये शक्त्यशक्त्योर्विनियोगाविनियोगयोश्चैकसमवायसंभवादेकस्यैवैष को ऽप्यचिन्त्यः सामर्थ्यातिशयो निखिलभेदप्रपञ्चसंपादनायै प्रभुः पावकस्येव पाकप्लोषादिप्रविभागनिमित्तं यदोपपद्यते [क्क्स्_55] तदा भेदकल्पनमकारणम्, एकस्मादपि तत्सिद्धेः --- इति पूर्वोपसंहारः । तदेतदृचाभ्यनूक्तम् --- ‘एतावानस्य महिमाऽ; इति । एतत्परिमाणमस्य सामर्थ्यम् --- यदेको ऽपि ‘सहस्रशीर्षाऽ; इति ‘यद्भूतं यच्च भव्यम्ऽ; इति । पूर्वर्ग्द्वयनिर्दिष्टविविधविरुद्धाभिमतधर्मकार्यव्यवहाराश्रयः कथमिति । ‘अतःऽप्रत्यक्षाभिमतात्, ‘पुरुष एवेदं सर्वम्ऽइति वादृष्टनिर्दिष्टात् । ‘उतामृतत्वस्यऽइति वा देवमनुष्यलोकभेदेन प्रपञ्चादेकैकस्मात्समस्ताच्च वृद्धतरः पुरुषः । तेनास्मिन् परिमितानां विरुद्धाभिमतानामप्यनन्ते न समावेशो न युज्यते । तदेव ज्यायस्त्वं दर्शयति --- ‘पादो ऽस्य विश्वाऽ; इति । कृत्स्नो ऽपि तावद्भूतप्रपञ्चो ऽस्य कनीयान् भाग इति, किं पुनः प्रत्येकम् । तथा हि --- ‘त्रिपात्ऽइवापरिमितमनन्तं मरणादिभूतप्रपञ्चधर्मशून्यं रूपं ‘दिविऽप्रद्योतावस्थायां वर्तते, प्रमोदावस्थायां वा, सूर्यमण्डले, द्युस्थाने वा । तत्र हि तदुपास्यम् । तद्धि तस्योपलब्धिस्थानमिति तत्रेत्युच्यते । अपरः कल्पः --- कल्पिते ऽपि कार्यभेदाद्यवस्थाया वा कारणभेदे किमिति न कार्यान्तरम्? किमिति वा न संकरः, विपरीता वा व्यवस्था? भेदे ऽपि पयसः, तिलेभ्य एव तैलं न सिकताभ्यः? भिना अपि चैककार्याश्चक्षुरालोकादयः, शरशृङ्गादयश्च । भेदे ऽपि च तिलेभ्यस्तैलं पयसो दधि, न तु पयसस्तैलं तिलेभ्यो दधि? यदि मतम् --- अचिन्त्येभ्यो भावसामर्थ्येभ्यः --- अचिन्त्यानुपपत्तितो भावसामर्थ्यानि ‘कस्मात्? कथम्?ऽ; इति, कार्यदर्शनोन्नेयव्यवस्थानि --- तेभ्यः कार्यस्य भेदः, व्यवस्था, न विपर्ययश्चेति । यद्येवम्, एकस्यैव सो ऽस्तु सामर्थ्यातिशयः --- यदनेकं व्यवस्थितमविपरीतं च कार्यम् । तन्मात्रेण तत्सिद्धेरप्रामाणिका भावानां भावकल्पनेति । स्यादेतत् --- वह्नेरपि शक्तिभेदनिबन्धनः कार्यभेदः । तन्नैकस्मादनेकं [क्क्स्_56] कार्यम् । तत्र यदि वह्निरपि कारणम्, कथं नैकस्मादनेकं कार्यम्? अथ शक्तीनामेव कारणत्वमभिप्रैति । तत्रोच्यते ---
यथैव भिन्नशक्तीनामभिन्नं रूपमाश्रयः

vahneriva yadā bhāvabhedakalpastadā mudhā /
ekatra kriyābhedopalabdheḥ, asaṃbhavasya cāsiddheḥ, adṛṣṭadarśanasya cābhedabādhane sāmarthyābhāvāt, viśeṣamātrahetutvāttasya ca tattvānyatvābhyāmanirvācyasya kalpanāspadatvāt, abhedādiva ca tādṛśāt kāryābhedasya bhedādapi tadvidhādbhedasyopapatteḥ, virodhasya cānaikāntikatvādasiddhatvādvā vyavasthāyāśca, viniyogabhedasya cānaikāntikatvāt, abhedādiva ca kalpitādbhedāttatsiddheḥ, bhedābhedayoścaikatra samavāye śaktyaśaktyorviniyogāviniyogayoścaikasamavāyasaṃbhavādekasyaivaiṣa ko 'pyacintyaḥ sāmarthyātiśayo nikhilabhedaprapañcasaṃpādanāyai prabhuḥ pāvakasyeva pākaploṣādipravibhāganimittaṃ yadopapadyate [kks_55] tadā bhedakalpanamakāraṇam, ekasmādapi tatsiddheḥ --- iti pūrvopasaṃhāraḥ / tadetadṛcābhyanūktam --- ‘etāvānasya mahimā'; iti / etatparimāṇamasya sāmarthyam --- yadeko 'pi ‘sahasraśīrṣā'; iti ‘yadbhūtaṃ yacca bhavyam'; iti / pūrvargdvayanirdiṣṭavividhaviruddhābhimatadharmakāryavyavahārāśrayaḥ kathamiti / ‘ataḥ'pratyakṣābhimatāt, ‘puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam'iti vādṛṣṭanirdiṣṭāt / ‘utāmṛtatvasya'iti vā devamanuṣyalokabhedena prapañcādekaikasmātsamastācca vṛddhataraḥ puruṣaḥ / tenāsmin parimitānāṃ viruddhābhimatānāmapyanante na samāveśo na yujyate / tadeva jyāyastvaṃ darśayati --- ‘pādo 'sya viśvā'; iti / kṛtsno 'pi tāvadbhūtaprapañco 'sya kanīyān bhāga iti, kiṃ punaḥ pratyekam / tathā hi --- ‘tripāt'ivāparimitamanantaṃ maraṇādibhūtaprapañcadharmaśūnyaṃ rūpaṃ ‘divi'pradyotāvasthāyāṃ vartate, pramodāvasthāyāṃ vā, sūryamaṇḍale, dyusthāne vā / tatra hi tadupāsyam / taddhi tasyopalabdhisthānamiti tatretyucyate / aparaḥ kalpaḥ --- kalpite 'pi kāryabhedādyavasthāyā vā kāraṇabhede kimiti na kāryāntaram? kimiti vā na saṃkaraḥ, viparītā vā vyavasthā? bhede 'pi payasaḥ, tilebhya eva tailaṃ na sikatābhyaḥ? bhinā api caikakāryāścakṣurālokādayaḥ, śaraśṛṅgādayaśca / bhede 'pi ca tilebhyastailaṃ payaso dadhi, na tu payasastailaṃ tilebhyo dadhi? yadi matam --- acintyebhyo bhāvasāmarthyebhyaḥ --- acintyānupapattito bhāvasāmarthyāni ‘kasmāt? katham?'; iti, kāryadarśanonneyavyavasthāni --- tebhyaḥ kāryasya bhedaḥ, vyavasthā, na viparyayaśceti / yadyevam, ekasyaiva so 'stu sāmarthyātiśayaḥ --- yadanekaṃ vyavasthitamaviparītaṃ ca kāryam / tanmātreṇa tatsiddheraprāmāṇikā bhāvānāṃ bhāvakalpaneti /

syādetat --- vahnerapi śaktibhedanibandhanaḥ kāryabhedaḥ / tannaikasmādanekaṃ [kks_56] kāryam / tatra yadi vahnirapi kāraṇam, kathaṃ naikasmādanekaṃ kāryam? atha śaktīnāmeva kāraṇatvamabhipraiti / tatrocyate ---
yathaiva bhinnaśaktīnāmabhinnaṃ rūpamāśrayaḥ
units.translation:
This concludes the earlier argument: when differences among things are imagined as their real nature, that is pointless, as with fire. One fire is observed to perform different actions; the impossibility of their belonging to one thing has not been established. The fact that one does not see something is not enough to defeat non-difference; it establishes only a particular feature. That feature, being indescribable as either identical with or different from the thing, may be only a conceptual construction. Effects of that kind can be explained by imagined identity just as well as by imagined difference. Contradiction is not decisive, since different causes can lead to different arrangements, and the deployment of things in different ways is not conclusive either. Just as an imagined difference may arise from an imagined non-difference, non-difference itself can be established through an imagined difference. Even opposed features—capacity and incapacity, use and non-use—can belong to one basis. This is the one wondrous and unsurpassed power that can produce the entire manifold of differences, just as fire accounts for distinctions such as cooking and burning. Since the same effects can be explained from one thing, imagining difference has no cause.

This is expressed in the verse: “This is his greatness.” This much is the measure of his power: though one, he is “thousand-headed” and is “what has been and what will be.” How can one thing support the various opposed qualities and effects described in the preceding two verses? The answer is: “From this”—from what is assumed to be perceived by the senses—“the person is all this,” as scripture says. Or “from this” may mean that, in comparison with the worlds of gods and human beings, the Person is greater than each world and than all of them together. Thus, it is not unreasonable that finite, apparently opposed qualities should be included in what is infinite. The verse shows this greatness: “All beings are one quarter of him.” The entire world of beings is only a small part of him; how much less is each individual thing? Indeed, the other three quarters are boundless and infinite, free of the conditions of worldly beings such as death. They abide in the radiant state above, or in the solar orb or heaven. That is where the object of worship is found; it is referred to as “there” because that is the place where it is realized.

There is another question: even if differences among causes are only imagined through differences in their effects, why should another kind of effect not arise, or why should there be no mixture or reversal in the order? Though milk and sesame are different, oil comes from sesame, not from sand; and curds come from milk, not oil. Things that differ may also share one effect, as the eye, light, and other conditions do in producing visual cognition, or as arrows and horns of a hare do. Even though sesame and milk differ, sesame produces oil and milk produces curds, not oil from milk and curds from sesame. Someone may say this happens because things have unthinkable powers. Those powers, inexplicable in themselves by asking “Why?” or “How?”, are understood from the effects: the distinct effects, their order, and the absence of reversal are inferred from those powers. If so, the one thing itself may have that unsurpassed power: the power to produce many effects in an ordered and non-reversed way. If that alone establishes the effects, there is no means of knowledge for imagining many separate things.

Someone may object that even in fire, different effects are grounded in different powers, so many effects do not arise from one thing. The reply is:

“Just as distinct powers have one and the same support...”

units.deva:
तथा नानाक्रियाहेतुरूपं किं नाभ्युपेयते । एकस्यानेककार्ययोगविरोधाच्छक्तिभेदः कल्प्यते । यदि चैकस्यानेकसंबन्धविरोधः, कथं नानाभूताभिः शक्तिभिरेकः संबध्यते? तत्र यथैकस्यार्थस्वभावस्य नानाशक्तियोगः, तथा नानाकार्ययोगो ऽपि किं नानुज्ञायते? अथ नानाकार्ययोगे विरोधः, न नानाशक्तियोगे । विशेषहेतुर्वाच्यः । अपि च शक्तीनामव्यतिरेकादेकमनेकात्मकमिष्टम् । तत्रैकत्वं स्वाश्रयसमवायिनानेकत्वेन च विरुध्यते । कार्यगतेन त्वाश्रयान्तरसमवायिना विरुध्यत इति सुभाषितम्! अथार्थान्तरत्वमेव शक्तीनाम्, आश्रयार्थो वाच्यः । संश्लेषश्चेत्, न भिन्नत्वे रूपाविभागलक्षणः संश्लेषः, भेद एव न स्यात् । न नैरन्तर्यम्, तच्छक्तिद्रव्यसंयुक्तस्य द्रव्यान्तरस्यापि तच्छक्तित्वप्रसङ्गात् । न हि द्रव्यस्यानन्तरं तच्छक्तेर्व्यवहितं भवति । न हि चक्षुर्द्रव्यस्यानन्तरं रूपस्य नानन्तरम् । विभुत्वाच्चाकाशादीनां सर्वार्थशक्तिव्यवधानाभावात्सर्वशक्तिप्रसङ्गः । तस्मादुपकारविशेषात्कुतश्चिदाश्रयः । तत्र यथा भिन्नासु शक्तिषु तद्भेदादुपकारान् भिन्नानेको ऽर्थस्वभावः करोति, तथा कार्याण्यपीति कस्मान्नेष्यते? एवं तावन्नानुमाने ऽपि भेदाधिगमः, नार्थापत्त्या च । ये तु मन्यन्ते --- सत्यमेतत्, न प्रत्यक्षं भेदाधिगमायालम् । इतरेतराभावांशो हि भावानां भेदः, न सो ऽक्षगोचरः । ‘भावांशेनैव संयोगो योग्यत्वादिन्द्रियस्य हिऽ; । तथा च न लिङ्गगम्यो ऽपि, अदृष्टसंगतित्वात् । अर्थापत्तिरपि कार्यव्यवस्थाहेतुका स्यात् । सा असिद्धे भेदे व्यवस्थाया (म्स् च्; कार्यव्यवस्थाया -- एदितिओन्) एवानुपपत्तेस्तत्रायुक्ता । तस्मात्सदुपलम्भहेतुभ्यः प्रमाणान्तरमेवाभावायोपासनीयम् । विधायकाद्वा प्रमाणान्तरमेव व्यवच्छेदकमभावाख्यम् । तन्निबन्धना [क्क्स्_57] हि भावानामसंकीर्णता (@मसंकीर्णस्वभावता -- एदितिओन्) । यदवोचन् ---

‘वस्त्वसंकरसिद्धिश्च तत्प्रामाण्यसमाश्रयाऽ; । इति । तान् प्रत्युच्यते ---
अन्योन्यसंश्रयाद्भेदो न प्रमान्तरसाधनः

tathā nānākriyāheturūpaṃ kiṃ nābhyupeyate /
ekasyānekakāryayogavirodhācchaktibhedaḥ kalpyate / yadi caikasyānekasaṃbandhavirodhaḥ, kathaṃ nānābhūtābhiḥ śaktibhirekaḥ saṃbadhyate? tatra yathaikasyārthasvabhāvasya nānāśaktiyogaḥ, tathā nānākāryayogo 'pi kiṃ nānujñāyate? atha nānākāryayoge virodhaḥ, na nānāśaktiyoge / viśeṣaheturvācyaḥ / api ca śaktīnāmavyatirekādekamanekātmakamiṣṭam / tatraikatvaṃ svāśrayasamavāyinānekatvena ca virudhyate / kāryagatena tvāśrayāntarasamavāyinā virudhyata iti subhāṣitam! athārthāntaratvameva śaktīnām, āśrayārtho vācyaḥ / saṃśleṣaścet, na bhinnatve rūpāvibhāgalakṣaṇaḥ saṃśleṣaḥ, bheda eva na syāt / na nairantaryam, tacchaktidravyasaṃyuktasya dravyāntarasyāpi tacchaktitvaprasaṅgāt / na hi dravyasyānantaraṃ tacchaktervyavahitaṃ bhavati / na hi cakṣurdravyasyānantaraṃ rūpasya nānantaram / vibhutvāccākāśādīnāṃ sarvārthaśaktivyavadhānābhāvātsarvaśaktiprasaṅgaḥ / tasmādupakāraviśeṣātkutaścidāśrayaḥ / tatra yathā bhinnāsu śaktiṣu tadbhedādupakārān bhinnāneko 'rthasvabhāvaḥ karoti, tathā kāryāṇyapīti kasmānneṣyate? evaṃ tāvannānumāne 'pi bhedādhigamaḥ, nārthāpattyā ca /

ye tu manyante --- satyametat, na pratyakṣaṃ bhedādhigamāyālam / itaretarābhāvāṃśo hi bhāvānāṃ bhedaḥ, na so 'kṣagocaraḥ / ‘bhāvāṃśenaiva saṃyogo yogyatvādindriyasya hi'; / tathā ca na liṅgagamyo 'pi, adṛṣṭasaṃgatitvāt / arthāpattirapi kāryavyavasthāhetukā syāt / sā asiddhe bhede vyavasthāyā (ms c; kāryavyavasthāyā -- edition) evānupapattestatrāyuktā / tasmātsadupalambhahetubhyaḥ pramāṇāntaramevābhāvāyopāsanīyam / vidhāyakādvā pramāṇāntarameva vyavacchedakamabhāvākhyam / tannibandhanā [kks_57] hi bhāvānāmasaṃkīrṇatā (@masaṃkīrṇasvabhāvatā -- edition) / yadavocan ---

‘vastvasaṃkarasiddhiśca tatprāmāṇyasamāśrayā'; / iti / tān pratyucyate ---
anyonyasaṃśrayādbhedo na pramāntarasādhanaḥ
units.translation:
Why not accept that one thing can be the cause of many different actions? A plurality of powers is imagined because it seems incompatible for one cause to produce many different effects. But if one thing can be related to many effects, why not accept many powers in that one thing? If there is a conflict in the one thing’s relation to many effects, why is there no conflict in its relation to many powers? A particular reason would need to be stated. Further, if powers are not different from their bearer, one thing is accepted as having many natures. In that case its oneness conflicts with the many qualities that belong to it. To say that it conflicts only with other things because those qualities are in another substrate is an empty answer. If the powers are entirely different things, then one must explain what supports them and how they are joined. If the relation is conjunction, that cannot explain a real connection where the two are distinct; otherwise there would be no difference at all. Nor is mere proximity enough: any other object connected with the same power-substance would then have to be that power as well. An eye is not followed by form only because it is next to it. Since space and other pervasive things are not obstructed from anything, the same argument would make them connected with every power. Thus one must posit a particular substrate because it contributes something specific. But if a different, multiple nature can make one object support several distinct powers, why cannot the same one object produce several different effects? Difference cannot be established by inference or presumption either. Some say that perception cannot reveal difference, because difference is the mutual absence of things, while only positive aspects are perceived. They say that conjunction is perceived through the positive aspect, and so the senses are suited only to positive things. Difference, then, cannot be inferred from a mark either, because the relation of a mark to what it indicates is not observed. Presumption could depend on the arrangement of effects, but that arrangement cannot be established unless difference has already been established; so it is circular. Therefore, they say, a separate means of knowledge is required to establish absence, or injunction itself is the means of knowledge that excludes other things and makes them non-mixed. The reply to them is:

“Because it depends on one another, difference is not established by another means of knowledge.”

units.deva:
नास्मिन्नयं नायमयमिति भेदाद्विना न धीः । न खलु यद्व्यवच्छिद्यते, यतश्च व्यवच्छिद्यते, तयोरप्रतिपत्तौ व्यवच्छेदगतिः । नानपेक्षितविषयनिषेध्यो निषेधो ऽस्ति । सन् वा शून्यतामापादयेत्, न भेदमित्युक्तम् । तेषामपि वचः ---

‘गृहीत्वा वस्तुसद्भावं स्मृत्वा च प्रतियोगिनम् । मानसं नास्तिताज्ञानं जायते ऽक्षानपेक्षयाऽ; ॥ तयोश्च प्रतिपत्तिर्यदि नासंकीर्णस्वभावयोः, अपि तु वस्तुमात्रत्वेन व्यवच्छेद्यव्यवच्छेदावधिविभागाभावात् । न निषेधसंभवो ऽर्थमात्रे ह्यविभागे । विषयत्वेनापेक्षिते न निषेध्यम् । निषेध्यत्वेनापेक्षिते न विषयविशेषः । तत्रात्यन्ताय निषेधः स्यात् । स च न सिद्धत्वेनासिद्धत्वेन वा युज्यत इत्युक्तम् । कस्यचित्तावत्कुतश्चिद् (कस्यचित्कुतश्चिद् म्स् च्; कस्यचित्कुतश्चिच्च एदितिओन्) भेदप्रतिपत्तौ सर्वस्य सर्वतो भेदगतिः स्यात्, अविशेषात् । तस्मादनेनासंकीर्णस्वभावेन भिन्नावेव प्रतिपद्य विषयनिषेध्यौ ‘नेदमिहऽ; ‘नायमयम्ऽ; इति व्यवच्छेदः प्रतिपत्तव्यः, संभवान्नियमाच्च । न चान्यथा प्रतियोगित्वम्, सामान्योपलब्धौ च स्थाणौ

पुरुषस्याभाव(म्स् अ; पुरुषाभाव@ एदितिओन्)प्रतिपत्त्यभावात् । तथा च सिद्धविषयनिषेध्याङ्गीकरणेन व्यवच्छेदमात्रविधायिन्यभावप्रतिपत्तिः प्रत्यात्ममुपलक्ष्यते । तथा च इतरेतराश्रयत्वम् --- असंकरपूर्वमभावज्ञानम्, ततश्चासंकरसिद्धिरिति । अपि च न प्रमाणानुत्पादमात्रादभावज्ञानम्, सुषुप्तादावनुत्पत्तेः । तस्मात्सत्सु प्रमाणकारणेषु प्रमाणानुत्पादो ऽभावज्ञानहेतुरिष्टः । न च तस्य स्वरूपभेदः कश्चित्, येन सामर्थ्यातिशयाच्चक्षुरादिवद्बोधकः, किं तु नान्तरीयकत्वात् । नान्तरेण प्रमेयाभावं सत्सु प्रमाणहेतुषु प्रमाणानुत्पादः । असत्सु तु सत्यपि प्रमेये तदभावात्स्यादिति । तथा च लिङ्गवज्ज्ञानापेक्षः प्रतिपत्तेर्जनकः, स च यदि वस्त्वन्तरज्ञानम्, [क्क्स्_58] नासिद्धे वस्तुभेदे सिध्यति । ज्ञेयभेदानुमेयो हि ज्ञेयानुमेयानां ज्ञानानां भेदः । तथा च वस्तुभेदसिद्धिपूर्विकैवाभावाद्भेदावगतिरितीतरेतराश्रयत्वम् । अथात्मनो ऽपरिणामः । न स स्तिमितावस्था, सर्वाप्रतिपत्तौ कस्यचिदभावस्यानवगतेः । तस्मात्सत्यपि वस्त्वन्तरज्ञानरूपपरिणामे तज्ज्ञानरूपपरिणामाभावो ऽभावज्ञानहेतुः । न चैष विशेषः प्राग्वस्तुभेदसिद्धेः सिध्यतीति तदेवेतरेतराश्रयत्वम् । ये त्वाहुः --- दर्शनादेव भावानां भेदः सिध्यति । तथा हि --- निर्विकल्पस्य प्रत्यक्षस्य सामान्यविषयत्वमपाकुर्वतोक्तम् --- ‘तदयुक्तं प्रतिद्रव्यं भिन्नरूपोपलम्भनाद्ऽ; इति । यस्तु संयोगात्समवायाद्वा संकरः, सो ऽभावाख्येन प्रमाणेनापनीयत इति । ते प्रागेव प्रत्युक्ताः । ये ऽपि --- विधायकप्रत्यक्षपुरःसरं प्रत्यक्षान्तरमेव वस्तुग्रहणप्रतियोगिस्मरणेतिकर्तव्यतानुगृहीताक्षप्रतिलब्धजन्म व्यवच्छेदकं मन्यन्ते । यथैव सविकल्पस्य वस्तुग्रहणस्य पश्चाज्जन्म, शब्दस्मरणव्यवधिश्च --- न चानैन्द्रियकत्वम्, इतिकर्तव्यताविशेषानुगृहीतादिन्द्रियात्तदुत्पत्तेः --- एवं नास्तीत्यपि ज्ञानस्येति ब्रुवन्तः । तान् प्रतीदमेव वक्तव्यम् --- अन्योन्यसंश्रयाद्भेदो न प्रमान्तरसाधनः । प्रत्यक्षान्तरसाधन इत्यर्थः । ‘अयमसौ न भवतिऽ; इति ज्ञानं प्रत्यक्षं वा प्रमाणान्तरं वा । सर्वथा विषयनिषेध्यविभागादृते न निषेधसंभव इति । किं च
मीयमानैकरूपेषु न निषेधो ऽवकाशवान्
units.iast:
nāsminnayaṃ nāyamayamiti bhedādvinā na dhīḥ /
na khalu yadvyavacchidyate, yataśca vyavacchidyate, tayorapratipattau vyavacchedagatiḥ / nānapekṣitaviṣayaniṣedhyo niṣedho 'sti / san vā śūnyatāmāpādayet, na bhedamityuktam / teṣāmapi vacaḥ ---

‘gṛhītvā vastusadbhāvaṃ smṛtvā ca pratiyoginam /
mānasaṃ nāstitājñānaṃ jāyate 'kṣānapekṣayā'; //

tayośca pratipattiryadi nāsaṃkīrṇasvabhāvayoḥ, api tu vastumātratvena vyavacchedyavyavacchedāvadhivibhāgābhāvāt / na niṣedhasaṃbhavo 'rthamātre hyavibhāge / viṣayatvenāpekṣite na niṣedhyam / niṣedhyatvenāpekṣite na viṣayaviśeṣaḥ / tatrātyantāya niṣedhaḥ syāt / sa ca na siddhatvenāsiddhatvena vā yujyata ityuktam / kasyacittāvatkutaścid (kasyacitkutaścid ms c; kasyacitkutaścicca edition) bhedapratipattau sarvasya sarvato bhedagatiḥ syāt, aviśeṣāt / tasmādanenāsaṃkīrṇasvabhāvena bhinnāveva pratipadya viṣayaniṣedhyau ‘nedamiha'; ‘nāyamayam'; iti vyavacchedaḥ pratipattavyaḥ, saṃbhavānniyamācca / na cānyathā pratiyogitvam, sāmānyopalabdhau ca sthāṇau

puruṣasyābhāva(ms a; puruṣābhāva@ edition)pratipattyabhāvāt / tathā ca siddhaviṣayaniṣedhyāṅgīkaraṇena vyavacchedamātravidhāyinyabhāvapratipattiḥ pratyātmamupalakṣyate / tathā ca itaretarāśrayatvam --- asaṃkarapūrvamabhāvajñānam, tataścāsaṃkarasiddhiriti / api ca na pramāṇānutpādamātrādabhāvajñānam, suṣuptādāvanutpatteḥ / tasmātsatsu pramāṇakāraṇeṣu pramāṇānutpādo 'bhāvajñānaheturiṣṭaḥ / na ca tasya svarūpabhedaḥ kaścit, yena sāmarthyātiśayāccakṣurādivadbodhakaḥ, kiṃ tu nāntarīyakatvāt / nāntareṇa prameyābhāvaṃ satsu pramāṇahetuṣu pramāṇānutpādaḥ / asatsu tu satyapi prameye tadabhāvātsyāditi / tathā ca liṅgavajjñānāpekṣaḥ pratipatterjanakaḥ, sa ca yadi vastvantarajñānam, [kks_58] nāsiddhe vastubhede sidhyati / jñeyabhedānumeyo hi jñeyānumeyānāṃ jñānānāṃ bhedaḥ / tathā ca vastubhedasiddhipūrvikaivābhāvādbhedāvagatiritītaretarāśrayatvam / athātmano 'pariṇāmaḥ / na sa stimitāvasthā, sarvāpratipattau kasyacidabhāvasyānavagateḥ / tasmātsatyapi vastvantarajñānarūpapariṇāme tajjñānarūpapariṇāmābhāvo 'bhāvajñānahetuḥ / na caiṣa viśeṣaḥ prāgvastubhedasiddheḥ sidhyatīti tadevetaretarāśrayatvam /

ye tvāhuḥ --- darśanādeva bhāvānāṃ bhedaḥ sidhyati / tathā hi --- nirvikalpasya pratyakṣasya sāmānyaviṣayatvamapākurvatoktam --- ‘tadayuktaṃ pratidravyaṃ bhinnarūpopalambhanād'; iti / yastu saṃyogātsamavāyādvā saṃkaraḥ, so 'bhāvākhyena pramāṇenāpanīyata iti / te prāgeva pratyuktāḥ /

ye 'pi --- vidhāyakapratyakṣapuraḥsaraṃ pratyakṣāntarameva vastugrahaṇapratiyogismaraṇetikartavyatānugṛhītākṣapratilabdhajanma vyavacchedakaṃ manyante / yathaiva savikalpasya vastugrahaṇasya paścājjanma, śabdasmaraṇavyavadhiśca --- na cānaindriyakatvam, itikartavyatāviśeṣānugṛhītādindriyāttadutpatteḥ --- evaṃ nāstītyapi jñānasyeti bruvantaḥ / tān pratīdameva vaktavyam --- anyonyasaṃśrayādbhedo na pramāntarasādhanaḥ /

pratyakṣāntarasādhana ityarthaḥ / ‘ayamasau na bhavati'; iti jñānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ vā pramāṇāntaraṃ vā / sarvathā viṣayaniṣedhyavibhāgādṛte na niṣedhasaṃbhava iti /

kiṃ ca
mīyamānaikarūpeṣu na niṣedho 'vakāśavān
units.translation:
There can be no cognition of “this is not here” or “this is not that” without difference. Unless the thing being excluded and the thing from which it is excluded are understood, there can be no understanding of exclusion. A negation does not negate an object that has not been considered. It was said that this would establish existence, or else emptiness, not difference. Even those who argue for the cognition of absence say:

“Having grasped that an object exists and remembered its counterpart,
a mental cognition of its absence arises without dependence on the senses.”

But if the object and its counterpart are not understood as having distinct natures, but only as objects in general, there is no basis for distinguishing what is to be excluded from what is doing the excluding. Where there is only an undivided object in general, negation is impossible. If something is taken as the subject of cognition, it cannot be what is denied; if it is taken as what is denied, it is not a distinct object. In that case the negation would be absolute, and it has already been said that this cannot be established as either existent or nonexistent.

If someone understands a difference between a particular thing and something else, then, without distinction, there would have to be difference between everything and everything else. Therefore, one must first understand the object and what is denied as distinct, with unmixed natures, and only then understand negation, as in “This is not here,” and “This is not that.” Negation occurs according to what is possible and is restricted accordingly. There is no other basis for something to be the counterpart of a negation. For example, even when one sees a post, one does not understand that a person is absent unless the difference between them is understood.

Thus, cognition of absence, which merely presents something as negated, assumes in every individual case that an object and the thing denied have already been accepted as established. This creates mutual dependence: first absence is known before the two things are distinguished, and then their distinction is established through that knowledge of absence.

Moreover, cognition of absence does not arise merely because a means of knowledge fails to arise. In deep sleep a means of knowledge does not arise, but this does not make one aware of any absence. Therefore, non-arising of a means of knowledge is accepted as a cause of knowing absence only when the causes of that means are present. But that non-arising has no distinct nature of its own that could make it a means of knowledge through its power, as the eye does. It is only a necessary concomitant: when the object is absent, a means of knowledge does not arise even when its causes are present; when the means of knowledge’s causes are absent, it may fail to arise even if the object is there.

Thus the cognition of absence depends on cognition of something else, like inference; and if that cognition of something else is knowledge of a different object, it cannot arise until the difference between objects has been established. The difference between objects, in turn, is supposed to be understood from the cognition of absence. That too is mutual dependence. Someone may say that the Self undergoes no transformation other than cognition of other objects. But this is not a state of blank stillness: if no cognition at all occurs, the absence of anything could not be known. Therefore, even when there is a cognition of something else as another object, the failure of a cognition of the object being denied is what causes the cognition of its absence. But this difference cannot be established until the difference between objects has first been established; the same circularity remains.

Some say that the difference between things is established directly by seeing them. The objection that determinate perception cannot concern a particular object, because each substance is perceived in a different form, has already been answered. They say that any confusion from conjunction or inherence is removed by the means of knowledge called cognition of absence. They were refuted earlier. Others hold that a second perception, preceded by an affirmative perception of an object and supported by recollection of what is excluded and by a particular action of the senses, establishes its absence. Just as determinate cognition of an object arises after the first perception and the recollection of its word, so the cognition “it is not” arises. It is not nonsensory, they say, because it arises from the senses aided by that particular activity.

The reply to them is the same: difference is not established by another means of knowledge, such as a second perception, because the two depend on one another. The cognition “this is not that” may be perception or another means of knowledge; in every case, without distinguishing the object from what is denied, negation cannot occur. Further:

“For objects that are established as having one nature through a means of knowledge,
there is no room for negation...”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 1 · Tarka — reasoning about perception, difference, and nonduality
units.label: Kāṇḍa 1 · 15
units.deva:
अपि च सन्मात्ररूपे सर्वत्र प्रतीयमाने तत्स्वभावेषु वस्तुषु नेतराभिमत इतराभिमतप्रमाणानुत्पादः, सत्स्वभावत्वात्तयोः । ‘सत्ऽइति च सर्वत्र प्रमाणसद्भावात् । प्रमाणाभावाच्चेतरेतराभावज्ञानमिति । ननु नार्थानां किञ्चिदभिन्नं रूपम् । प्रत्यभिज्ञानाद्धि तदवगम्यते (तदवगम्येत म्स् अ; तद्गम्येत एदितिओन्) । न चार्थमात्रं दृष्टवतो ऽर्थान्तरे स एवायमिति प्रत्यभिज्ञास्ति यथैकां गां दृष्टवतो गवान्तरे । सच्छब्दप्रत्ययानुवृत्तिस्तु पाचकादिवद्योगनिबन्धना । प्रमाणविषयो हि ‘सन्ऽ; [क्क्स्_59] इत्युच्यते । नैतत्सारम् । न चेदभिन्नरूपप्रतिपत्तिः, निर्विषयत्वमेव प्रमाणस्यापद्येत । यतो न व्यवच्छेदमन्तरेण भेदप्रतीतिः । न व्यवच्छेदः केवलः, न विधिसहितः, न विधेः पश्चात्प्रमाणस्य व्यापारः । न विधिरेव व्यवच्छेद इति वर्णितम् । तत्र यद्येकमपि न गम्यते निर्विषयतैव स्यात् । अप्रत्यभिज्ञानं च यदि गोवैलक्षण्यादुच्येत सत्यपि सन्मात्ररूपानुगमे, गवान्तरे ऽपि तन्न स्यात्, देवदत्तवैलक्षण्यात् । न हि यादृशो देवदत्तस्य पुनर्दर्शने एकत्वप्रत्ययस्तादृशो गवान्तरे । अथास्ति तत्र तावत्पूर्वापरानुसन्धानम्, न तु सतः सदन्तरे । किं च भोः अनुसन्धानादेकत्वम्, नाभिन्नरूपसंविदः । नेदानीमभिन्नदेशकालो ऽर्थ एकः स्यात् । देशकालभेदे हि सो ऽयमिति पूर्वापरानुसंधानम् । गोमण्डले च महिषमण्डलविलक्षणे देशभेदे ऽप्यभिन्नरूपानुगतात् प्रथमादेव निर्विकल्पकात्प्रत्ययादेकार्थप्रतिपत्तिरिष्यते । न च तत्र कालभेदाभावात्सो ऽयमित्यवमर्शः । यथोक्तम् ---

निर्विकल्पकबोधे ऽपि द्व्यात्मकस्यापि वस्तुनः । ग्रहणं लक्षणाख्येयं ज्ञात्रा शुद्धं तु गृह्यते ॥ न च यथा मणिकं दृष्टवतो मणिकान्तरे ऽनुसन्धिः तथा शरावं दृष्ट्वा तत्र मृज्जातिरप्यपह्नूयेत । अथास्ति तत्रापि, न तु यथा मणिकान्तरे सामान्यरूपाणां भूयस्त्वादुत्कटः, अल्पसामान्यानुगमात् । सदन्तरे ऽपि तथैव स्यात् । विस्तरेण चैतदुपरिष्टादभिधास्यत इत्यलमतिप्रसङ्गेन । भेदाभेदावभासे द्वे विज्ञाने चेत्परीक्ष्यताम् । यदि मतम् --- विद्येते तावदनुवृत्तव्यावृत्ताभे द्वे विज्ञाने । न हि तयोरभावे ऽनुवृत्तव्यावृत्तव्यवहार संभवः । न च विज्ञानरूपादन्यो ऽर्थव्यवस्थाहेतुः । तस्याहेतुत्वे ऽभेदो ऽपि न सिध्येत् । नैतत्सारम् । न हि विज्ञानमित्येवार्थं (@मित्येवार्थतत्त्वं -- एदितिओन्) व्यवस्थापयति । तदपि हि परीक्ष्यम् --- युक्त्या विरुध्यते नेति, प्रमाणोत्थं नेति । न खल्वलातचक्रादिविज्ञानेभ्यो ऽर्थतत्त्वव्यवस्था । स्यादेतत् । [क्क्स्_60] न प्रत्यक्षं युक्त्यापबाध्यते । सत्यम् । प्रत्यक्षतैव भेदज्ञानस्य नेत्यावेदितम्, यथा क्षेपीयस्सर्वतोदिक्संयोगकारितस्यालातचक्रज्ञानस्य । तत् सदप्यप्रमाणोत्थं प्रत्यक्षसरूपं स्वप्नदृश्यालातचक्रादिज्ञानवन्न तत्त्वावगमनिमित्तम् । ननूक्तेन प्रकारेण प्रमाणादन्यतो ऽपि भेदज्ञानस्योदयो न संभवति । को वान्यथाह? न हि परमार्थतो भेदावगमो ऽस्ति । यदि स्यात्, कथं भेदो ऽपह्नूयेत? अपह्नवे वा कथं तदवगमः । नावगम्यमस्ति, अवगम्यते चेति दुर्घटम् । किं तर्हीदम्? अविद्या विभ्रमः । यथावभासं वेद्यसद्भावे च न विभ्रमः, किं तु सम्यग्ज्ञानम् । असतो चावगमो ऽनुपपन्नः । तस्मान्न परमार्थतः सत्त्वेन निरुच्यते, नाप्यसत्त्वेन, लोके सिद्धत्वात्सर्वप्रवादेष्वित्युक्तम् । अपि च ज्ञानद्वये ऽस्मिंश्चतस्रः कल्पनाः संभवन्ति --- ज्ञानभेदात्सामान्यव्यक्तिविभागेन वस्तुद्वयम्, यथाहुः संसर्गवादिनः । एकं वा सामान्यविशेषात्मकं वस्तु, यथाहुरनेकान्तवादिनः । विशेषा एव वा वस्तूनि । तेषामात्यन्तिकभेदनिश्चयासामर्थ्यात्तदुपादानस्तद्विषय एवाभेदः कल्पनाज्ञानगोचरः । दृष्टा हि भिन्नेष्वभेदकल्पना ‘वनम्ऽ; इति --- यथाहुरात्यन्तिकभेदवादिनः । अभेदो वा परमार्थः । तस्यानवच्छिन्नस्यानन्तस्य तथा निश्चेतुमशक्तेरनादित्वाच्चाविद्यायास्तदुपादानास्तद्विषया भेदपरिकल्पनाः । दृष्टा हि तरङ्गभेदादभिन्ने चन्द्रमसि भेदकल्पना । तन्नापरीक्ष्य तत्त्वनिश्चयः । तत्र परीक्षायाम् ---
न तावद्द्वयमैकात्म्यप्रख्यानानवकल्पनात्

api ca sanmātrarūpe sarvatra pratīyamāne tatsvabhāveṣu vastuṣu netarābhimata itarābhimatapramāṇānutpādaḥ, satsvabhāvatvāttayoḥ / ‘sat'iti ca sarvatra pramāṇasadbhāvāt / pramāṇābhāvāccetaretarābhāvajñānamiti / nanu nārthānāṃ kiñcidabhinnaṃ rūpam / pratyabhijñānāddhi tadavagamyate (tadavagamyeta ms a; tadgamyeta edition) / na cārthamātraṃ dṛṣṭavato 'rthāntare sa evāyamiti pratyabhijñāsti yathaikāṃ gāṃ dṛṣṭavato gavāntare / sacchabdapratyayānuvṛttistu pācakādivadyoganibandhanā / pramāṇaviṣayo hi ‘san'; [kks_59] ityucyate / naitatsāram / na cedabhinnarūpapratipattiḥ, nirviṣayatvameva pramāṇasyāpadyeta / yato na vyavacchedamantareṇa bhedapratītiḥ / na vyavacchedaḥ kevalaḥ, na vidhisahitaḥ, na vidheḥ paścātpramāṇasya vyāpāraḥ / na vidhireva vyavaccheda iti varṇitam / tatra yadyekamapi na gamyate nirviṣayataiva syāt / apratyabhijñānaṃ ca yadi govailakṣaṇyāducyeta satyapi sanmātrarūpānugame, gavāntare 'pi tanna syāt, devadattavailakṣaṇyāt / na hi yādṛśo devadattasya punardarśane ekatvapratyayastādṛśo gavāntare /

athāsti tatra tāvatpūrvāparānusandhānam, na tu sataḥ sadantare / kiṃ ca bhoḥ anusandhānādekatvam, nābhinnarūpasaṃvidaḥ / nedānīmabhinnadeśakālo 'rtha ekaḥ syāt / deśakālabhede hi so 'yamiti pūrvāparānusaṃdhānam / gomaṇḍale ca mahiṣamaṇḍalavilakṣaṇe deśabhede 'pyabhinnarūpānugatāt prathamādeva nirvikalpakātpratyayādekārthapratipattiriṣyate / na ca tatra kālabhedābhāvātso 'yamityavamarśaḥ / yathoktam ---

nirvikalpakabodhe 'pi dvyātmakasyāpi vastunaḥ /
grahaṇaṃ lakṣaṇākhyeyaṃ jñātrā śuddhaṃ tu gṛhyate //

na ca yathā maṇikaṃ dṛṣṭavato maṇikāntare 'nusandhiḥ tathā śarāvaṃ dṛṣṭvā tatra mṛjjātirapyapahnūyeta / athāsti tatrāpi, na tu yathā maṇikāntare sāmānyarūpāṇāṃ bhūyastvādutkaṭaḥ, alpasāmānyānugamāt / sadantare 'pi tathaiva syāt / vistareṇa caitadupariṣṭādabhidhāsyata ityalamatiprasaṅgena /
bhedābhedāvabhāse dve vijñāne cetparīkṣyatām /
yadi matam --- vidyete tāvadanuvṛttavyāvṛttābhe dve vijñāne / na hi tayorabhāve 'nuvṛttavyāvṛttavyavahāra saṃbhavaḥ / na ca vijñānarūpādanyo 'rthavyavasthāhetuḥ / tasyāhetutve 'bhedo 'pi na sidhyet / naitatsāram / na hi vijñānamityevārthaṃ (@mityevārthatattvaṃ -- edition) vyavasthāpayati / tadapi hi parīkṣyam --- yuktyā virudhyate neti, pramāṇotthaṃ neti / na khalvalātacakrādivijñānebhyo 'rthatattvavyavasthā / syādetat / [kks_60] na pratyakṣaṃ yuktyāpabādhyate / satyam / pratyakṣataiva bhedajñānasya netyāveditam, yathā kṣepīyassarvatodiksaṃyogakāritasyālātacakrajñānasya / tat sadapyapramāṇotthaṃ pratyakṣasarūpaṃ svapnadṛśyālātacakrādijñānavanna tattvāvagamanimittam / nanūktena prakāreṇa pramāṇādanyato 'pi bhedajñānasyodayo na saṃbhavati / ko vānyathāha? na hi paramārthato bhedāvagamo 'sti / yadi syāt, kathaṃ bhedo 'pahnūyeta? apahnave vā kathaṃ tadavagamaḥ / nāvagamyamasti, avagamyate ceti durghaṭam / kiṃ tarhīdam? avidyā vibhramaḥ / yathāvabhāsaṃ vedyasadbhāve ca na vibhramaḥ, kiṃ tu samyagjñānam / asato cāvagamo 'nupapannaḥ / tasmānna paramārthataḥ sattvena nirucyate, nāpyasattvena, loke siddhatvātsarvapravādeṣvityuktam /

api ca jñānadvaye 'smiṃścatasraḥ kalpanāḥ saṃbhavanti --- jñānabhedātsāmānyavyaktivibhāgena vastudvayam, yathāhuḥ saṃsargavādinaḥ / ekaṃ vā sāmānyaviśeṣātmakaṃ vastu, yathāhuranekāntavādinaḥ / viśeṣā eva vā vastūni / teṣāmātyantikabhedaniścayāsāmarthyāttadupādānastadviṣaya evābhedaḥ kalpanājñānagocaraḥ / dṛṣṭā hi bhinneṣvabhedakalpanā ‘vanam'; iti --- yathāhurātyantikabhedavādinaḥ / abhedo vā paramārthaḥ / tasyānavacchinnasyānantasya tathā niścetumaśakteranāditvāccāvidyāyāstadupādānāstadviṣayā bhedaparikalpanāḥ / dṛṣṭā hi taraṅgabhedādabhinne candramasi bhedakalpanā / tannāparīkṣya tattvaniścayaḥ / tatra parīkṣāyām ---
na tāvaddvayamaikātmyaprakhyānānavakalpanāt
units.translation:
Moreover, if bare existence were present everywhere, and things had existence as their nature, then neither one favored means of knowledge nor another disfavored means of knowledge could arise, since both would have existence as their nature. The word “existent” is applied everywhere because every means of knowledge is present; the cognition that things are mutually absent arises when the means of knowledge is absent. Someone may object that things have no common nature. Such a common nature is understood through recognition: a person who has seen one thing does not recognize a different thing as “that very same thing,” just as someone who has seen one cow does not recognize another cow as the same individual. The recurring cognition associated with the word “existent” is instead based on practical use, like the word “cook.” An object within the scope of a means of knowledge is called “existent.”

That is not sound. If there were no understanding of a common nature, the means of knowledge would have no object at all, since cognition of difference requires exclusion. Exclusion by itself is not the operation of a means of knowledge; nor is exclusion together with affirmation, nor is the operation of a means of knowledge after affirmation. It has already been explained that affirmation alone is not exclusion. If not even one thing were understood, the means of knowledge would have no subject matter.

If recognition fails because cows are unlike one another, then the same should apply to different cows, due to their difference from Devadatta. The recognition that arises when Devadatta is seen again is not the same as the cognition of “that very same cow” when one sees another cow. Someone may reply that, in the first case, there is a linking of what was seen before and what is seen now, but no such linking between one existent thing and another. But, my friend, does unity arise from the linking itself, rather than from cognition of a common nature? Then an object at different places and times would not be one. Recognition of “that very same thing” relies precisely on difference of place and time between the earlier and later perception.

In a herd of cows, even though there is a difference of place from a herd of buffaloes, the very first, indeterminate cognition apprehends a single object because a common nature recurs. There is no recollection of “that very same one” there, since there is no difference in time. As it is said:

“Even in indeterminate cognition, an object of two aspects is grasped;
the knower grasps it as having a mark, but as pure in its nature.”

Nor is this like someone who has seen one jewel remembering that it is the same jewel upon seeing another. When one sees a dish, one does not deny the clay-kind present in it. If the common nature is especially prominent among several jewels, then the common feature is weak in comparison; it should be exactly the same with one existent thing and another. This will be explained in detail later; enough of this digression.

If one says that the appearance of difference and non-difference consists in two cognitions, let us examine that. Someone may say that there are two cognitions, one of what continues and one of what is excluded. If neither of these existed, the ordinary dealings involving continuity and difference could not occur...

There is no cause for establishing the nature of an object other than cognition; if cognition had no causal role, even oneness could not be established. This is not sound: it is not cognition alone that establishes the nature of an object. Cognition itself must be examined—whether it is consistent with reasoning and whether it arises from a valid means of knowledge. The reality of an object is not established merely by cognitions such as seeing a firebrand whirl in a circle. Someone may say that perception cannot be contradicted by reasoning. That is true; nevertheless, it has already been shown that perception itself does not establish difference as real. For example, the circular appearance of a rapidly whirled firebrand is produced by contact with all directions in a short time. Although it seems perceptual, it does not arise from a valid means of knowledge in the way that a dream image or an illusory firebrand circle does not reveal reality.

One may object that, in the manner explained, cognition of difference cannot arise from any means of knowledge. Who says otherwise? There is no cognition of difference in ultimate reality. If there were, how could difference be denied? If it were denied, how could it be cognized? It is contradictory to say that it is not cognized and yet is cognized. What, then, is this? It is ignorance, an error. If the object exists as it appears, this is not error but correct knowledge. And cognition of something nonexistent is impossible. Therefore reality is not defined as either existent or nonexistent; it is established in ordinary life and across the various philosophical systems, as has been said.

Moreover, when these two cognitions are considered, four possible accounts arise. First, there are two objects, a universal and a particular, corresponding to the difference between the cognitions, as those who hold that things are connected say. Second, there is one object whose nature consists of both universal and particular, as those who hold that reality has many aspects say. Third, only particulars exist; but because their absolute difference cannot be ascertained, an imagined identity is formed that is both derived from them and about them. The identity of distinct things is seen in the concept “forest,” as those who hold absolute difference say. Fourth, non-difference alone is ultimate reality, unbounded and infinite; because its nature cannot be determined in this way, and because ignorance is beginningless, imagined differences arise from it and concern it. Difference is imagined in the moon, which is not different, as when the moon’s reflection appears in waves. Therefore, the truth cannot be settled without examination. In that examination:

“Two cannot be accepted, since the one Self cannot be fully understood...”
