nanvanyathāyaṃ bhedaḥ --- agrahaṇasamyaggrahaṇābhyām / agrahaṇalakṣaṇācchādikā suṣupte, asamyaggrahaṇamitarayoḥ / tathā hi --- abhinnasya vastuno 'pradeśasya grahaṇe tathābhāvasya cāgrahaṇātpṛthaktvena pratyavabhāsaḥ / naitatsāram / yadi tāvadasamyaggrahaṇamātraṃ tadapaṭutvaṃ vā jñānasya kenaciddrūpeṇa vā grahaṇam, na sarvātmanā / tatra dūrasthe sūkṣme ca bhavatyapaṭu jñānaṃ sāmānyajñānam / na ca tadavidyā / na ca kiñcijjñānaṃ sarvātmanārthasya grāhakamiti sarvajñānamithyātvāpātaḥ / abhedasyāgrahaṇe 'pi bhedasyāvartane 'pi bhedasyāsaṃvitterna nivartanīyamasti vidyayā / na khalvabhedāgrahaṇaṃ nivartanīyam / na hi tatkiñcidaparādhyati / bhedastu vividhaduḥkhāyatanam / athāsamyaggrahaṇaṃ pṛthakpratyavabhāso 'pṛthagātmanaḥ, abhyupetā tarhi viparyayakhyātiḥ --- apṛthak pṛthak prakāśata iti /

athocyeta --- na brūmaḥ pṛthak prakāśate, kiṃ tu pṛthagiva prakāśata iti / ka ivārthaḥ? yadi yathā pṛthagbhūtamaprakāśamānaikatvaṃ prakāśate tathaikamapyātmatattvamagṛhyamāṇaikatvaṃ prakāśata iti / kenacidaṃśena grahaṇaṃ sarvātmanā cāgrahaṇamuktaṃ bhavati, tatra coktam / atha prakāśata iva, na tu prakāśate / prakāśane ka upamārthaḥ? tannibandhanavyavahārapravṛttiḥ / tannibandhanaścedvyavahāraḥ / prāptaṃ prakāśanam --- nāsati kāraṇe kāryaṃ bhavatīti / athābhedāgraha eva pṛthaktvagrahābhimānaḥ / tadasat, agrahaṇasyābhāvasya svarūpeṇa pararūpeṇa vā grahaṇānabhyupagamāt / aprakāśamāne ca pṛthaktve kutastadavagrahaḥ? abhinne ca bhedābhimānaṃ parityajyābhedāgrahaṇe bhedagrahābhimānamūrīkurvatā kiṃ parihṛtaṃ syāt? tasmātsuṣṭhūcyate --- ‘layavikṣepabhedaśca na syādagrahamātrake'; iti /

[kks_151] nanvanātmarūpeṇa pratipatterna dṛśyate kiñcitphalam / tatrādṛṣṭakalpanā syāt / ātmarūpapratipattestu dṛṣṭaṃ phalaṃ tatsvarūpasiddhiḥ / ucyate --- na yasya kasyaciddarśanād dṛṣṭārthatā, kiṃ tu puruṣārthasaṃsparśinaḥ / tena hi tadvidhirnirākāṅkṣā bhavati / na ca puruṣārrhabhedastattvātattvapratipattyoḥ / yathā hi viśuddhamadvaitamātmānaṃ pratipadyamānastathābhūto na śokena saṃspṛśyate, śocanīyābhāvāt / na karmāśayamupacinoti, kartavyābhāvāt / na kvaciddrajyati kiñcid dveṣṭi vā, viṣayābhāvāt / ‘evaṃ jīvanneva vidvānvimukto bhavati / tathā atathābhūtamapi tathābhāvanāpuraḥsaraṃ sākṣādiva pratipadyamānaḥ / abhūto 'pyarthaḥ paribhāvanātiśayādbhūtavyavahāraheturbhavati / idameva cātra yujyate, pratyakṣādīnāmavirodhāt, karmavidhīnāṃ ca bhūtārthatvāt / paramārthe hi prapañcaśūnyatve pratyakṣādīni pramāṇāni bādhyeran / karmavidhayaścābhūtakalpanopādānavyavahārasiddhārthagocarāḥ syuḥ / tasmādaparamārthenaivādvaitātmajñānavidhiryujyate /
jānātistattvabodhe cenna mithyādiviśeṣaṇāt
units.translation:
The meanings are not figurative, since they are subjects of ritual action. As for the injunction to know the Self, all that it conveys is this: by knowledge the Self is made manifest, taken as a support, and brought into the range of practical understanding. Such manifestation has been observed both as the thing’s own nature and as something other than it, as when a shell appears in the form of silver. It has been explained that this is not mere non-apprehension but the apprehension of one thing as another. If either account is possible, why must we accept only correct knowledge of reality and not the mistaken appearance? Otherwise, the injunction to know the Self would have no result. Its purpose is to dissolve the appearance of the non-Self, since the nature of a thing is understood when its non-Self form is dissolved. If the Self does not shine forth as the manifold of names and forms, what is there to dissolve?

Someone may say that ignorance is of two kinds: it conceals illumination and projects another form. The projecting kind operates in dream and waking; in deep sleep there is concealment, characterized by absorption. The result of the injunction to know is the removal of the concealing ignorance. That is not sound, since a person does not desire the removal of concealment in the same way as the removal of projection. Projection has the nature of various forms of suffering, while absorption is repeatedly praised in scripture as bliss because it removes diverse suffering; it should instead be desired. Moreover, if one does not accept mistaken perception, there is no distinction between kinds of ignorance: in all three states there would be only non-apprehension. Therefore ignorance is divided into non-apprehension and mistaken apprehension, standing in a relation of cause and effect. Both are present in dream and waking, while in deep sleep ignorance is the non-apprehension that is their cause. As it is said:

“The states of waking and dreaming are bound by cause and effect;
the wise one in deep sleep is bound by cause alone;
neither of the two is established in the fourth state.”

Someone may object that the distinction is made differently: between non-apprehension and correct apprehension. Deep sleep is concealment characterized by non-apprehension; in the other two states there is incorrect apprehension. The undivided, unlocated object appears as if it were divided because its undivided nature is not apprehended. That is not sound. If incorrect or imperfect cognition alone were ignorance—whether cognition is weak or grasps something in one respect but not every respect—then knowledge from a distance, knowledge of subtle things, and general cognition would all be ignorance. Yet that is not so. Nor does any cognition grasp an object in every respect; it would follow that every cognition is false. Even when non-difference is not apprehended, if difference does not appear, there is nothing to be removed by knowledge. Mere non-apprehension does not need to be removed, since it does no harm. But difference does...

...is the basis of various suffering. If “incorrect apprehension” means that what is not separate appears as separate, then the doctrine of error by apprehending one thing as another has been accepted: what is not separate appears as separate. Someone may respond, “We do not say that it actually appears separate, only that it appears as if separate.” What does “as if” mean? It means that just as something truly separate appears separate when its oneness is not manifested, so this one reality appears as if it were separate when its oneness is not apprehended. In that case, it has been admitted that something is grasped in one respect and not grasped in its entirety, which has already been discussed. Or perhaps one says that it does not actually appear, but only seems as if it appeared. What does that comparison mean? It means that ordinary transactions arise on its basis. If they arise on its basis, then the appearance itself has been admitted: an effect does not arise without a cause. Perhaps the assumption of separateness consists only in not apprehending non-difference. That is unsound, since one has not accepted that an absence is apprehended either as its own nature or as another nature. If difference does not shine forth, how can it be grasped? And if one gives up the claim that the imagined apprehension of difference arises when non-difference is not apprehended, but then accepts that difference is apprehended, what has one avoided? Therefore it was rightly said:

“If there were only non-apprehension, there could be no distinction between absorption and projection.”

Someone may object that no visible result comes from knowing the Self as what it is not; its result would have to be assumed. But knowing the Self as it is has a visible result: establishing its own nature. The reply is that a result is not visible merely because something has been seen; it must touch a human purpose. That is what makes the injunction to do it complete and independent. There is no difference in human purpose between true and false cognition. Someone who understands the pure, nondual Self is no longer touched by sorrow, because there is nothing to grieve over; does not accumulate actions, because there is nothing to do; and feels neither attachment nor aversion, because there are no objects. “Thus, while still living, the knower is liberated.” Similarly, a person who has not become that way, but directly apprehends the Self as if it were so through the intensity of repeated contemplation, may have an unreal object function as a real one in ordinary transactions.

This is what fits the present discussion, since it avoids conflict with perception and the other means of knowledge, and with ritual injunctions that concern actual, factual things. If the ultimate reality were an absolute absence of the manifold world, perception and the other means would be contradicted. Ritual injunctions would concern objects that exist only as imagined, and transactions based on unreal things. Therefore the injunction to know the nondual Self is fitting only as a nonultimate teaching. If the verb “to know” means knowledge of what is real, it cannot be qualified by terms such as “false” and the like...

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 172
units.deva: नात्मा ज्ञातस्तथा स्याच्चेन्न तद्रूपाविधानतः । प्रमाणान्तरसिद्धत्वे नतरामन्यथा यदि
units.iast:
nātmā jñātastathā syāccenna tadrūpāvidhānataḥ /
pramāṇāntarasiddhatve natarāmanyathā yadi
units.translation: If the Self were not known in that way, it would be because its nature was not taught. If it is established by another means of knowledge, then all the more…

gloss.en: because its nature is not stated
if established by another means of knowledge

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 173
units.deva: शब्दार्पितेन रूपेण तस्य ज्ञानं विधीयते । अतत्त्वेनापि तेनास्य विज्ञानमवकल्पते
units.iast:
śabdārpitena rūpeṇa tasya jñānaṃ vidhīyate /
atattvenāpi tenāsya vijñānamavakalpate
units.translation: Knowledge of the Self in the form presented by the words is prescribed. Through that knowledge, the Self can be apprehended even if the form is not ultimately true.

gloss.en: in the form presented by words
even in a form that is not ultimately real

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 174
units.deva: यदि मतम् --- ‘स विजिज्ञासितव्यःऽ; इति जानातिस्तत्त्वपरिच्छेद एव वर्तते । तेन नाभूतसमारोपेण ज्ञानविधिः स्यादिति । तन्न, मिथ्यात्वादिभिर्ज्ञानं विशेष्यते --- मिथ्याज्ञानं सम्यग्ज्ञानं संशयज्ञानमिति । तदेकनियमे नोपपद्येत, पौनरुक्त्याद्विरोधाच्च । स्यादेतत् --- अस्वरूपेण प्रतिपत्तौ न तदात्मज्ञानम्, अन्यज्ञानमेव भवति । तत्त्वज्ञानं च विधीयते । तस्मात्तत्त्वसिद्धिरिति । तच्च न । न खल्वेतावदेव तत् --- ‘आत्मा ज्ञातव्यः इति । [क्क्स्_152] यदि स्यात्तद्रूपज्ञानविधिः । तच्च न, उभयथानुपपत्तेः । प्रमाणान्तरसिद्धं चेदात्मरूपं न तज्ज्ञानं विधेयम् । अथासिद्धम्, अशक्यमेव तत् । स्यादेतत् --- ‘अपहतपाप्मा विजरो विमृत्युःऽ; ‘इदं सर्वं यदयमात्माऽइति शब्दसमर्पितरूपस्य तस्य ज्ञानं विधीयते, तेन च तत्त्वेनापि तत्संभवति समारोपितेनापि, तेन न नियोगतस्तथाभूतज्ञानविधेस्तथाभावो ऽस्य प्रतीयते । ज्ञानं यदि च दृष्टार्थं प्राप्तं दृष्टत एव तत् । आत्मरूपविजिज्ञासोरजिज्ञासोर्वृथैव तत्
units.iast:
yadi matam --- ‘sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ'; iti jānātistattvapariccheda eva vartate / tena nābhūtasamāropeṇa jñānavidhiḥ syāditi / tanna, mithyātvādibhirjñānaṃ viśeṣyate --- mithyājñānaṃ samyagjñānaṃ saṃśayajñānamiti / tadekaniyame nopapadyeta, paunaruktyādvirodhācca / syādetat --- asvarūpeṇa pratipattau na tadātmajñānam, anyajñānameva bhavati / tattvajñānaṃ ca vidhīyate / tasmāttattvasiddhiriti / tacca na / na khalvetāvadeva tat --- ‘ātmā jñātavyaḥ iti / [kks_152] yadi syāttadrūpajñānavidhiḥ / tacca na, ubhayathānupapatteḥ / pramāṇāntarasiddhaṃ cedātmarūpaṃ na tajjñānaṃ vidheyam / athāsiddham, aśakyameva tat / syādetat --- ‘apahatapāpmā vijaro vimṛtyuḥ'; ‘idaṃ sarvaṃ yadayamātmā'iti śabdasamarpitarūpasya tasya jñānaṃ vidhīyate, tena ca tattvenāpi tatsaṃbhavati samāropitenāpi, tena na niyogatastathābhūtajñānavidhestathābhāvo 'sya pratīyate /

jñānaṃ yadi ca dṛṣṭārthaṃ prāptaṃ dṛṣṭata eva tat /
ātmarūpavijijñāsorajijñāsorvṛthaiva tat
units.translation:
One might argue: in the sentence “It is to be known,” the verb “to know” concerns only determining the truth; hence an injunction to know could not be an instruction to impose something unreal. This is not so. Knowledge is qualified by terms such as “false,” “correct,” and “doubtful,” as in “false cognition,” “correct cognition,” and “doubtful cognition.” If the verb had only one fixed sense, these uses would be impossible, and its repetition would be redundant or contradictory.

Someone may object: if something is apprehended as other than it really is, that is not knowledge of the Self; it is knowledge of something else. What is enjoined is knowledge of the truth, and therefore the truth of the Self is established. No. The words do not merely say, “The Self is to be known.” If they did, an injunction to know it in that particular form would follow. But this is untenable in either case. If the Self’s nature is already established by another means of knowledge, knowledge of it cannot be enjoined. If it is not established, then such knowledge is impossible.

One might say that the words “free from evil, ageless, immortal” and “all this is indeed the Self” present the Self’s nature, and knowledge of the Self in that form is enjoined. But such knowledge is possible whether the presented form is true or superimposed; the injunction does not establish that the Self is truly so. And if the knowledge has a directly visible result, then that result is already available directly. It would be pointless to prescribe it for one who desires to know the nature of the Self, or for one who does not.

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 175
units.deva: तदुपायो न चेज्ज्ञातस्तस्यैवास्तु विधिस्ततः । अवघातादिविधयो नादृष्टस्पर्शवर्जिताः
units.iast:
tadupāyo na cejjñātastasyaivāstu vidhistataḥ /
avaghātādividhayo nādṛṣṭasparśavarjitāḥ
units.translation: If the means to that end is not known, let an injunction prescribe it; injunctions for pounding and the like also involve an unseen result.

gloss.en: injunctions concerning pounding and the like

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 176
units.deva: अलौकिकमिदं ज्ञानमतो यदि विधीयते । न रूपसिद्धये तावद्यतः कर्तव्यता विधेः
units.iast:
alaukikamidaṃ jñānamato yadi vidhīyate /
na rūpasiddhaye tāvadyataḥ kartavyatā vidheḥ
units.translation: If this extraordinary knowledge is enjoined, it is not to establish the Self’s nature; an injunction concerns something to be done.

gloss.en: is the domain of an injunction

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 177
units.deva: कर्तव्यता च दृष्टार्थे दृष्टादेव प्रसिद्ध्यति । अलौकिके ऽर्थरूपे ऽतः शब्देन प्रतिपादिते
units.iast:
kartavyatā ca dṛṣṭārthe dṛṣṭādeva prasiddhyati /
alaukike 'rtharūpe 'taḥ śabdena pratipādite
units.translation: An obligation concerning something with a directly visible result is established from that result itself. Therefore, when the nature of an extraordinary object is presented by words…

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 178
units.deva: ज्ञाने ज्ञेयाभ्युपायत्वात्स्वयमेवोन्मुखः पुमान् । तदुपाये त्वविज्ञाते विधिना स प्रवर्त्यताम्
units.iast:
jñāne jñeyābhyupāyatvātsvayamevonmukhaḥ pumān /
tadupāye tvavijñāte vidhinā sa pravartyatām
units.translation: When knowledge is the means to the known object, a person turns toward it of their own accord; but when the means to that end is unknown, let an injunction prompt them.

gloss.en: because it is a means to what is to be known

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 179
units.deva: नियोगानुप्रवेशो ऽतो विहन्त्येव प्रमाणताम् । भूतर्थ इति नोपास्यो भूतार्थगतिमिच्छता
units.iast:
niyogānupraveśo 'to vihantyeva pramāṇatām /
bhūtartha iti nopāsyo bhūtārthagatimicchatā
units.translation: Participation in an injunction therefore undermines its validity. One who seeks knowledge of an already existent reality should not contemplate it as something to be accomplished.

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 180
units.deva:
यदि च ज्ञानस्य दृष्टं फलम्, तत एव प्रवृत्तिसिद्धे व्यर्थो विधिः । यो ह्यात्मरूपमनुभवितुकामः, स तस्य ज्ञाने स्वयमेव यतते । यस्तु न तथा, तस्य तद्व्यर्थमिति विधिशतेनापि स न प्रवर्त्यते । अथोपायाज्ञानाद्दृष्टफले ऽपि न प्रवर्तते स्वयम्, अतो विधीयत इति । तच्च वार्तम् । यतः स एवोपायो विधीयताम्, यत्रायमज्ञानान्न प्रवृत्तः । ज्ञाने तु दृष्टफलत्वात्प्रवर्तत [क्क्स्_153] एव । स्यादेतत्, अवघातादिषु दृष्टफलेष्वपि दृष्टो विधिः । सत्यम्, न त्वदृष्टसंस्पर्शरहितः । तत्रापि हि नियमादृष्टं फलं तण्डुलेषु तत्प्रणाड्या वा प्रधानपूर्वसिद्धिरदृष्टैव । अथ मतम् --- अद्वैतात्मज्ञानमदृष्टपूर्वमलौकिकम् । अतो ऽनन्तरफलमपि विधीयत इति । तत्रोच्यते --- किमर्थं विधीयते । प्रमाणान्तरागोचरस्य स्वरूपप्रतिपत्त्यर्थम्, आहोस्विदनुष्ठानार्थम्? तत्र न स्वरूपसिद्ध्यर्थम्, अनुष्ठानफलो हि विधिर्नानुष्ठानाय, दृष्टार्थत्वादेव तत्सिद्धेः । तस्मादलौकिके ऽपहतपाप्मादिरूप आत्मतत्त्वे शब्दात्प्रतिपन्ने तस्य साक्षाज्ज्ञानं प्रति तदनुभवोपायत्वात्स्वयमेव पुरुषस्याभिमुख्यं भवतीति व्यर्थं तद्विधानम्, यथाश्चर्यभूते कस्मिंश्चिदर्थे आगमात्प्रतिपन्ने तस्य साक्षात्करणे स्वयमेवोन्मुखत्वं भवति । तदुपायेषु त्वज्ञातेषूपायत्वज्ञापनाय विधानं युज्यते । तदेवं ज्ञाने नियोगानुपपत्तेर्नियोगे च वस्तुरूपावगमे प्रामाण्यायोगाद्व्यवस्थितात्मतत्त्वप्रतिपत्तिमिच्छता शब्दान्न तस्य नियोगानुप्रवेशो ऽभ्युपगन्तव्य इति । इदानीं द्वितीयप्रतिपत्तिविधिनिरासायाह ---

अत एव न विज्ञानसंतानविधिनिष्ठता । तत्रापि पूर्ववन्न स्यात्स्वरूपावगतिप्रमा
units.iast:
yadi ca jñānasya dṛṣṭaṃ phalam, tata eva pravṛttisiddhe vyartho vidhiḥ / yo hyātmarūpamanubhavitukāmaḥ, sa tasya jñāne svayameva yatate / yastu na tathā, tasya tadvyarthamiti vidhiśatenāpi sa na pravartyate / athopāyājñānāddṛṣṭaphale 'pi na pravartate svayam, ato vidhīyata iti / tacca vārtam / yataḥ sa evopāyo vidhīyatām, yatrāyamajñānānna pravṛttaḥ / jñāne tu dṛṣṭaphalatvātpravartata [kks_153] eva / syādetat, avaghātādiṣu dṛṣṭaphaleṣvapi dṛṣṭo vidhiḥ / satyam, na tvadṛṣṭasaṃsparśarahitaḥ / tatrāpi hi niyamādṛṣṭaṃ phalaṃ taṇḍuleṣu tatpraṇāḍyā vā pradhānapūrvasiddhiradṛṣṭaiva / atha matam --- advaitātmajñānamadṛṣṭapūrvamalaukikam / ato 'nantaraphalamapi vidhīyata iti / tatrocyate --- kimarthaṃ vidhīyate / pramāṇāntarāgocarasya svarūpapratipattyartham, āhosvidanuṣṭhānārtham? tatra na svarūpasiddhyartham, anuṣṭhānaphalo hi vidhirnānuṣṭhānāya, dṛṣṭārthatvādeva tatsiddheḥ / tasmādalaukike 'pahatapāpmādirūpa ātmatattve śabdātpratipanne tasya sākṣājjñānaṃ prati tadanubhavopāyatvātsvayameva puruṣasyābhimukhyaṃ bhavatīti vyarthaṃ tadvidhānam, yathāścaryabhūte kasmiṃścidarthe āgamātpratipanne tasya sākṣātkaraṇe svayamevonmukhatvaṃ bhavati / tadupāyeṣu tvajñāteṣūpāyatvajñāpanāya vidhānaṃ yujyate / tadevaṃ jñāne niyogānupapatterniyoge ca vasturūpāvagame prāmāṇyāyogādvyavasthitātmatattvapratipattimicchatā śabdānna tasya niyogānupraveśo 'bhyupagantavya iti /

idānīṃ dvitīyapratipattividhinirāsāyāha ---

ata eva na vijñānasaṃtānavidhiniṣṭhatā /
tatrāpi pūrvavanna syātsvarūpāvagatipramā
units.translation:
If knowledge has a directly visible result, activity is already assured by that result, and the injunction is pointless. Someone who desires to experience the nature of the Self will make the effort to know it of their own accord. For someone who does not desire this, knowledge would be pointless, and not even a hundred injunctions could make that person act. One might reply that, although the result is visible, a person does not act because they do not know the means; hence an injunction is given. That is badly argued. The means should be enjoined only where a person does not act from ignorance of the means. But in this case, because knowledge has a directly visible result, the person acts already.

One might say that injunctions are seen even for actions such as pounding, which have visible results. True, but those actions are not entirely free of an unseen result. In that case, an unseen result is necessarily produced in the grains, or in the sequence by which the principal result is accomplished. Or someone might argue: knowledge of the nondual Self is unprecedented and beyond ordinary experience; therefore even its immediate result must be enjoined. We ask: for what purpose is it enjoined? Is it to establish the Self’s nature, which is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge, or to prompt a practice? It is not to establish the Self’s nature, because an injunction concerns a result achieved through practice; practice is not itself the purpose when its result is already directly available. Therefore, when scripture has taught the nature of the Self as an extraordinary reality, free from evil and so forth, a person naturally turns toward direct knowledge of it, because that knowledge is the means of experiencing it. An injunction to know it is therefore pointless—just as when scripture teaches something astonishing, a person naturally seeks to see it directly. But where the means to an end are unknown, an injunction is reasonable to teach that they are the means.

Thus, because an injunction to know is untenable, and because an injunction cannot be a valid means of knowing the nature of a thing, anyone who seeks a settled understanding of the Self’s nature must not accept that its apprehension depends upon an injunction in scripture. The author now refutes the view that an injunction prescribes a second kind of apprehension:

“For that very reason, it does not culminate in an injunction to maintain a continuous stream of cognitions. There too, as before, there would be no valid understanding of the Self’s nature…”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 181
units.deva: स्वरूपनिष्ठाच्छब्दात्तु प्रमितस्य वचो ऽन्तरात् । उपासनविधानं स्यात्प्राप्तेस्तदपि वा वृथा
units.iast:
svarūpaniṣṭhācchabdāttu pramitasya vaco 'ntarāt /
upāsanavidhānaṃ syātprāptestadapi vā vṛthā
units.translation: After something has been known from words that focus on its own nature, an injunction to contemplate it may arise from another statement; that too would be pointless, since it has already been attained.

gloss.en: from words focused on its own nature

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 182
units.deva: अभ्यासेन प्रत्ययस्य प्रकर्षस्याभिवीक्षणात् । तस्माद्भवत्यकार्ये ऽर्थे वेदान्तानां प्रमाणता
units.iast:
abhyāsena pratyayasya prakarṣasyābhivīkṣaṇāt /
tasmādbhavatyakārye 'rthe vedāntānāṃ pramāṇatā
units.translation: Because cognition is observed to become stronger through repeated practice, the Upaniṣads are therefore authoritative about an object that is not something to be done.

gloss.en: concerning an object that is not to be produced

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 2 · Niyoga — whether Vedānta knowledge depends on injunction
units.label: Kāṇḍa 2 · 183
units.deva: यदपि मतम् --- ‘स क्रतुं कुर्वीतऽप्रज्ञां कुर्वीतऽ; ‘निदिध्यासितव्यःऽ; इति, यत्रापि स्वरूपनिष्ठतैव लक्ष्यते ‘तत्त्वमसिऽ; इति तत्रापि ‘सदस्मि --- इति चेतो धारयेत्ऽइति विवक्षितत्वाच्छ्रवणादन्यदनुचिन्तनं ध्यानं प्रत्ययप्रवाहो विधीयते कर्मवदेवामृतत्वफलम् । [क्क्स्_154] तदप्यत एव न युज्यते, पूर्वोक्तात्तत्त्वावगतिप्रमाणाभावप्रसङ्गादन्यनिष्ठत्वाद्वाक्यस्य । अथ तु वाक्यान्तरात्तत्त्वनिष्ठादधिगते तद्विषयप्रत्ययप्रवाहविधानमिष्यते । भवतु । न कश्चिद्दोषः । तथा च ‘विज्ञाय प्रज्ञां कुर्वीतऽइत्यात्मतत्त्वविज्ञानस्य सिद्धतां दर्शयति । तदपि वा व्यर्थमेव, प्राप्तार्थत्वात् । साक्षात्करणफलं हि तत्तदनुचिन्तनं दृष्टार्थम्, न ततो ऽन्यत्फलमाकाङ्क्ष्यते । अमृतत्वं हि न स्वरूपाविर्भावादन्यदिति प्राग्वर्णितम् । दृष्टा च ज्ञानाभ्यासस्य सम्यग्ज्ञानप्रसादहेतुता लोके । भावनाविशेषाद्धि अभूतमप्यनुभवमापद्यते, किं पुनर्भूतम् । ‘स क्रतुं कुर्वीतऽ; इति तु न सकलविशेषातिगात्मतत्त्वानुचिन्तनं विधीयते तद्भावफलम्, अपि तु नामरूपोपाधिमनोमयप्राणशरीरादिरूपानुध्यानमैश्वर्यफलम्, क्रमेण वा साक्षात्करणफलम् । ‘तमेव धीरो विज्ञायऽ; इति न प्रज्ञाकरणविधिः । ‘तमेवऽइत्यन्यनिवृत्तेः श्रुतत्त्वान्निवृत्तौ तात्पर्यं गम्यते, ‘रक्तः पटो भवतिऽइति तया रक्तपरत्वं वाक्यस्य । अत्र आकाशादितत्त्वभेदपूर्वमविभागः प्रतिपादितः, तत्र तथैव प्रज्ञाकरणप्रसङ्गे ‘तमेवऽ; इति विधीयते । तथा च पूर्वार्धे --- ‘विरजः पर आकाशादज आत्मा महान् ध्रुवःऽ; । इत्याकाशादिभ्यः परत्वेनात्मतत्त्वं दर्शितम् । तस्य तथैव प्रज्ञाकरणप्रसङ्गे तन्निवृत्तये ‘तमेवऽ; इत्युच्यते । अन्यथा न एवशब्दस्य फलम्, न च निवर्त्यं विज्ञायेत । तथा च तदेवोत्तरेण प्रपञ्च्यते ‘नानुध्यायाद्बहूञ्छब्दान्ऽ; इत्येकवाक्यता । अन्यथा वाक्यं भिद्येत । शब्दमात्रे चानुध्यानाप्रसङ्गात् शब्दपूर्वत्त्वात्तस्य शब्दार्थविषयमेवेदमिति । एवम् ‘आत्मेत्येवोपासीतऽइत्येवकारश्रुतेस्तदर्थविधिः । ‘निदिध्यासितव्यःऽ; इत्यपि ‘आत्मनस्तु कामायऽ; इत्युपक्रमात् ‘इदं सर्वं [क्क्स्_155] यदयमात्माऽइत्युपसंहारादात्मस्वरूपपरमेकं वाक्यम् । तदन्तर्गताः ‘द्रष्टव्यः श्रोतव्यो निदिध्यासितव्यःऽ; इति न पृथग्विधयः कृत्यप्रत्यययोगे ऽपि । कृत्यप्रत्ययस्यार्थान्तरे ऽपि स्मरणादर्हादौ स्तुत्यर्थाः यथोपांशुयाजवाक्यान्तर्गताः ‘विष्णुरुपांशु यष्टव्यःऽइत्येवमादयः । ‘ऐतदात्म्यमिदं सर्वं तत्सत्यं स आत्मा तत्त्वमसिऽइति भूत एव पर्यवसितं वाक्यम् । तत्र ‘सदस्मि --- इति धारयेत्ऽ; इति कल्पनेयम् । तस्मात्त्रिविधस्यापि ज्ञानस्य विधेयत्वायोगात्, विना च विधेर्वाक्यार्थप्रतिपत्तेः, अपौरुषेयत्वेन निरपेक्षत्वाद्भूते ऽप्यर्थे वेदान्तानां प्रामाण्यसिद्धिः । तथा च ‘तत्तु समन्वयात्ऽइति चोदनालक्षणाद्धर्मात्तुशब्देन विशेष्यं ब्रह्म समन्वयगम्यमुक्तम् । समन्वयो हि पदार्थानां संसर्गो विनियोगस्ततो ब्रह्म गम्यते, न चोदनात इत्यर्थः । नन्वविशेषेण कार्ये ऽर्थे वेदस्य प्रामाण्यं वर्णितम् --- ‘चोदनालक्षणो ऽर्थो धर्मःऽ; इति । चोदनालक्षणो वेदार्थ इत्यर्थः । नैतत्सारम् । एवं हि सिद्धप्रामाण्यवेदार्थविचारो ऽयं स्यात्तदुत्तरलक्षणवत् । तत्रानन्तरं प्रामाण्यप्रतिपादनं न युज्येत, ‘वृत्तं प्रमाणलक्षणम्ऽ; इति च । मन्त्रार्थवादेषु च कार्यार्थत्वेन विप्रतिपत्तिर्न स्यात् । सा चोपरिष्टादेव निरसिष्यते बहु चात्र वक्तव्यमित्यलं प्रसङ्गेन । यथान्यमानव्यतिभेदमुक्ता मतिः प्रमाणत्वमुपैति कार्ये । अपौरुषेयागमलब्धजन्मा तथैव सिद्धे निरपेक्षभावात्

yadapi matam --- ‘sa kratuṃ kurvīta'prajñāṃ kurvīta'; ‘nididhyāsitavyaḥ'; iti, yatrāpi svarūpaniṣṭhataiva lakṣyate ‘tattvamasi'; iti tatrāpi ‘sadasmi --- iti ceto dhārayet'iti vivakṣitatvācchravaṇādanyadanucintanaṃ dhyānaṃ pratyayapravāho vidhīyate karmavadevāmṛtatvaphalam / [kks_154] tadapyata eva na yujyate, pūrvoktāttattvāvagatipramāṇābhāvaprasaṅgādanyaniṣṭhatvādvākyasya / atha tu vākyāntarāttattvaniṣṭhādadhigate tadviṣayapratyayapravāhavidhānamiṣyate / bhavatu / na kaściddoṣaḥ / tathā ca ‘vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta'ityātmatattvavijñānasya siddhatāṃ darśayati / tadapi vā vyarthameva, prāptārthatvāt / sākṣātkaraṇaphalaṃ hi tattadanucintanaṃ dṛṣṭārtham, na tato 'nyatphalamākāṅkṣyate / amṛtatvaṃ hi na svarūpāvirbhāvādanyaditi prāgvarṇitam / dṛṣṭā ca jñānābhyāsasya samyagjñānaprasādahetutā loke / bhāvanāviśeṣāddhi abhūtamapyanubhavamāpadyate, kiṃ punarbhūtam / ‘sa kratuṃ kurvīta'; iti tu na sakalaviśeṣātigātmatattvānucintanaṃ vidhīyate tadbhāvaphalam, api tu nāmarūpopādhimanomayaprāṇaśarīrādirūpānudhyānamaiśvaryaphalam, krameṇa vā sākṣātkaraṇaphalam / ‘tameva dhīro vijñāya'; iti na prajñākaraṇavidhiḥ / ‘tameva'ityanyanivṛtteḥ śrutattvānnivṛttau tātparyaṃ gamyate, ‘raktaḥ paṭo bhavati'iti tayā raktaparatvaṃ vākyasya / atra ākāśāditattvabhedapūrvamavibhāgaḥ pratipāditaḥ, tatra tathaiva prajñākaraṇaprasaṅge ‘tameva'; iti vidhīyate / tathā ca pūrvārdhe --- ‘virajaḥ para ākāśādaja ātmā mahān dhruvaḥ'; / ityākāśādibhyaḥ paratvenātmatattvaṃ darśitam / tasya tathaiva prajñākaraṇaprasaṅge tannivṛttaye ‘tameva'; ityucyate / anyathā na evaśabdasya phalam, na ca nivartyaṃ vijñāyeta / tathā ca tadevottareṇa prapañcyate ‘nānudhyāyādbahūñchabdān'; ityekavākyatā / anyathā vākyaṃ bhidyeta / śabdamātre cānudhyānāprasaṅgāt śabdapūrvattvāttasya śabdārthaviṣayamevedamiti / evam ‘ātmetyevopāsīta'ityevakāraśrutestadarthavidhiḥ / ‘nididhyāsitavyaḥ'; ityapi ‘ātmanastu kāmāya'; ityupakramāt ‘idaṃ sarvaṃ [kks_155] yadayamātmā'ityupasaṃhārādātmasvarūpaparamekaṃ vākyam / tadantargatāḥ ‘draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ'; iti na pṛthagvidhayaḥ kṛtyapratyayayoge 'pi / kṛtyapratyayasyārthāntare 'pi smaraṇādarhādau stutyarthāḥ yathopāṃśuyājavākyāntargatāḥ ‘viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ'ityevamādayaḥ / ‘aitadātmyamidaṃ sarvaṃ tatsatyaṃ sa ātmā tattvamasi'iti bhūta eva paryavasitaṃ vākyam / tatra ‘sadasmi --- iti dhārayet'; iti kalpaneyam / tasmāttrividhasyāpi jñānasya vidheyatvāyogāt, vinā ca vidhervākyārthapratipatteḥ, apauruṣeyatvena nirapekṣatvādbhūte 'pyarthe vedāntānāṃ prāmāṇyasiddhiḥ / tathā ca ‘tattu samanvayāt'iti codanālakṣaṇāddharmāttuśabdena viśeṣyaṃ brahma samanvayagamyamuktam / samanvayo hi padārthānāṃ saṃsargo viniyogastato brahma gamyate, na codanāta ityarthaḥ /

nanvaviśeṣeṇa kārye 'rthe vedasya prāmāṇyaṃ varṇitam --- ‘codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ'; iti / codanālakṣaṇo vedārtha ityarthaḥ / naitatsāram / evaṃ hi siddhaprāmāṇyavedārthavicāro 'yaṃ syāttaduttaralakṣaṇavat / tatrānantaraṃ prāmāṇyapratipādanaṃ na yujyeta, ‘vṛttaṃ pramāṇalakṣaṇam'; iti ca / mantrārthavādeṣu ca kāryārthatvena vipratipattirna syāt / sā copariṣṭādeva nirasiṣyate bahu cātra vaktavyamityalaṃ prasaṅgena /

yathānyamānavyatibhedamuktā matiḥ pramāṇatvamupaiti kārye /
apauruṣeyāgamalabdhajanmā tathaiva siddhe nirapekṣabhāvāt
units.translation:
Someone may argue that scripture says, “One should form an intention,” “One should cultivate understanding,” and “One should meditate.” Even where a sentence like “You are that” appears to teach rest in one’s own nature, it might intend the injunction, “One should hold the mind with the thought, ‘I am Being.’” After hearing the words, one is then enjoined to continue a stream of thought about their meaning, just as one performs a ritual action, with immortality as the result. That is not appropriate: because the sentence is directed toward something else, it would no longer provide evidence for knowing reality, as was explained earlier. If knowledge of reality is instead understood from another sentence that teaches rest in one’s own nature, then let meditation on the object of that knowledge be prescribed. There is no fault in that. A statement such as “Having known, one should cultivate understanding” itself shows that knowledge of the Self is already established. Yet even this prescription is unnecessary, because meditation has the visible result of direct realization; no further result is sought from it. Immortality, as has been explained, is nothing other than the manifestation of one’s own nature. It is also seen in ordinary life that repeated practice of knowledge helps correct understanding become clear: through a particular intensity of imagining, even something unreal can come to be experienced, so how much more so something real.

The statement “One should form an intention” does not prescribe meditation on the Self, which transcends every distinction. Rather, it prescribes meditation on name and form, on the mind-made Self, on the Self whose body is the breath, and the like, for the result of sovereignty, or for direct realization attained gradually. “The wise one should know that alone” is not an injunction to produce knowledge. The word “that alone” excludes other things, showing that the emphasis is on withdrawing from them, just as “the cloth is red” emphasizes the redness of the cloth.

Here, the text first describes the differences among the elements beginning with space, and then teaches their non-difference. In that context, where one might otherwise understand “one should cultivate knowledge,” it says “that alone,” prescribing the exclusion of those other things. Earlier it says, “The Self is unborn, great, and stable, beyond space and the other elements.” In the context of cultivating knowledge of it, it says “that alone” to turn the mind away from those other things. Otherwise the word “alone” would have no function, and nothing would be excluded. The following statement, “One should not meditate on many words,” continues the same sentence and makes its unity clear. Otherwise the sentence would be divided. And since meditation cannot concern mere sounds alone, it must concern their meaning, which is expressed through words.

In the same way, “One should meditate on the Self alone” prescribes that meaning, as shown by the word “alone.” The sentence “One should see, hear, reflect upon, and meditate upon the Self” is also a single sentence, since it begins with “for the sake of the Self alone” and concludes, “All this is the Self.” The verbal forms “to be seen,” “to be heard,” and “to be meditated upon” do not each create separate injunctions, even though they have the grammatical form of things to be done. Such forms are also used for praise in other contexts, as in statements within a sentence about the Upāṃśu sacrifice: “Viṣṇu is to be worshipped in the Upāṃśu,” and similar phrases. The sentence, “All this has that as its Self; that is the truth; that is the Self; you are that,” states a fact. The interpretation “One should hold the mind with the thought, ‘I am Being’” is only imagined.

Thus knowledge of all three kinds cannot be the object of an injunction. A sentence can be understood without an injunction, and, because the Veda has no human author and is independent, its authority is established even concerning facts that already exist. This is why the Brahma Sūtra says, “But Brahman is established through the connected purport.” The word “but” distinguishes Brahman, whose purport is established through the connection of the texts, from dharma, which is characterized by an injunction. The connection of words is a relation among meanings; Brahman is understood through that connection, not from an injunction.

Someone may object that the authority of the Veda was described without distinction as applying to things to be done: “Dharma is that which is characterized by an injunction,” meaning that the meaning of the Veda is what is characterized by an injunction. That is not sound. If so, this would be an inquiry into the meaning of a Veda whose authority had already been established, just as a later definition presupposes an earlier one. Then a subsequent discussion to establish its authority would make no sense, nor would the statement, “The function of a means of knowledge is its definition.” There would also be no disagreement about whether mantras and explanatory passages refer to actions. That disagreement is refuted later. There is much more to say on this, but enough of this digression.

“As cognition becomes authoritative concerning what is to be done
when distinguished from other means of knowledge,
so too does cognition born of the authorless scripture
become authoritative concerning what is established, through its independence.”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 1
units.deva:
॥ इति नियोगकाण्डस् तृतीयः ॥ [क्क्स्_156] ॥ चतुर्थः (सिद्धि)काण्डः ॥ एवं तावत्प्रतिपत्तिकर्तव्यताप्रामाण्यव्याजेन यैरप्रामाण्यमुक्तं तत्प्रतिबोधनाय कृतः प्रयत्नः; इदानीं त्वप्रामाण्यमेवाहुर्ये तद्बोधनाय प्रयत्यते । तत्र पूर्वपक्षः ---

नन्वन्वितपदार्थत्वाद्वाक्यार्थस्य पदार्थताम् । अप्राप्य न स्याद्वाक्यार्थः पदार्थत्वे ऽन्यमानकः
units.translation:
Thus far, effort has been made to answer those who call scripture invalid, while appearing to accept it as valid when it prescribes acts of understanding. Now the author turns to those who simply declare it invalid.

The opponent’s position is:

“Since a sentence’s meaning is a connected set of word-meanings, it cannot be the meaning of words; when the sentence meaning is not established by another means of knowledge, it cannot be reached through the words.”

gloss.en: under the pretext of validity depending on an act of understanding
because it consists of connected word-meanings
not established by another means of knowledge

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 2
units.deva:
न तावद्ब्रह्मान्तर्याम्यादिपदं प्रमाणम्, संबन्धज्ञानापेक्षया पूर्वसिद्धे प्रत्ययहेतुत्वेन । नापि वाक्यम्; न हि तत्साक्षाद्वाचकम्; पदार्थद्वारा तु तत् प्रतिपत्तिः; अपदार्थे ज्ञानस्याभावात् । ते हि संसर्गाद्गुणप्रधानभावेनेतरपदार्थविशिष्टमेकं पदार्थं गमयन्ति । तत्र पदार्थ एव विशिष्टो वाक्यार्थो भवति । न चानधिगतेषु प्रमाणान्तरेण पदार्थत्वम्; सम्बन्धज्ञानापेक्षणात् इत्युक्तम् । तत्रापदार्थत्वे न वाक्यविषयत्वम्; अनवबोधकं तेषां वाक्यम् । पदार्थत्वे प्रमाणान्तराधिगतेरनुवादकम् । तत्रात्यन्तापरिदृष्टब्रह्माद्यर्थप्रमाणाभिमतेषु वाक्येषु तद्वाचीनि पदानि स्युः, न वा । यदि न सन्ति न त इतरैः संसृज्येरन् न भिद्येरन्निति न तेषां प्रमेयाः लोष्टादिवत् । अथ तु सन्ति, तथापि तैरधिगतसंबन्धैर्न प्रतिपाद्येरन् अप्रतिपन्नाश्च न विशिष्टवाक्यार्थप्रतिपत्तिहेतवः; तत्र यथा ऽवनात्पिक आनीयतम्ऽ; इति पिकपदार्थज्ञाने ऽवबोधकत्वं तथा तेषामपि । तस्मान्न चोदनातो ऽपूर्वपदार्थावगमः; सा हि विधिप्रतिषेधाभ्यां क्रियासु पुरुषमधिकरोति; त्रैविध्यवृद्धपरिग्रहस्तु जपोपयोगात्, उपनिषदो वेदान्ताः; --- इति तत्र विनियोगात् । तत्रोच्यते ---

सामान्येन पदार्थत्वे सिद्धे ऽसाधारणैर्गुणैः । शक्यापूर्वविशेषस्य लोकवत् प्रतिपादना
units.iast:
na tāvadbrahmāntaryāmyādipadaṃ pramāṇam, saṃbandhajñānāpekṣayā pūrvasiddhe pratyayahetutvena / nāpi vākyam; na hi tatsākṣādvācakam; padārthadvārā tu tat pratipattiḥ; apadārthe jñānasyābhāvāt / te hi saṃsargādguṇapradhānabhāvenetarapadārthaviśiṣṭamekaṃ padārthaṃ gamayanti / tatra padārtha eva viśiṣṭo vākyārtho bhavati / na cānadhigateṣu pramāṇāntareṇa padārthatvam; sambandhajñānāpekṣaṇāt ityuktam / tatrāpadārthatve na vākyaviṣayatvam; anavabodhakaṃ teṣāṃ vākyam / padārthatve pramāṇāntarādhigateranuvādakam / tatrātyantāparidṛṣṭabrahmādyarthapramāṇābhimateṣu vākyeṣu tadvācīni padāni syuḥ, na vā / yadi na santi na ta itaraiḥ saṃsṛjyeran na bhidyeranniti na teṣāṃ prameyāḥ loṣṭādivat / atha tu santi, tathāpi tairadhigatasaṃbandhairna pratipādyeran apratipannāśca na viśiṣṭavākyārthapratipattihetavaḥ; tatra yathā 'vanātpika ānīyatam'; iti pikapadārthajñāne 'vabodhakatvaṃ tathā teṣāmapi / tasmānna codanāto 'pūrvapadārthāvagamaḥ; sā hi vidhipratiṣedhābhyāṃ kriyāsu puruṣamadhikaroti; traividhyavṛddhaparigrahastu japopayogāt, upaniṣado vedāntāḥ; --- iti tatra viniyogāt /

tatrocyate ---

sāmānyena padārthatve siddhe 'sādhāraṇairguṇaiḥ /
śakyāpūrvaviśeṣasya lokavat pratipādanā
units.translation:
The words “Brahman,” “the inner controller,” and the like are not, by themselves, a means of knowledge, because their power to produce cognition depends on knowing the relation between word and meaning beforehand. Nor is a sentence such a means: it does not directly express its meaning. Understanding it proceeds through the meanings of its words, since there is no cognition of what is not conveyed by words. Through their relations and their relative prominence, the words convey one object qualified by the meanings of the other words. That qualified object is the meaning of the sentence.

But an object whose meaning has not been established by another means of knowledge cannot already be a known word-meaning; it has been explained that knowing the word–meaning relation is required. If it has no word-meaning, the sentence does not concern it and cannot make it known. If it does have a word-meaning, then the sentence merely repeats what another means of knowledge has established. Thus, in sentences believed to be means of knowledge about Brahman and other objects that have never been perceived, either there must be words that denote those objects or there must not. If there are no such words, they cannot be joined or distinguished from the other words, and therefore are not objects of knowledge at all, like clods and the like. If such words do exist, even a person who knows their conventional meaning cannot have them convey what has not been understood; without that understanding, they cannot produce comprehension of the qualified meaning of a sentence. They would have no more power to make something known than the word “cuckoo” has for a person who does not know what it means in the instruction “Bring the cuckoo from the forest.”

Therefore an injunction does not establish the meaning of a previously unknown word. It assigns a person to actions through prescriptions and prohibitions. The threefold interpretation adopted by the elders is applied there because it is useful in recitation: “The Upaniṣads are the concluding portions of the Veda,” and the like. The reply is:

“Once something is established in general as the meaning of a word, its distinctive properties can convey a novel particular, just as in ordinary usage.”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 3
units.deva: [क्क्स्_157] यथा लोके ‘द्वीपविशेषे एवंनामानो मरतकमयपादाः पद्मरागमयचञ्चवः सौवर्णराजतपक्षाः पक्षिणःऽइति पक्षिसामान्यं प्रमाणान्तरधिगतमनन्यसाधारणेन धर्मकलापेन संसृज्यमानं प्रमाणान्तरानधिगतं विशेषरूपमासादयति, वाक्येन च प्रमीयते प्रमाणान्तरानधिगतेन विशेषरूपेण --- सर्वस्यैव हि वाक्यस्यानधिगतो विशेष एव प्रमेयः तथा कारणसामान्यं वा सत्सामान्यं वा ‘यतो वा इमानि भूतानि जायन्तेऽ; इति ‘अस्थूलमनण्वह्रस्वम्ऽइत्यादिपदार्थैः संसर्गाद्भेदाच्च प्रमाणान्तरानधिगतं विशेषरूपमासादयति, वाक्यस्य च प्रमेयं भवति । तदेवं लोकसिद्धपदार्थान्वयेनैवापूर्वार्थप्रतिपत्तेर्नानवबोधकत्वमनुवादकत्वं वा । सर्वप्रत्ययवेद्ये वा ब्रह्मरूपे व्यवस्थिते । प्रपञ्चस्य प्रविलयः शब्देन प्रतिपाद्यते
units.iast:
[kks_157] yathā loke ‘dvīpaviśeṣe evaṃnāmāno maratakamayapādāḥ padmarāgamayacañcavaḥ sauvarṇarājatapakṣāḥ pakṣiṇaḥ'iti pakṣisāmānyaṃ pramāṇāntaradhigatamananyasādhāraṇena dharmakalāpena saṃsṛjyamānaṃ pramāṇāntarānadhigataṃ viśeṣarūpamāsādayati, vākyena ca pramīyate pramāṇāntarānadhigatena viśeṣarūpeṇa --- sarvasyaiva hi vākyasyānadhigato viśeṣa eva prameyaḥ tathā kāraṇasāmānyaṃ vā satsāmānyaṃ vā ‘yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante'; iti ‘asthūlamanaṇvahrasvam'ityādipadārthaiḥ saṃsargādbhedācca pramāṇāntarānadhigataṃ viśeṣarūpamāsādayati, vākyasya ca prameyaṃ bhavati / tadevaṃ lokasiddhapadārthānvayenaivāpūrvārthapratipatternānavabodhakatvamanuvādakatvaṃ vā /

sarvapratyayavedye vā brahmarūpe vyavasthite /
prapañcasya pravilayaḥ śabdena pratipādyate
units.translation:
In ordinary speech one might say: “On a certain island are birds of this name, with emerald feet, ruby beaks, and wings of gold and silver.” The general notion “bird” is already known by another means of knowledge; when it is combined with a set of distinctive properties not known by any other means, it acquires a particular form not previously known. This particular form is understood through the sentence even though no other means of knowledge establishes it. Indeed, the object of every sentence is precisely the distinctive particular that has not already been known.

Likewise, from terms such as “the source from which all these beings arise” and “not gross, not minute, not short,” a general notion such as “cause” or “existence” combines through relation and distinction to acquire a particular form not known by another means; that particular becomes the object of the sentence. Thus, by connecting words with meanings already established in ordinary usage, one understands a novel meaning; the sentence is neither unintelligible nor merely repetitive. Or, once the nature of Brahman, which is known through all cognition, has been established, scripture teaches the dissolution of the manifold world.

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 4
units.deva: प्रविलीनप्रपञ्चेन तद्रूपेण न गोचरः । मानान्तरस्येति मतमाम्नायैकनिबन्धनम्
units.iast:
pravilīnaprapañcena tadrūpeṇa na gocaraḥ /
mānāntarasyeti matamāmnāyaikanibandhanam
units.translation: In that form, with the manifold world dissolved, it is not within the scope of another means of knowledge. Therefore it is held to depend solely on scripture.

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 5
units.deva:
अथवा न लोके ऽत्यन्तमप्रसिद्धं ब्रह्म, सर्वप्रत्ययवेद्यत्वात्, ब्रह्मणो व्यतिरेकेण प्रत्येतव्यस्याभावात्, विशेषप्रत्ययानां च सामान्यरूपानुगमात्, भेदोपसंहारावशिष्टं च सत्यं ब्रह्म --- इति प्रतिपादनात्, ‘वाचारम्भणं विकारो नामधेयं मृत्तिकेत्येव सत्यम्ऽ; इति दृष्टान्तात् । किं तर्हि शब्देन प्रतिपाद्यते? प्रपञ्चाभावः । तत्र प्रपञ्चपदार्थो ऽपि सिद्धः, निषेधो ऽपि सिद्धः, तयोः संसर्गात्तदभावप्रतिपत्तिः । आम्नायैकनिबन्धनत्वं तु तस्योच्यते, प्रत्यक्षादीनामविद्यासंभिन्नत्वात्; प्रत्यस्तमितनिखिलभेदेन रूपेणाविषयीकरणाद्भेदप्रत्यस्तमयस्याम्नायावगम्यत्वादिति । परः पुनः प्रत्यवतिष्ठते ---
ननु चापुरुषार्थत्वं भूतनिष्ठे प्रसज्यते । यत् खलु वाक्यं न पुरुषं क्वचिद्धितसाधने प्रवर्तयति अहितसाधनाच्च [क्क्स्_158] निवर्तयति, केवलं सिद्धमर्थमन्वाचष्टे, तदपुरुषार्थम्; अपुरुषार्थत्वाच्चोन्मत्तप्रलापवदप्रमाणम्; तथा च प्रायेण वेदान्ताः । उच्यते ---
प्रमाणस्य न चैतावत्पुरुषार्थैकनिष्ठता
units.iast:
athavā na loke 'tyantamaprasiddhaṃ brahma, sarvapratyayavedyatvāt, brahmaṇo vyatirekeṇa pratyetavyasyābhāvāt, viśeṣapratyayānāṃ ca sāmānyarūpānugamāt, bhedopasaṃhārāvaśiṣṭaṃ ca satyaṃ brahma --- iti pratipādanāt, ‘vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ mṛttiketyeva satyam'; iti dṛṣṭāntāt / kiṃ tarhi śabdena pratipādyate? prapañcābhāvaḥ / tatra prapañcapadārtho 'pi siddhaḥ, niṣedho 'pi siddhaḥ, tayoḥ saṃsargāttadabhāvapratipattiḥ / āmnāyaikanibandhanatvaṃ tu tasyocyate, pratyakṣādīnāmavidyāsaṃbhinnatvāt; pratyastamitanikhilabhedena rūpeṇāviṣayīkaraṇādbhedapratyastamayasyāmnāyāvagamyatvāditi /

paraḥ punaḥ pratyavatiṣṭhate ---
nanu cāpuruṣārthatvaṃ bhūtaniṣṭhe prasajyate /
yat khalu vākyaṃ na puruṣaṃ kvaciddhitasādhane pravartayati ahitasādhanācca [kks_158] nivartayati, kevalaṃ siddhamarthamanvācaṣṭe, tadapuruṣārtham; apuruṣārthatvācconmattapralāpavadapramāṇam; tathā ca prāyeṇa vedāntāḥ / ucyate ---
pramāṇasya na caitāvatpuruṣārthaikaniṣṭhatā
units.translation:
Or perhaps Brahman is not utterly unknown in ordinary experience, since it is known through every cognition. There is nothing to be known apart from Brahman, and the particular cognitions all participate in a general form. It has been shown that Brahman, remaining when all distinctions are gathered away, is the real. This is illustrated by the statement: “A modification is only a name arising from speech; the clay alone is real.” What, then, is scripture teaching? The absence of the manifold world. The meanings “manifold world” and “negation” are each already established; from their relation one understands the world’s absence. It is said that this understanding rests solely on scripture because perception and the other means of knowledge are mixed with ignorance, while the disappearance of all distinctions—where the world is no longer an object—is known through scripture alone.

The opponent replies:

If the Veda speaks about what already exists, then it would have no purpose for human beings. A sentence that neither prompts a person to pursue a means to their welfare nor turns them away from a source of harm, but merely reports an established fact, serves no human purpose. Since it has no human purpose, it is not a valid means of knowledge, like the ravings of a madman. Most of the Upaniṣads would then be like that.

We reply:

“A means of knowledge is not exclusively directed toward a human purpose…”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 6
units.deva:
(उपेक्षामपि हि फलं प्रमाणस्य प्रचक्षते) । (अनेन श्लोकार्धेनात्र भवितव्यमित्यभ्यूहः; परं तु मातृकासु न दृश्यते । --- एदितोर्)
अपि चाज्ञानतः शोकी दुःखी जीवः प्रकाशते
units.iast:
(upekṣāmapi hi phalaṃ pramāṇasya pracakṣate) / (anena ślokārdhenātra bhavitavyamityabhyūhaḥ; paraṃ tu mātṛkāsu na dṛśyate / --- editor)
api cājñānataḥ śokī duḥkhī jīvaḥ prakāśate
units.translation:
(For some also state that disregard is a result of a means of knowledge. The editor conjectures that this half-verse should occur here, but it is not found in the manuscripts.)

Moreover, the embodied self, ignorant and sorrowful, appears as one who suffers.

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 7
units.deva: तन्निवृत्तिश्च विज्ञानं पुरुषार्थः स्वयं मतम् । कस्मिंश्चिदर्थे विज्ञाते कुतूहलवतां नृणाम्
units.iast:
tannivṛttiśca vijñānaṃ puruṣārthaḥ svayaṃ matam /
kasmiṃścidarthe vijñāte kutūhalavatāṃ nṛṇām
units.translation: The cessation of that [ignorance] is cognition, which is itself held to be a human good. When people are curious about something and come to know it…

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 8
units.deva: आकुलानां ज्ञानजन्म पुरुषार्थत्वसंमतम् । अक्षादौ च यथारूपनिष्ठे नापुरुषार्थता
units.iast:
ākulānāṃ jñānajanma puruṣārthatvasaṃmatam /
akṣādau ca yathārūpaniṣṭhe nāpuruṣārthatā
units.translation: Knowledge that arises for those who are perplexed is accepted as a human good. Cognition centered on the senses and the like is not without purpose.

gloss.en: is accepted as a human good
in the senses and the like

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 9
units.deva: न च प्रवृत्तिनिष्ठत्वं तथास्मिन् केन वार्यते । ज्ञेयस्य पुरुषार्थत्वं तत्र चेदत्र तत्समम्
units.iast:
na ca pravṛttiniṣṭhatvaṃ tathāsmin kena vāryate /
jñeyasya puruṣārthatvaṃ tatra cedatra tatsamam
units.translation: And what prevents this sentence from being directed toward action as well? If what is to be known is a human good there, the same applies here.

gloss.en: of what is to be known

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 10
units.deva: पुरुषार्थः स्वयं ब्रह्म प्रशान्तं विजरादिकम् । अतस्तत्त्वमसीत्येवमनुशिष्याय शिष्यते
units.iast:
puruṣārthaḥ svayaṃ brahma praśāntaṃ vijarādikam /
atastattvamasītyevamanuśiṣyāya śiṣyate
units.translation: Brahman itself is the human good: utterly peaceful, ageless, and so forth. Therefore the teacher instructs the student only with “You are that.”

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 11
units.deva: परप्रवृत्तेरङ्गत्वं प्रत्यक्षादेर्मतं यदि । अत्रापि साक्षात्करणप्रवृत्तावङ्गतेष्यताम्
units.iast:
parapravṛtteraṅgatvaṃ pratyakṣādermataṃ yadi /
atrāpi sākṣātkaraṇapravṛttāvaṅgateṣyatām
units.translation: If perception and the other means of knowledge are held to be components of another person’s action, then here too they should be accepted as components of the activity that leads to direct realization.

gloss.en: of perception and the other means
in the activity leading to direct realization

units.sectionTitle: Kāṇḍa 4 · Siddhi — scriptural knowledge and the attainment of liberation
units.label: Kāṇḍa 4 · 12
units.deva:
न तावन्नियोगतः प्रमाणस्य पुरुषार्थफलता । न खलु हितोपादानाहितहाने एव प्रमाणफले; उपेक्षामपि हि प्रमाणफलं प्रमाणविद आचक्षते । न च पुरुषार्थता प्रमाणलक्षणम्, प्रमाहेतुत्वं तु । तस्मान्न पुरुषार्थाभावेनाप्रामाण्यम् । अपि च ‘शोक्यहम्ऽदुःख्यहम्ऽ; ऽधनादीनि मम नष्टानिऽइति विशुद्धब्रह्मात्मनो जीवस्य मिथ्याज्ञानम्; एतन्निवृत्तिरूपं च विशुद्धानन्दप्रकाशब्रह्मात्मतत्वज्ञानम् । तत् स्वरूपेणैव पुरुषार्थः; अनिष्टनिवृत्तिरूपत्वादिष्टाविर्भावाच्च । यद्यपि च संस्कारात्तस्यानुवृत्तिस्तथापि शाब्दज्ञानमनुसंतन्वतो विदुषो न पूर्ववद्भवति निवर्तते चात्यन्ताय । दृष्टा च ज्ञानोत्पत्तेरेव पुरुषार्थता क्वचित् कुतूहलाकुलितानामज्ञातेऽर्थे । न हि [क्क्स्_159] तज्ज्ञानात् परमन्यदर्थ्यते । न च प्रवृत्तिनिवृत्तिविषयस्यैव पुरुषार्थतेति नियमः; प्रत्यक्षादीनि हि प्रमाणानि; न च तावत्प्रवृत्तिनिवृत्तिपराणि सिद्धवस्तुविषयाणि; न च पुरुषार्थतां जहति । यदि मतम् --- प्रत्यक्षादिज्ञेयं हि सिद्धं वस्तु पुरुषार्थः सलिलादिः, तदुपकारात्; ततः प्रत्यक्षादीनां पुरुषार्थता भूतनिष्ठानामपि । अत्रापि च शब्दप्रमेयं स्वयमेव ब्रह्म पुरुषार्थो जरादिविविधाशिवोपशमात् परमानन्दप्रकाशत्वाच्च सुप्रसन्नम् । अत एव ऽतत्त्वमसिऽइति श्वेतकेतुमुखेनाशासनीयाय पुरुषाय श्रुत्याभिन्नमुपदिश्यते; अभिन्नं हि तदनुशासनीयात् । भेदेन च प्रतीयमानं न पुरुषार्थः । तत्त्वे तादात्म्यज्ञाने च तथाभावात् विश्वाशिवोपशमात् परमशिवभावाच्च परिपूर्णः पुरुषार्थो आप्तो भवति । यदि मतम् --- 
प्रत्यक्षादीन्यपि प्रवृत्यङ्गान्येव,
प्रमिते ऽर्थे हानोपादानादिलक्षणायाः प्रवृत्तेस्तन्मूलत्वात्;
ईदृशं प्रवृत्यङ्गत्वमत्राप्यस्त्येव, शब्दात् प्रमिते ब्रह्मणि साक्षात्करणाय प्रवृत्तेरिष्टत्वादिति ॥ एषा वेदान्ततत्त्वप्रविचयचतुरप्रस्फुरन्न्यायतेजा मार्गं मुक्तेर्निरुन्धन्निबिडमपि तमो ऽनादि निर्दारयन्ती । सद्यः प्रक्षालयन्ती घनमपि जगतां तीर्थदुस्तर्कपङ्कं व्याख्यातोत्खातविश्वा शिवनिरतिशयश्रेयसे ब्रह्मसिद्धिः

na tāvanniyogataḥ pramāṇasya puruṣārthaphalatā / na khalu hitopādānāhitahāne eva pramāṇaphale; upekṣāmapi hi pramāṇaphalaṃ pramāṇavida ācakṣate / na ca puruṣārthatā pramāṇalakṣaṇam, pramāhetutvaṃ tu / tasmānna puruṣārthābhāvenāprāmāṇyam / api ca ‘śokyaham'duḥkhyaham'; 'dhanādīni mama naṣṭāni'iti viśuddhabrahmātmano jīvasya mithyājñānam; etannivṛttirūpaṃ ca viśuddhānandaprakāśabrahmātmatatvajñānam / tat svarūpeṇaiva puruṣārthaḥ; aniṣṭanivṛttirūpatvādiṣṭāvirbhāvācca / yadyapi ca saṃskārāttasyānuvṛttistathāpi śābdajñānamanusaṃtanvato viduṣo na pūrvavadbhavati nivartate cātyantāya / dṛṣṭā ca jñānotpattereva puruṣārthatā kvacit kutūhalākulitānāmajñāte'rthe / na hi [kks_159] tajjñānāt paramanyadarthyate / na ca pravṛttinivṛttiviṣayasyaiva puruṣārthateti niyamaḥ; pratyakṣādīni hi pramāṇāni; na ca tāvatpravṛttinivṛttiparāṇi siddhavastuviṣayāṇi; na ca puruṣārthatāṃ jahati / yadi matam --- pratyakṣādijñeyaṃ hi siddhaṃ vastu puruṣārthaḥ salilādiḥ, tadupakārāt; tataḥ pratyakṣādīnāṃ puruṣārthatā bhūtaniṣṭhānāmapi / atrāpi ca śabdaprameyaṃ svayameva brahma puruṣārtho jarādivividhāśivopaśamāt paramānandaprakāśatvācca suprasannam / ata eva 'tattvamasi'iti śvetaketumukhenāśāsanīyāya puruṣāya śrutyābhinnamupadiśyate; abhinnaṃ hi tadanuśāsanīyāt / bhedena ca pratīyamānaṃ na puruṣārthaḥ / tattve tādātmyajñāne ca tathābhāvāt viśvāśivopaśamāt paramaśivabhāvācca paripūrṇaḥ puruṣārtho āpto bhavati / yadi matam --- 
pratyakṣādīnyapi pravṛtyaṅgānyeva,
pramite 'rthe hānopādānādilakṣaṇāyāḥ pravṛttestanmūlatvāt;
īdṛśaṃ pravṛtyaṅgatvamatrāpyastyeva, śabdāt pramite brahmaṇi sākṣātkaraṇāya pravṛtteriṣṭatvāditi //


eṣā vedāntatattvapravicayacaturaprasphurannyāyatejā mārgaṃ mukternirundhannibiḍamapi tamo 'nādi nirdārayantī / sadyaḥ prakṣālayantī ghanamapi jagatāṃ tīrthadustarkapaṅkaṃ vyākhyātotkhātaviśvā śivaniratiśayaśreyase brahmasiddhiḥ
units.translation:
The validity of a means of knowledge does not have to result in a human good through an injunction. Its results are not limited to accepting what is beneficial and rejecting what is harmful; those who understand the means of knowledge also count indifference as one of its results. Being directed toward a human goal is not the defining mark of a means of knowledge; its defining mark is that it causes true cognition. Therefore it is not invalid merely because it does not produce a human good.

Moreover, the notions “I am sorrowful,” “I am suffering,” and “my wealth and other things have been lost” are mistaken cognitions of the living Self, whose nature is the pure Brahman. Their removal is knowledge of the true nature of Brahman as the pure Self, shining with bliss. That knowledge itself is a human good, since it removes what is unwanted and makes what is desired manifest. Even if an impression of the old cognition continues for a time, it does not recur as before for a knower who sustains verbal knowledge of the truth; it is removed completely. The arising of knowledge itself is seen to be a human good in some cases, as when people are overwhelmed by curiosity about something unknown. Nothing further is sought beyond knowing it.

Nor is it a rule that only what concerns action or restraint can be a human good. Perception and the other means of knowledge concern established things; they are not directed toward action or restraint, yet they do not lose their status as means of knowledge or their connection with human purposes. Someone may say that objects known through perception, such as water, are human goods because they are useful, and thus perception is useful as the means to them. In this case too, Brahman itself, which is known through words, is the human good: it removes the many evils of age and the like and shines forth as supreme bliss. That is why scripture, through Śvetaketu, teaches identity with Brahman to the person who is to be instructed, with the words “You are that.” The Self is not different from the one being taught. What appears as difference is not a human good. Through knowledge of identity with the truth, one becomes complete in human purpose: the evils of the world subside and the highest good is attained.

Someone may object that perception and the other means of knowledge are also only auxiliaries to action, since after an object is known one acts to accept or reject it. The same relation to action exists here: after Brahman is understood through words, one undertakes direct realization, which is desired.

“This Brahmasiddhi, whose light of reasoning shines with skill in investigating the truth of Vedānta, tears apart dense, beginningless darkness and clears the path to liberation. It immediately washes away the thick mud of false reasoning that has clouded the world. Its truths have been explained and the universe brought to light, for the highest and unsurpassed good.”
